days.title: Understanding English Grammar and Sentence Anatomy
outcomes: Distinguish a word class from a grammatical function.
Segment a transparent word into a root and relevant affixes.
Identify a whole subject phrase, its head and a simple predicate.
Distinguish direct objects, predicative complements and adjuncts in taught examples.
Explain a meaning difference caused by changing subject and object.

days.title: Nouns and Noun Structures
outcomes: Form the taught regular, irregular and compound plurals.
Choose count-unit expressions for ordinary noncount nouns.
Explain a contextual countability change and a British collective-agreement choice.
Write singular, plural and double-genitive constructions accurately.
Analyse noun modifiers, apposition and a meaning-preserving nominalisation.

days.title: Articles, Determiners and Quantification
outcomes: Choose a/an by sound and distinguish indefinite form from specificity.
Explain identifiable and generic references using articles or zero article.
Apply conventional institutional and geographical article patterns with regional qualification.
Use distributive determiners and quantifiers with compatible noun senses.
Explain the meaning differences in some/any, few/a few and little/a little.

days.title: Pronouns, Reference and Agreement
outcomes: Choose taught personal, possessive and reflexive forms according to role and meaning.
Explain reciprocal, demonstrative, indefinite, interrogative and relative uses.
Track anaphoric, cataphoric and deictic reference without assuming prior noun mention is compulsory.
Use singular they and identify genuine reference ambiguity.
Distinguish referring and dummy subjects and explain ordinary local reflexive interpretation.

days.title: The English Verb System
outcomes: Identify principal forms, auxiliary uses and finite/non-finite status in taught patterns.
Construct ordinary questions and negatives with appropriate inversion or do-support.
Distinguish direct objects, indirect objects, predicative complements and selected locative complements.
Explain lexical valency restrictions rather than convert every verb mechanically.
Distinguish stative/dynamic senses and active ergative alternations from passive voice.

days.title: Present-Time Expressions and Aspect
outcomes: Form present simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive affirmatives, questions and negatives.
Explain a habit/state/activity/result contrast in context.
Identify the finite auxiliary and the participle forms in a perfect progressive.
Choose a construction from an intended temporal meaning rather than one signal word.
Edit a present-time paragraph using Days 1–6 concepts.

days.title: Past-Time Expressions and Narrative Grammar
outcomes: Form past simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive questions and negatives.
Distinguish foreground event, background and earlier situation.
Explain when simple past can replace past perfect after a sequencing connector.
Use used to, habitual would and be used to with their distinct meanings.
Write a coherent narrative with justified viewpoint changes.

days.title: Perfect, Progressive and Complex Aspectual Relationships
outcomes: Build and analyse perfect-progressive auxiliary sequences.
Explain completion, continuing activity and recent-result interpretations without absolute claims.
Choose for, since, by and until according to the intended relationship.
Distinguish ordinary stative readings from dynamic uses of the same verb.
Use already, yet, just, lately and recently with appropriate context and register.

days.title: Future Reference and Sequence of Tenses
outcomes: Choose and explain future expressions for plans, offers, schedules and predictions.
Form negatives and questions with will and be going to.
Build future progressive, perfect and perfect-progressive sequences.
Distinguish a time adjunct clause from an embedded question.
Report a future-from-past viewpoint while preserving dates and communicative force.

days.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
outcomes: Identify the finite verb and its agreement controller in long subjects.
Distinguish coordination, accompaniment and notional agreement.
Explain collective and indefinite-pronoun patterns with regional and register qualifications.
Analyse relative-clause, inverted and existential agreement.
Choose agreement for quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking nouns without absolute shortcuts.

days.title: Adjectives, Adverbs, Degree and Comparison
outcomes: Distinguish attributive, predicative and postpositive adjective uses.
Form and interpret comparisons without double marking or category mismatches.
Choose adjective/adverb forms according to the actual construction.
Explain how context and placement determine an adverb's scope.
Recognise sense-dependent gradability and legitimate variation.

days.title: Prepositions, Particles and Verb Patterns
outcomes: Interpret temporal, spatial and abstract preposition meanings.
Identify preposition heads and their complements.
Distinguish particles, prepositional verbs and phrasal-prepositional verbs.
Place personal-pronoun objects correctly with separable particle verbs.
Use cumulative review to identify a specific earlier distinction needing revision.

days.title: Phrases and Their Internal Structure
outcomes: Identify the five central phrase classes and their heads.
Distinguish determiners, modifiers and complements inside phrases.
Represent premodification, postmodification, coordination and embedding with clear brackets.
Apply substitution, movement and question-answer diagnostics cautiously.
Explain why phrase class and grammatical function are different descriptions.

days.title: Clauses and Sentence Architecture
outcomes: Identify main and subordinate clauses, including non-finite structures.
Distinguish clause form from communicative function.
Classify sentence architecture using the stated finite-clause convention.
Repair fragments, fused sentences and comma splices without changing logical relationships.
Represent clause boundaries and embedding with accessible bracketed parsing.

days.title: Relative, Nominal and Adverbial Clauses
outcomes: Distinguish defining relatives from supplementary relatives and explain their punctuation.
Choose and omit relative markers only where the construction licenses them.
Analyse content clauses, embedded questions and fused-relative expressions without confusing form and function.
Use finite and infinitival complements with the intended subject and meaning.
Express time, reason, result, purpose, concession, condition, comparison and manner through suitable subordinate structures.

days.title: Coordination, Conjunctions and Logical Relationships
outcomes: Identify the units coordinated in a sentence.
Choose a connector that expresses a stated logical relation.
Punctuate clauses with however and therefore.
Construct balanced correlative alternatives and diagnose agreement problems.

days.title: Modal Verbs and Modality
outcomes: Form modal questions and negatives without unnecessary do-support.
Distinguish permission, obligation, ability and inference in context.
Interpret modal-perfect constructions and their time reference.
Use hedging to limit a claim without disguising the evidence.

days.title: Conditionals, Hypothesis and Mood
outcomes: Distinguish open conditions from remote and counterfactual alternatives.
Construct common conditional patterns without treating them as exhaustive formulas.
Express wishes, preferences and regrets with appropriate time reference.
Use conditional inversion and mandative constructions with register awareness.
Explain how clause form, modal meaning and discourse context interact.

days.title: Active, Passive, Causative and Related Constructions
outcomes: Build be-passives with appropriate tense, aspect and modal auxiliaries.
Choose an agentless, reporting, get- or double-object passive in context.
Use have, get, make, let and help with their own complement patterns.
Distinguish an active intransitive change of state from a passive.
Explain lexical and discourse restrictions on meaning-preserving transformations.

days.title: Gerunds, Infinitives, Participles and Non-Finite Clauses
outcomes: Identify -ing, to-infinitival, bare-infinitival and past-participial forms in context.
Build active, passive and perfect non-finite verb phrases without confusing form with time.
Explain meaning changes after verbs such as remember, stop and try.
Revise purpose and participial clauses while preserving their intended subject.
Use basic control/raising diagnostics while recognising theory-dependent terminology.

days.title: Direct and Indirect Speech
outcomes: Distinguish direct quotation from indirect content reporting.
Construct embedded questions with suitable word order.
Choose a defensible backshift from the reporting context.
Preserve participants, time, place and modal force in a report.
Use say, tell, ask, suggest and advise with appropriate complements.

days.title: Modifiers, Parallelism and Grammatical Ambiguity
outcomes: Identify a modifier’s target and a non-finite clause’s understood subject.
Explain at least two readings of an ambiguous attachment.
Distinguish not all from none and place only for an intended focus.
Construct coordination compatible with its shared head.
Verify that a proposed revision preserves meaning.

days.title: Advanced English Sentence Structures
outcomes: Apply negative-adjunct and conditional inversion accurately.
Distinguish fronted subjects, objects and adjuncts.
Construct and interpret it-clefts and pseudo-clefts.
Recognise dummy it and existential there.
Use emphatic auxiliaries and recoverable ellipsis.
Choose marked or neutral order for a stated communicative purpose.

days.title: Punctuation, Capitalisation and Orthographic Conventions
outcomes: Repair genuine clause-boundary errors.
Distinguish defining from supplementary punctuation.
Use apostrophes without confusing possession and plurality.
Punctuate quotations and embedded questions by their structure.
Apply a stated spelling and capitalisation policy without rejecting legitimate variants.

days.title: Usage, Collocations and Frequently Confused Constructions
outcomes: Choose confusable words by sense and construction.
Use lexical complements without inventing absolute following-word rules.
Explain contextual countability and agreement.
Identify legitimate regional and register variation.
Write an evidence-based editing note that preserves intended meaning.

days.title: Grammar Beyond the Sentence
outcomes: Trace reference chains across several sentences.
Recover omitted grammatical material without creating fragments.
Explain purposeful changes of tense and voice.
Use transitions only for supported logical relations.
Revise compression and hedging without changing scope or certainty.

days.title: Grammar in Précis, Paraphrasing and Formal Expression
outcomes: Reduce an original passage while preserving its essential qualifications.
Identify meaning changes in paraphrases.
Combine attributed claims without inventing causation.
Translate meaning notes into idiomatic English.
Draft an explicit formal request with a deadline.

days.title: Advanced Error Analysis and Sentence Reconstruction
outcomes: Diagnose multiple independent grammatical faults.
Recognise suspicious but grammatical structures in context.
Use a meaning ledger for transformations.
Revise sentences and paragraphs without adding certainty or changing reference.
Explain corrections, exceptions and alternative solutions with evidence.

days.title: Comprehensive Grammar Examination
outcomes: Analyse grammatical categories and functions inside unfamiliar sentences.
Select defensible forms in explicit contexts and recognise genuine no-error cases.
Transform and edit while retaining tense, scope, participants and modality.
Produce connected formal writing with clear reference and qualified claims.
Use the concept-level report to choose a fresh revision activity.

days.title: Final Mastery Assessment and Continuing Development
outcomes: Apply grammar across the six diagnostic skill domains and explain the limits of numerical comparison.
Correct and transform unfamiliar sentences without altering essential meaning.
Produce a qualified formal report and a faithful concise précis.
Interpret first responses, exposure, retention and writing self-review separately.
Build a specific continuing revision plan and select appropriate permanent resources.

concepts.title: Grammar, meaning and units of structure
concepts.definition: Grammar describes the patterns by which words and larger units combine and change form. A grammatical analysis asks how an expression is built; interpretation asks what it means in a particular context. Neither question can be answered reliably by word order alone.

glossary.definition: A grammatical unit organised around a verb, with finite or non-finite structure.
glossary.example: The staff waited is finite; to wait outside is non-finite.

glossary.definition: The central element that determines a phrase’s category.
glossary.example: In the small office, office heads the noun phrase.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d01-m01 Grammar, meaning and units of structure H gv5-topic-d01-c01 gv5-topic-d01-c02 gv5-topic-d01-c04 Grammar describes the patterns by which words and larger units combine and change form. A grammatical analysis asks how an expression is built; interpretation asks what it means in a particular context. Neither question can be answered reliably by word order alone. Begin with a familiar message: The nurse opened the window. Its words work together to identify someone, an event and something affected. Reversing nurse and window changes who does what, even though most words remain unchanged. Grammar therefore carries meaning. Vocabulary also matters: The window congratulated the nurse follows a recognisable structural pattern but normally needs an imaginative context. Structural well-formedness and ordinary real-world plausibility are different judgements. When evaluating an unfamiliar sentence, identify which judgement you are making before calling it wrong. A phrase is a unit organised around a head, its central word; it can contain one word or several. In the unusually quiet room, room heads a noun phrase, quiet heads an adjective phrase and unusually is an adverb. A clause organises a situation around a verb, often with a subject and complements. The nurse opened the window is a finite clause. To open the window is a non-finite clause: its verb has no independent tense. This course introduces these terms now and analyses their internal structure in Days 13–15. A full written sentence normally contains a main clause and appropriate boundary punctuation. A subordinate clause can be part of that sentence: The nurse opened the window because the room was warm. Because introduces a reason but does not make the first event happen in the grammar itself; the writer asserts that causal relationship. Short answers, labels and conversational fragments can be meaningful without a full main clause. No entry on a sign and After lunch in reply to When? are useful expressions; formal paragraph writing normally requires fuller structures. Grammatical correctness, contextual acceptability and editorial style must be distinguished. A sentence may be grammatical but too informal for a report, or perfectly clear in conversation but unclear without its shared setting. Standard British and American forms can differ without one being a mistake. A descriptive account records established patterns; a prescriptive convention recommends choices for a stated purpose. In this course, British English supplies the editorial default, while alternatives are identified explicitly. An asterisk in a grammar book often marks an unacceptable intended reading; it does not prove every imaginable use impossible. main clause + because + subordinate clause The second clause supplies the writer’s reason for the first situation. The courier arrived. A main clause forms a complete neutral written statement. The courier arrived after the office closed. A subordinate time clause locates the arrival relative to the closure. To reach the archive before noon, Sara took an earlier bus. The opening non-finite clause states a purpose; Sara is understood as the person reaching the archive. The inspector questioned the driver. The driver questioned the inspector. Both are grammatical; exchanging subjects and objects changes the roles and meaning. Close the window is a grammatical imperative with an ordinarily unexpressed subject. Do not add you merely to satisfy a simplified statement that every sentence must display a subject. Because the lift had stopped. We used the stairs. Because the lift had stopped, we used the stairs. For a continuous formal statement, attach the reason clause to its main clause. The clerk opened the file the supervisor read it. The clerk opened the file, and the supervisor read it. Two main clauses need an appropriate boundary or grammatical link. clause A grammatical unit organised around a verb, with finite or non-finite structure. The staff waited is finite; to wait outside is non-finite. head The central element that determines a phrase’s category. In the small office, office heads the noun phrase. source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5 source-58353073c867f7 source-15b65ce5c1b751 source-445532eb0f5c35

concepts.title: Inside words: morphemes, roots, stems and word formation
concepts.definition: A morpheme is a smallest unit carrying lexical meaning or grammatical information. A root supplies the central lexical material; a stem is the form to which an inflection is attached. Inflection supplies grammatical forms, while derivation creates a new lexical item.

glossary.definition: A grammatical form change within a lexical item.
glossary.example: Worked is a past form of work.

glossary.definition: Formation of a new lexical item, often by an affix.
glossary.example: Careful is derived from care.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d01-m02 Inside words: morphemes, roots, stems and word formation A gv5-topic-d01-c03 gv5-topic-d01-c06 A morpheme is a smallest unit carrying lexical meaning or grammatical information. A root supplies the central lexical material; a stem is the form to which an inflection is attached. Inflection supplies grammatical forms, while derivation creates a new lexical item. Compare help, helpful and helpfulness. Help carries the central meaning; -ful helps form an adjective, and -ness helps form a noun. These added parts cannot normally stand alone as words, so they are bound morphemes. Help can stand alone, making it a free morpheme. Meaningful parts are not the same as syllables: helpfulness has three readily identifiable morphemes, but a long word need not contain a meaningful part for each syllable. Avoid splitting letters into pieces unless each piece has a defensible role in contemporary English. Inflection relates forms of one lexical item: file/files, walk/walked/walking and small/smaller. Derivation changes the vocabulary item: teach/teacher or happy/unhappy/happiness. Derivation can change word class, as happy to happiness does, but need not: happy and unhappy are both adjectives. In teachers, teach is the root, teacher is the stem receiving the plural ending and -s marks plural number. A base is the material to which an affix attaches at a particular step; it can already contain other affixes. These labels describe different analytical roles rather than competing spellings. A prefix precedes its base, as un- in unfair; a suffix follows it, as -ment in agreement. Compounding combines lexical bases: raincoat or classroom. Conversion uses an established form in a new class without an overt affix: a text and to text. Spelling does not supply a perfect guide to structure: compounds may be closed, hyphenated or written separately. Learn a new word together with its meaning, word class and usual pattern. A productive pattern permits new formations readily, but a familiar suffix cannot be added freely to every possible base. Roots and stems can be irregular or show changes of spelling and sound. The past went is an inflectional form of go even though it is not built by visibly adding -ed. Morphological analysis is therefore more than chopping off endings. Contemporary structure also differs from etymology, the historical origin of a word: learners need not reconstruct ancient roots before understanding a current English form. This introductory model intentionally avoids deciding every disputed boundary, such as the status of English possessive -’s; that construction receives a phrase-level account on Day 2. root + derivational suffix + inflectional suffix teach + -er + -s forms a plural noun meaning people who teach. The gardeners repaired the gate. garden + -er forms a person noun; plural -s gives gardeners. The unfair decision was withdrawn. un- derives unfair from fair without changing adjective class. Please email the revised schedule. Email is used as a verb here; its form does not require a new derivational ending. reviewed reviewer Reviewed is an inflected verb form; reviewer is a derived noun. The shared ending letters are not interchangeable. Some grammatical contrasts have no visible added suffix: sheep may be singular or plural. Interpret the word with its determiner, verb and context. The team has went home. The team has gone home. Perfect auxiliary has requires a past participle; went is the past-simple form. Her explanation was very clearlyness. Her explanation was very clear. Inventing a suffix does not create a standard adjective; clear is the needed predicative form here. inflection A grammatical form change within a lexical item. Worked is a past form of work. derivation Formation of a new lexical item, often by an affix. Careful is derived from care. source-a016595c7d84bc source-f97a2154fcf48e source-ebed13706aced2 source-c81befbecce753 source-5532e2d7078060

concepts.title: Word classes and the difference between category and function
concepts.definition: A word class is a grammatical category identified through a combination of form, distribution and possible combinations. A function is a role within a larger structure. Noun is a category; subject and modifier are functions. A word’s meaning alone does not establish its class.

glossary.definition: A category such as noun, verb or adjective.
glossary.example: In They plan carefully, plan is a verb.

glossary.definition: A role such as subject, object or modifier.
glossary.example: The noun phrase those plans functions as subject in Those plans changed.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d01-m03 Word classes and the difference between category and function A H gv5-topic-d01-c05 gv5-topic-d01-c07 A word class is a grammatical category identified through a combination of form, distribution and possible combinations. A function is a role within a larger structure. Noun is a category; subject and modifier are functions. A word’s meaning alone does not establish its class. Nouns commonly head expressions naming people, things or ideas: teacher, bridge, patience. Verbs organise actions, events or states: repair, happen, know. Adjectives commonly describe or classify nouns: a narrow bridge. Adverbs modify activities, qualities, other adverbs or wider statements: works carefully, unusually narrow, fortunately. These are major open classes: new members enter them readily. Many words have more than one class, so classify their use in a particular sentence. The spelling clean occurs as an adjective in a clean room and as a verb in clean the room. Other classes include determiners, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections. Determiners help specify a noun’s reference or quantity: the report, this report, some reports. Pronouns can head expressions such as she, someone or mine. Prepositions head relational expressions: under the table, after lunch. Conjunctions link units: paper and ink; because it rained. Interjections express reactions: Oh! These are relatively closed classes, although change is possible. Closed does not mean semantically empty: compare before lunch with after lunch, where one small word changes the time relationship. Use several clues together. Plural marking often identifies nouns; comparison often identifies gradable adjectives; auxiliary patterns identify verbs. Each clue has exceptions. News is singular, wooden normally lacks comparative wooden-er, and fast is an adverb in move fast despite lacking -ly. A noun can modify another noun: in a stone wall, stone remains a noun functioning as a premodifier. An adjective can follow a linking verb: the wall is old. Category and position therefore interact, but neither simply equals the other. Detailed patterns are developed in the dedicated noun, verb and adjective lessons. Grammars differ in some category boundaries. Traditional accounts often call my a possessive adjective; this course usually calls it a possessive determiner because it occupies a determiner position. Some modern accounts treat pronouns as a subclass of nouns or distinguish determinative as a word class from determiner as a function. Recognise the labels without assuming the analysis has changed the sentence’s meaning. The immediate goal is a defensible explanation supported by behaviour: name the category, then state its function in the expression. Do not turn every describing word into an adjective or every -ly word into an adverb. determiner + adjective + noun The adjective modifies the noun; the determiner specifies reference. noun + noun The first noun can function as a modifier without changing class. Those careful researchers checked the figures. Those is a determiner, careful an adjective and researchers the noun head. The college will finance the project. Finance is a lexical verb after modal will; the project is its object. The finance office remained open unusually late. Finance is a noun modifier, open is an adjective complement, and unusually modifies adverb late. a friendly guide She spoke quietly. Friendly is an adjective despite -ly; quietly is an adverb. Endings are clues, not decisive rules. One spelling can belong to different classes: They water the plants uses a verb, while The water is cold uses a noun. Explain the local pattern rather than assign one permanent label to the spelling. A stone wall: stone must be an adjective because it describes wall. Stone is a noun functioning as a modifier of wall. Category and modifying function must be distinguished. He answered calm. He answered calmly. In this intended manner description, the adverb calmly modifies answered; calm is the adjective form. word class A category such as noun, verb or adjective. In They plan carefully, plan is a verb. function A role such as subject, object or modifier. The noun phrase those plans functions as subject in Those plans changed. source-58353073c867f7 source-b7519a9fb89ab0 source-fb277fd6f4e9a7

concepts.title: Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns
concepts.definition: The subject is a grammatical element identified by structural behaviour, not simply the person doing an action. The predicate is what is predicated of that subject. Objects, predicative complements and adjuncts perform different roles within clause structure.

glossary.definition: An element normally selected by a transitive verb, typically a noun phrase.
glossary.example: The visitors read the notice.

glossary.definition: An added circumstance or comment rather than a selected complement.
glossary.example: Yesterday is a time adjunct in We met yesterday.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d01-m04 Subjects, predicates and the first sentence patterns H gv5-topic-d01-c08 gv5-topic-d01-c09 The subject is a grammatical element identified by structural behaviour, not simply the person doing an action. The predicate is what is predicated of that subject. Objects, predicative complements and adjuncts perform different roles within clause structure. Start with The librarian opened the parcel. The librarian is the subject; opened the parcel is the predicate. Opened is the verb and the parcel is the direct object. In a neutral declarative clause, English usually places these in subject–verb–object order, abbreviated SVO. Identify the whole subject phrase before naming its head: in The new librarian opened the parcel, the new librarian is the subject and librarian is its head. Keeping those two answers separate prevents a common analysis mistake. The predicate can be short or extended with additional information. Not every clause has an object. The visitors waited follows subject–verb, or SV. The room became quiet contains a linking verb and a subject complement: quiet describes the room rather than a separate affected object. A complement can be a noun phrase: Leena is a doctor. In The coach gave the players advice, the players is an indirect object and advice is the direct object. In They considered the advice useful, useful is an object complement, describing the advice. Learn these contrasts as meaningful patterns rather than force all sentences into SVO. Adjuncts add circumstances or comments: The visitors waited outside yesterday. Outside gives place and yesterday gives time. A complement is selected by a head’s pattern; an adjunct supplies a less tightly selected addition. With put, a location normally completes the pattern: Put the parcel on the desk. Deletion is a helpful clue, not an infallible test, since some selected complements can be left understood. A passive subject can be affected rather than an agent: The parcel was opened by the librarian. Subject is therefore a syntactic function, while agent and patient describe semantic roles. The course uses verb narrowly for the verbal element and predicate broadly for everything predicated of the subject. In broader syntactic terminology, objects are also complements because the verb selects them; when distinguishing clause patterns, subject complement and object complement mean predicative descriptions. State which sense of complement is intended. Dummy it in It is raining and dummy there in There are two seats occupy subject positions without naming an ordinary participant. Questions and some emphatic clauses change ordinary word order, so the first noun before a verb is not a universal subject test. These constructions receive detailed treatment later. S + V + O A transitive clause: The mechanic repaired the bicycle. S + linking V + subject complement A predicative clause: The bicycle looks new. The musicians rehearsed. SV: the musicians is subject; rehearsed is the verb and complete predicate. The volunteers painted the classroom yesterday. SVO plus time adjunct: yesterday is outside the object noun phrase. The board considered the proposed timetable impractical. The proposed timetable is direct object; impractical is its predicative complement. The chairperson became a teacher. The chairperson appointed a teacher. Both are grammatical. Became takes a subject complement; appointed takes an object in this use. Imperatives normally omit an expressed subject: Read the notice. Questions can put an auxiliary before the subject: Did the visitors wait? Analyse the whole pattern. The head of the two departments approve the plan. The head of the two departments approves the plan. The head of the two departments is the subject; singular head controls ordinary agreement here. The room seems quietly. The room seems quiet. The intended description of the room is the adjective quiet, functioning as subject complement. direct object An element normally selected by a transitive verb, typically a noun phrase. The visitors read the notice. adjunct An added circumstance or comment rather than a selected complement. Yesterday is a time adjunct in We met yesterday. source-15b65ce5c1b751 source-d8d773260d5fa1 source-d6af2eef369812 source-4bea8b5c1c8314

concepts.title: Noun meanings and the formation of plurals
concepts.definition: A noun is a word class whose members typically head noun phrases. Meaning labels such as concrete, abstract, collective and material describe overlapping kinds of nouns; number is the grammatical contrast between singular and plural where that contrast is available.

glossary.definition: A noun naming a group as a group.
glossary.example: The committee met on Tuesday.

glossary.definition: The singular/plural distinction expressed in relevant forms and agreement.
glossary.example: One child became three children.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d02-m01 Noun meanings and the formation of plurals A B gv5-topic-d02-c01 gv5-topic-d02-c02 A noun is a word class whose members typically head noun phrases. Meaning labels such as concrete, abstract, collective and material describe overlapping kinds of nouns; number is the grammatical contrast between singular and plural where that contrast is available. A common noun identifies a kind: river, student or proposal. A proper noun is conventionally a name: Aisha, Lahore or the Indus. Concrete nouns refer to things ordinarily perceived through the senses, such as a bell; abstract nouns refer to qualities, states or ideas, such as fairness. A collective noun names a group, such as committee. A material noun names a substance, such as copper. These labels overlap: committee is common and collective, while copper is common, concrete and material in its substance meaning. They are not seven exclusive boxes into which every noun must fit. Regular count plurals normally add -s or -es: roads, boxes, wishes. Consonant plus y usually changes to -ies, as city/cities; vowel plus y normally keeps y, as key/keys. Plural forms must be learned with the noun when spelling is irregular: child/children, woman/women, mouse/mice, tooth/teeth. Some nouns keep one form for both numbers: one sheep, six sheep. Check the whole expression before choosing a verb, since the spelling alone may not reveal number. Apostrophes do not form ordinary plurals: three shops, not three shop’s. Some borrowed nouns retain foreign-origin patterns: analysis/analyses, criterion/criteria and phenomenon/phenomena. Others have established alternatives: indexes and indices or appendixes and appendices. Meaning and field can affect which plural is conventional; consult a current dictionary or disciplinary style guide rather than assume the older-looking form is always superior. Compound plurals usually mark the noun that functions as head: two car parks and three sisters-in-law. In lexicalised compounds the exact form can be conventional, so memorising the complete singular/plural pair is safer than applying a spelling slogan to every multiword expression. Proper names can acquire count uses without losing their connection to naming. Two Aishas may mean two people called Aisha; a Picasso may mean a work by Picasso. This is a contextual shift, not evidence that proper nouns never take articles or plurals. Semantic categories also shift with sense: glass is a substance in broken glass and a count object in three glasses. Number, countability and reference interact but are distinct. A grammatically plural word is not necessarily a group noun, and a collective singular does not necessarily denote just one person. Analyse the particular lexical sense and noun phrase. singular count noun → plural form Usually add -s/-es, but retain the noun’s established irregular form. head noun inside a compound → plural head sister-in-law → sisters-in-law; car park → car parks. The children planted three trees. Children is an irregular plural; trees is a regular plural. Two analyses reached different conclusions. Analyses is the plural of analysis; it is distinct from the verb analyses. Several sisters-in-law attended the reunion. The plural marks sisters, the head of this compound. The workshop needs glass. The workshop needs three glasses. Both are grammatical. The first requests a material; the second requests countable objects or containers. A noun’s spelling may remain unchanged: this sheep is restless but these sheep are restless. The determiner and verb make number explicit. The report uses two criterions. The report uses two criteria. The established plural of criterion is criteria. Three citys joined the scheme. Three cities joined the scheme. A consonant before final y normally produces the plural spelling -ies. collective noun A noun naming a group as a group. The committee met on Tuesday. grammatical number The singular/plural distinction expressed in relevant forms and agreement. One child became three children. source-5e8743788d0639 source-fb277fd6f4e9a7 source-a95ed69b7ca939 source-b6c1a3fe28cfd4

concepts.title: Countability, special number patterns and group agreement
concepts.definition: Countability describes how a noun sense combines with numbers and determiners. A count use presents separate units; a noncount use presents a mass, substance, activity or abstraction without ordinary unit counting. The distinction is grammatical and depends on lexical meaning and context.

glossary.definition: A noun use not ordinarily counted by a/an or a numeral directly.
glossary.example: We need reliable information.

glossary.definition: Agreement influenced by the meaning or construal of the subject.
glossary.example: The team are sharing their opinions presents individual members.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d02-m02 Countability, special number patterns and group agreement B P gv5-topic-d02-c03 gv5-topic-d02-c04 gv5-topic-d02-c05 Countability describes how a noun sense combines with numbers and determiners. A count use presents separate units; a noncount use presents a mass, substance, activity or abstraction without ordinary unit counting. The distinction is grammatical and depends on lexical meaning and context. Count nouns permit expressions such as a chair and several chairs. Noncount nouns in ordinary senses combine with some or much rather than a/an and do not take ordinary plural -s: information, advice, furniture, equipment, evidence and research. Use a piece of information, two items of equipment, three chairs or several studies when units matter. Evidence is not counted as evidences in ordinary general prose; a piece of evidence or several kinds of evidence states the intended unit. Learn each noun in a complete phrase, especially where another language uses a different countability pattern. A noun may have count and noncount senses. Experience means accumulated knowledge in She has experience, but an experience names a particular event. Two coffees can mean two servings; different wines can mean types. These changes are conventional, not permission to count every noncount noun freely. Advice and information normally retain their noncount pattern in everyday and academic prose. Much research is natural formal English. Where specialised dictionaries document a restricted plural, such as researches for particular investigations, identify that sense and register; use studies or research projects as the transparent general default. Some nouns have special number patterns. News and mathematics take singular agreement in their ordinary topic meanings despite final -s. Scissors, trousers, goods and belongings normally have plural form and agreement. One pair of scissors is singular because pair heads the expression; two pairs of scissors are plural. People is normally plural when meaning persons, while peoples can refer to distinct populations. Police normally takes a plural verb when referring to officers collectively. A noun’s final letters do not therefore predict either its countability or the verb automatically. Check its meaning and its head phrase. British group nouns can take singular agreement for a unit or plural agreement for members: The team is ready; The team are changing into their different uniforms. American English generally prefers singular agreement with a formally singular collective; the members of the team makes a plural construal explicit in either variety. Avoid claiming that a country has one exceptionless rule for all collectives. Keep the intended perspective clear when choosing pronouns. A group’s membership can be many people even when its grammar is singular; grammatical number and real-world number are different kinds of information. Day 10 develops these agreement choices further. piece/item/measure + of + noncount noun A countable unit expression allows explicit counting without inventing a plural of the material noun. The technician replaced two items of equipment. Items supplies countable units; equipment retains its ordinary noncount form. The news is encouraging, but the police are cautious. News is grammatically singular; police normally requires plural agreement. The committee are exchanging their separate notes. A British member-focused plural is appropriate; the members of the committee is a clear alternative. She has little experience. She described two memorable experiences. Both are grammatical. The first concerns knowledge; the second concerns separate events. A countability shift needs an established interpretation: two teas readily means servings, but two advices is not the ordinary way to request two recommendations. We received three useful informations. We received three useful pieces of information. Count pieces, not information, in this ordinary informational sense. The new trousers is too long. The new trousers are too long. Trousers is plural in this use. A new pair of trousers would instead have singular pair as its head and take is. noncount noun A noun use not ordinarily counted by a/an or a numeral directly. We need reliable information. notional agreement Agreement influenced by the meaning or construal of the subject. The team are sharing their opinions presents individual members. source-a95ed69b7ca939 source-5e8743788d0639 source-287989cd31ff3a source-8cf60a1688508e source-5bdfd5772dae31

concepts.title: Genitives, possession and noun relationships
concepts.definition: The genitive is a construction commonly marked by -’s or an apostrophe in writing. It expresses several relationships, including possession, association, authorship and time. An of-construction is another way to relate noun phrases, but the two patterns are not always interchangeable.

glossary.definition: A grammatical construction marking a relation between noun phrases.
glossary.example: The researcher’s notes identify notes through the researcher.

glossary.definition: An of-construction followed by a genitive expression.
glossary.example: A friend of hers called.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d02-m03 Genitives, possession and noun relationships B O gv5-topic-d02-c06 The genitive is a construction commonly marked by -’s or an apostrophe in writing. It expresses several relationships, including possession, association, authorship and time. An of-construction is another way to relate noun phrases, but the two patterns are not always interchangeable. With an ordinary singular noun, write the student’s notebook. With a regular plural ending in s, write the students’ notebooks. With an irregular plural, write the children’s notebooks. First determine how many owners or associates are meant, then place the apostrophe. The apostrophe is not a general signal that a word ends in s. Compare two teachers, one teacher’s desk and two teachers’ desks: the three expressions communicate different grammatical information. Possessive pronouns such as hers, ours and theirs do not take an additional apostrophe. The genitive often acts like a determiner: Amina’s bicycle identifies a bicycle through its relation to Amina. The relationship is not always literal ownership. Amina’s article may mean the article she wrote; tomorrow’s meeting relates the event to a time; the committee’s decision identifies its institutional source. The report’s conclusion and the conclusion of the report are both normal. People and organisations often favour the -’s pattern, while long phrases or some part–whole relationships may favour of. These are usage tendencies, not a grammatical rule that inanimate nouns can never take -’s. Place the marker at the end of a relevant compound or phrase: my sister-in-law’s address. In a shared genitive, Sara and Imran’s proposal can identify one joint proposal; Sara’s and Imran’s separate proposals makes separate association explicit. The exact punctuation and wording can become awkward with pronouns or long coordination, so recast rather than rely on punctuation to carry an unclear meaning. Names ending in s allow editorial alternatives such as James’s and James’; follow a consistent style and recognise both. Do not mark one conventional style as universally ungrammatical. A double-genitive construction combines of with a genitive: a friend of Amina’s or a colleague of mine. It can select one member of an associated set and differs from of + object pronoun. A portrait of Amina depicts Amina; a portrait of Amina’s associates the portrait with her, often as owner or creator, depending on context. The marker’s ability to occur at a phrase edge motivates analysing it as a clitic in many modern grammars; traditional teaching often calls it a possessive ending. Knowing both labels is useful, but the practical task remains deciding the intended relationship and the exact phrase the marker belongs to. singular noun + ’s; regular plural in -s + ’ the visitor’s coat; the visitors’ coats a + noun + of + genitive a neighbour of mine; a friend of Leena’s The doctor’s bag was beside the doctors’ coats. The first genitive is singular; the second is regular plural. The company’s response arrived after a week’s delay. The genitives express an institutional source and a duration. A colleague of my brother’s has rented the flat. The outer expression selects a colleague through the genitive phrase my brother’s. a photograph of Nida a photograph of Nida’s Both are grammatical; depiction is the usual first reading, while the second associates ownership or authorship with Nida. Names ending in s have style-dependent written genitives. James’s answer and James’ answer should not be used as competing right/wrong choices without a specified editorial convention. The childrens’ room is upstairs. The children’s room is upstairs. Children is an irregular plural without final plural -s, so the marker is ’s. This notebook is her’s. This notebook is hers. The possessive pronoun hers has no apostrophe. genitive A grammatical construction marking a relation between noun phrases. The researcher’s notes identify notes through the researcher. double genitive An of-construction followed by a genitive expression. A friend of hers called. source-fb41efc1d03fc7

concepts.title: Noun phrases, modifiers, apposition and nominalisation
concepts.definition: A noun phrase is organised around a noun or pronoun head and may contain determiners, modifiers and complements. Nominalisation forms or uses a noun to express an event, process or quality. Apposition places related noun phrases together to identify or describe a referent.

glossary.definition: A construction placing noun phrases together with a shared identifying or descriptive relationship.
glossary.example: Farah, the coordinator, welcomed us.

glossary.definition: Use or formation of a noun to express an event, process or quality.
glossary.example: Approve becomes approval.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d02-m04 Noun phrases, modifiers, apposition and nominalisation B H N gv5-topic-d02-c07 gv5-topic-d02-c08 A noun phrase is organised around a noun or pronoun head and may contain determiners, modifiers and complements. Nominalisation forms or uses a noun to express an event, process or quality. Apposition places related noun phrases together to identify or describe a referent. Expand a simple noun step by step: report; the report; the detailed report; the detailed report on housing. Report remains the head. The specifies reference, detailed modifies it before the head and on housing adds information after the head. These dependents belong inside the same noun phrase. When the phrase acts as subject, recognise the whole unit rather than report alone. Expansion helps a writer be precise, but putting every available detail before a head makes a phrase difficult to read. Place information where its relationship is clearest. Nouns can function as premodifiers: a research centre, a school library and an application form. The first noun does not become an adjective merely because it modifies another noun. A noun–noun expression can name many relationships: a school bus serves a school, a stone wall is made of stone and a history teacher teaches history. The relation must be learned from meaning and convention. Noun modifiers are often singular, but established plural modifiers occur in a sports centre and a savings account. Do not mechanically delete every -s before a second noun. Apposition offers another way to identify: my colleague Farah integrates the name into the phrase, while Farah, our new coordinator, adds a supplementary description. Punctuation depends on whether information identifies or supplements, so do not add commas merely because a second noun phrase appears. Noun phrases can also contain complements such as the decision to postpone the inspection, where the infinitival clause specifies the decision’s content. Longer phrases may embed other phrases: applications from graduates of local colleges. Their hierarchical structure matters more than a flat list of nearby words. Nominalisation allows an action or quality to become a noun: the council approved the plan becomes the council’s approval of the plan; the road is wide relates to the width of the road. This can make an event a topic that later sentences discuss. It can also hide who acted: the approval alone leaves the decision-maker unstated. Preserve agency, time and modality when rewriting. The proposal for a new inspection system is different from the proposal’s inspection system: the former identifies proposed content, while the latter may assign a system to a proposal awkwardly. Choose a structure for the relationship you intend, not merely because it sounds formal. determiner + premodifiers + noun head + postmodifiers/complements The two recent reports on flooding are one expanded noun phrase. verb clause → related nominalisation The council approved the plan → the council’s approval of the plan. The research centre needs a new application form. Research and application are noun modifiers, not necessarily adjectives. Our neighbour, a retired engineer, repaired the pump. The supplementary appositive describes the already identified neighbour. The committee’s rejection of the revised timetable surprised the applicants. Rejection nominalises reject; the genitive preserves the rejecting body and of preserves the rejected content. The students protested. The students’ protest continued. Both are grammatical. The event is a verb predicate in the first and a noun-phrase topic in the second. Plural modifiers may be conventional: a sports centre is standard. Dictionary-backed established compounds override a beginner’s singular-modifier tendency. The libraries research needs more funding. Intended: research carried out by the library. The library’s research needs more funding. The intended source relation is expressed by a genitive, not an unexplained plural modifier. The council’s approved of the plan was unexpected. The council’s approval of the plan was unexpected. The genitive requires a noun head here; approval is the relevant nominalisation. apposition A construction placing noun phrases together with a shared identifying or descriptive relationship. Farah, the coordinator, welcomed us. nominalisation Use or formation of a noun to express an event, process or quality. Approve becomes approval. source-58353073c867f7 source-fb277fd6f4e9a7 source-fb41efc1d03fc7 source-d6af2eef369812

concepts.title: Articles, identification and general reference
concepts.definition: Articles are a, an and the. A/an introduces one member of a countable class; the normally signals that the intended referent is identifiable in the situation or discourse. Zero article means that no article occurs, not that the noun phrase has no grammatical structure.

glossary.definition: Presentation of a referent as identifiable in context.
glossary.example: The report on your desk identifies a particular report.

glossary.definition: Reference to a particular entity rather than any suitable member of a class.
glossary.example: A certain visitor called refers to a particular visitor.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d03-m01 Articles, identification and general reference B K gv5-topic-d03-c01 gv5-topic-d03-c02 gv5-topic-d03-c03 Articles are a, an and the. A/an introduces one member of a countable class; the normally signals that the intended referent is identifiable in the situation or discourse. Zero article means that no article occurs, not that the noun phrase has no grammatical structure. Start with a singular count use: a report, an interview. A/an depends on the next sound rather than the next letter: a university, an hour, an unusual report and a useful report. The next sound may belong to an adjective, not to the noun. An introduces one unspecified member for the listener, but the speaker may already know which one: I spoke to a specialist yesterday can describe a specific person. Do not confuse indefinite form with a speaker having no particular individual in mind. Use the when the intended referent is identifiable. A visitor rang the bell. The visitor asked for directions introduces the person and then refers back. First mention is not the only source of identification: Please close the door can work when the relevant door is obvious. A bridging link also helps: We entered a house. The kitchen was bright. The kitchen is identifiable through its relationship to the house even though kitchen has not appeared before. If several doors or kitchens are equally relevant, add enough description to establish which is meant. General reference has several structures. Tigers are mammals uses a bare plural for the class generally. A tiger is a mammal describes a representative member. The tiger is endangered presents the species as a category; this singular generic pattern is conventional but cannot replace every bare-plural generalisation mechanically. Noncount nouns often have zero article for general reference: Water is essential. The water in this bottle is warm identifies a particular quantity. A noun being abstract does not itself forbid the: Justice matters, but the justice of the decision was disputed. Definiteness, specificity and uniqueness are related ideas, not synonyms. The author of this report can identify a unique role even if the reader does not know the author’s name. I need a book about wetlands can be nonspecific, whereas I bought a book about wetlands may refer to a particular purchased book. Context decides whether a description sufficiently identifies its referent; grammar does not supply a universal first-mention checklist. A/an normally accompanies a singular count use, but determiners and constructions permit other patterns, developed below. The article belongs to the noun phrase and does not tell you the noun’s function by itself. a/an + singular count noun One member of a class, with the article chosen by the following sound. the + identifying noun phrase The writer presents the referent as recoverable from context, discourse or descriptive information. A pilot phoned. The pilot left a message. First indefinite mention is followed by an identifiable reference to the same person. The roof of the library needs repairs. The of-phrase helps identify the intended roof without an earlier mention of roof. Copper conducts electricity; the copper in this cable is damaged. The first clause is generic; the second identifies a particular material quantity. I am looking for a particular engineer whom I met yesterday. I am looking for an engineer who can repair this device. Both are grammatical. The first describes a specific person; the second can mean any suitable engineer. Letters alone do not decide a/an: an MP uses the initial sound /em/, while a USB cable begins with /juː/. Accent and how an abbreviation is spoken can change the appropriate choice. She is an university lecturer. She is a university lecturer. University begins with a consonant sound despite its initial vowel letter. The oxygen is necessary for human life. Intended: oxygen generally. Oxygen is necessary for human life. A general noncount reference normally uses zero article; the would need an identifying context. definiteness Presentation of a referent as identifiable in context. The report on your desk identifies a particular report. specificity Reference to a particular entity rather than any suitable member of a class. A certain visitor called refers to a particular visitor. source-5de3dcfc2c8b36 source-a95ed69b7ca939

concepts.title: Articles with institutions, names and abstract nouns
concepts.definition: Article patterns depend on noun meaning, conventional names and the activity being described. A geographical or institutional expression must be learned as a whole pattern, with regional alternatives identified where they affect interpretation.

glossary.definition: Absence of an article in a grammatical noun-phrase construction.
glossary.example: Children need clean water.

glossary.definition: A conventional noun use referring to an institution’s typical activity or participant status.
glossary.example: At school can mean attending as a pupil.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d03-m02 Articles with institutions, names and abstract nouns B P gv5-topic-d03-c04 Article patterns depend on noun meaning, conventional names and the activity being described. A geographical or institutional expression must be learned as a whole pattern, with regional alternatives identified where they affect interpretation. Compare school as an institution and a school as a building or organisation. The children are at school normally describes participation as pupils. I waited outside the school identifies a particular location. British English commonly uses in hospital for a patient, while in the hospital can identify a building; American English commonly uses in the hospital for the patient meaning too. Bed has a conventional zero-article sleep use: go to bed. These are established constructions, not evidence that every building used for its purpose loses its article. A person may go to the bank for ordinary banking. Names have conventional article patterns. Many personal names, cities, countries and individual mountains have zero article: Sana, Karachi, Pakistan and Mount Kenya. Some country names conventionally include the, including the United Kingdom and the United States. Rivers, seas, oceans and mountain ranges commonly take the: the Indus, the Arabian Sea and the Himalayas. A plural name or a descriptive political name can therefore differ from a simple country name. Learn the complete name, rather than infer the article from national importance or size. Local institutional names also have their own conventions. Abstract and material nouns can be general, specific or conventionally countable in different senses. Education is important is general; the education she received was expensive identifies particular education. She had an excellent education uses a recognised count interpretation of an educational experience. The same contrast explains life and a life, knowledge and a detailed knowledge of the region. Do not add a/an to ordinary information or advice merely because an adjective intervenes. Useful advice remains noncount. Meals, languages, sports and subjects often have zero article in general activity uses, but a restrictive description can identify an instance: the lunch we ordered arrived late. Article omission also occurs in names, headlines, notices, coordinated expressions and role descriptions. They elected her chair is a recognised complement construction; it does not license They bought chair for an ordinary object. Proper names may acquire modified or count uses, as a young Mozart or the London of her childhood, and such expressions need contextual interpretation. British and American conventions should be described at the construction level. At university is a useful British educational pattern; at college is common in American contexts. A writer choosing a particular national convention should preserve it while recognising legitimate standard alternatives. at school / in hospital in relevant British institutional uses The noun evokes the institutional activity or participant status. the + specified abstract/material noun The phrase identifies a particular instance, kind or quantity. Her son is at school, but she is at the school for a meeting. The first describes pupil status; the second identifies a location. The expedition crossed the Indus before travelling towards Islamabad. The river name takes the; the city name normally does not. A detailed knowledge of local law would help; knowledge alone is not enough. The first has an established qualified count expression; the second is a general noncount use. He is in hospital after an operation. He is in the hospital after an operation. The first is the usual British patient pattern; the second is also the normal American patient pattern, as well as a possible building reference. Institutional zero article is lexical and regional: go to prison does not imply that every prison-related noun phrase must omit the. The prison beside the river needs the when it identifies a building. She lives in the Pakistan. She lives in Pakistan. The ordinary country name Pakistan does not take an article. He gave me a valuable information. He gave me valuable information. Information retains its ordinary noncount pattern despite the adjective valuable. zero article Absence of an article in a grammatical noun-phrase construction. Children need clean water. institutional use A conventional noun use referring to an institution’s typical activity or participant status. At school can mean attending as a pupil. source-5de3dcfc2c8b36 source-a95ed69b7ca939 source-8cf60a1688508e

concepts.title: Determiners, distribution and quantity
concepts.definition: A determiner helps specify reference or quantity within a noun phrase. Articles, demonstratives, possessive determiners, numbers and many quantifiers take part in this system. Their distribution depends on number, countability and the meaning of the construction.

glossary.definition: A meaning that applies separately to members of a set.
glossary.example: Each candidate receives a number.

glossary.definition: An expression indicating number, amount or proportion.
glossary.example: Several, much and all are quantifiers in relevant noun-phrase uses.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d03-m03 Determiners, distribution and quantity B K gv5-topic-d03-c05 gv5-topic-d03-c06 gv5-topic-d03-c09 A determiner helps specify reference or quantity within a noun phrase. Articles, demonstratives, possessive determiners, numbers and many quantifiers take part in this system. Their distribution depends on number, countability and the meaning of the construction. Demonstratives distinguish near or currently prominent reference from more distant reference: this form, that form, these forms, those forms. Possessive determiners include my, your, her, our and their; they normally replace an article in the central determiner position: my report, not the my report. Whose and which can introduce noun phrases in questions: Which route is open? What kind of evidence is available? In this course, these uses are called determiner uses. Some school descriptions use labels such as demonstrative adjective; identifying the noun-phrase role matters more than confusing terminology with correctness. Cardinal numbers state quantities, such as three rooms; ordinal numbers order members, such as the third room. Quantifiers specify amount or number more loosely: many rooms, much space, several applications and enough evidence. Many combines with plural count nouns; much combines with noncount nouns. Much is especially ordinary in negatives and questions, and also in formal positive phrases such as much research. A lot of can combine with either pattern. Enough precedes a noun but follows an adjective: enough time and clear enough. Its meaning is sufficiency for a stated or understood purpose, not simply a large quantity. Each and every distribute attention across individual members: each proposal is different; every proposal needs a signature. Each can stand alone and can occur with of: each of the proposals. Every normally needs a singular count head; use every one of the proposals rather than every of them. Both refers to two together; either selects or permits one of two, and neither excludes the two alternatives. All is not limited to two: all the proposals. These words can interact with negation: not all proposals passed means some did not, whereas no proposals passed excludes every one. Their meanings cannot be reduced to interchangeable substitutes for many. The of-pattern distinguishes a whole general class from a specified set: many students but many of the students. Compare all students, all the students and all of the students; all allows some patterns that each or several do not. Both my colleagues and both of my colleagues are possible. Distributive quantity and grammatical agreement interact, but agreement receives full treatment on Day 10. Either can also mean both in expressions such as on either side of the road, so interpretation must follow the construction. A determiner is not defined as a word that must always be directly adjacent to its noun; adjectives and other modifiers may intervene. quantifier + plural count/noncount noun Choose many applicants or much evidence according to the noun’s sense. quantifier + of + specified noun phrase Many of the applicants selects from an identified set. Each of the three files needs a label. Each distributes the requirement to individual files and takes an of-phrase. Both our buses have enough space. Both identifies the two buses; enough gives a sufficiency judgement about noncount space. Not all of the recommendations were adopted. Negation excludes complete adoption without saying that none were adopted. There is enough time. There is plenty of time. Both are grammatical; enough says time meets a requirement, while plenty suggests more than sufficient time. Either side of a road can mean each of its two sides. This established construction differs from choosing either of two proposed routes. Every of the forms needs a signature. Every one of the forms needs a signature. Every does not take this of-phrase directly. We have time enough to complete the task. Neutral everyday word order requested. We have enough time to complete the task. Enough normally precedes a noun in neutral prose; time enough is possible in marked or literary contexts and is not universally ungrammatical. distributive A meaning that applies separately to members of a set. Each candidate receives a number. quantifier An expression indicating number, amount or proportion. Several, much and all are quantifiers in relevant noun-phrase uses. source-b7519a9fb89ab0 source-2b69beb54eca89 source-5de3dcfc2c8b36

concepts.title: Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation
concepts.definition: Quantity expressions differ in the expectations they create as well as the nouns they permit. Some and any interact with questions, negation and unrestricted choice; few and little often imply insufficiency, whereas a few and a little present a positive quantity.

glossary.definition: Any meaning that no particular choice is restricted.
glossary.example: Choose any two questions.

glossary.definition: The part of an expression over which a grammatical meaning operates.
glossary.example: Not all does not normally mean none.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d03-m04 Some, any, few and little: meaning under quantity and negation B K P gv5-topic-d03-c07 gv5-topic-d03-c08 Quantity expressions differ in the expectations they create as well as the nouns they permit. Some and any interact with questions, negation and unrestricted choice; few and little often imply insufficiency, whereas a few and a little present a positive quantity. Use a few with plural count nouns and a little with noncount nouns: a few pages, a little time. Removing a changes the usual implication: few pages suggests not many, often fewer than hoped; little time suggests not much. A few and a little assert that some quantity is available, often enough for a modest purpose. The real situation matters: a few mistakes can be reassuring in a long report but serious in a safety procedure. Grammatical form expresses a perspective; it does not calculate whether a quantity is objectively good or bad. Some often introduces an indefinite quantity in an affirmative statement: We bought some paper. Any is common in negatives and open questions: We did not buy any paper; Do you have any paper? These are tendencies, not a rule banning some from questions. Would you like some tea? is an ordinary offer, and Have you got some spare paper? can suggest an expected positive answer. Any also has a free-choice use: Choose any seat means there is no restriction on which seat you select. That use is compatible with a singular count noun. In careful edited comparison, fewer commonly accompanies plural count nouns and less accompanies noncount nouns: fewer delays, less disruption. Established exceptions include measurements, sums and time spans regarded as amounts: less than ten minutes and less than twenty pounds. Less is also widespread with plural count nouns, especially in informal usage; a formal editor may prefer fewer ordinary individual items. Do not mark less than five miles wrong by applying a count-noun slogan to a measurement. Meaning and editorial convention are both relevant. More and most do not have separate count and noncount forms. Scope helps explain quantity expressions that seem similar. I did not read some of the reports can identify a particular subset that went unread, while I did not read any of the reports normally says none were read. Some can be stressed to create a contrast, so intonation and context contribute to interpretation. Few and little are negative in orientation and can license expressions associated with negation: Few applicants have ever complained. A few applicants have complained instead presents an existing positive set. Avoid classifying either sentence by a memorised positive-versus-negative word list without interpreting what is asserted about the set. few/a few + plural count noun; little/a little + noncount noun The article changes the usual negative or positive orientation. not + any + relevant set Ordinarily expresses absence of even one member or amount in that set. We have a little fuel, so we can reach the next village. A little presents a positive amount, linked here to sufficiency. Few applicants had read all the instructions. Few presents a small proportion and is negative in orientation. The repair took less than thirty minutes but required fewer tools. Minutes is a measured span; tools are separate counted objects. There is little evidence. There is a little evidence. Both are grammatical. The first emphasises scarcity; the second acknowledges a positive amount. Some is normal in offers and questions with a positive expectation: Would you like some water? Do not replace it automatically with any. There are a little applicants waiting. There are a few applicants waiting. Applicants is a plural count noun, so a few is the compatible expression. We received few information. We received little information. Information is noncount in this ordinary use; little expresses a small amount. free-choice any Any meaning that no particular choice is restricted. Choose any two questions. scope The part of an expression over which a grammatical meaning operates. Not all does not normally mean none. source-129df932b28c56 source-d8d7c7adb6ed42 source-39615bb337754a source-2b69beb54eca89

concepts.title: Personal forms, case and reflexive meaning
concepts.definition: Personal pronouns mark speaker, addressee or other referents. Their forms can distinguish grammatical case, such as I/me and she/her. Reflexive forms such as myself and themselves can refer back to a local subject or emphasise a participant; those uses must be distinguished from ordinary object forms.

glossary.definition: A grammatical distinction in forms such as I/me associated with their structural role.
glossary.example: I called them; they called me.

glossary.definition: A reflexive form adding emphasis to a participant rather than serving as a required object.
glossary.example: The director herself replied.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d04-m01 Personal forms, case and reflexive meaning C P gv5-topic-d04-c01 gv5-topic-d04-c03 Personal pronouns mark speaker, addressee or other referents. Their forms can distinguish grammatical case, such as I/me and she/her. Reflexive forms such as myself and themselves can refer back to a local subject or emphasise a participant; those uses must be distinguished from ordinary object forms. Compare She thanked him with He thanked her. She and he are subject forms; him and her are object forms. The forms show grammatical relationships even when the people remain the same. I, we and they contrast with me, us and them; you and it do not show this case contrast in spelling. Possessive determiners accompany a noun, as my folder and their house, while independent possessives can stand without that noun, as mine and theirs. Hers, ours, yours and theirs have no additional apostrophe. Learn each form together with a short sentence rather than memorising a list without its function. Coordination does not automatically change the case expected in careful edited prose: Sara and I attended; the tutor spoke to Sara and me. Temporarily removing Sara and can help reveal the ordinary subject or object pattern, although coordination has additional informal usage conventions. Do not insert I simply because it sounds polite. After be, object forms are normal standard usage: It is me and That is her. It is I survives as a highly formal alternative; calling every object form after be wrong confuses a restrictive traditional preference with present-day grammar. When subject and object refer to the same participant in a simple clause, a reflexive often expresses that relation: Leena blamed herself. Leena blamed her normally directs blame towards a different female referent. Reflexives can also emphasise: Leena herself checked the figures; Leena checked the figures herself. The emphatic form adds contrast or responsibility and is not the subject on its own. By herself can mean alone or without help. Do not assume that every first-language reflexive construction needs an English reflexive: She washed and dressed is ordinary when no special emphasis on doing it unaided is intended. Case choices interact with register and construction. Than me is standard in comparisons, while than I am uses an expanded clause; compare their actual meanings rather than enforcing a bare subject form. Informal coordinated subjects with me occur in established speech, but Sara and I is the conservative edited choice. Some independent or polite reflexives occur, such as people like yourself; they are not all governed by the simple same-clause rule for direct-object reflexives. This course therefore teaches the local subject–object contrast as a reliable basic pattern while identifying emphatic, polite and discourse-sensitive uses separately. subject + verb + reflexive object Leena blamed herself presents subject and object as the same person. coordinated object after a preposition The invitation is for Bilal and me in careful edited prose. The curator gave us her notes; the final copy is hers. Us is an object form, her accompanies a noun, and hers is an independent possessive. The scientist herself recalculated the result. Herself is emphatic; the scientist remains the subject phrase. Farah is taller than me, but her brother is taller than I am. Both comparison patterns are standard; the latter includes an explicit clause. Amina photographed herself. Amina photographed her. Both are grammatical; the ordinary local reading is self-directed in the first and directed at another female referent in the second. A polite expression such as someone like yourself can be standard without a local reflexive antecedent. This does not make Myself attended the seminar an ordinary neutral replacement for I attended the seminar. In careful edited prose: The manager spoke to I. The manager spoke to me. A personal pronoun complement of to normally takes the object form. Intended: the speaker injured the speaker. I cut me while chopping vegetables. I cut myself while chopping vegetables. The reflexive marks the ordinary local same-subject-and-object relationship. case A grammatical distinction in forms such as I/me associated with their structural role. I called them; they called me. emphatic reflexive A reflexive form adding emphasis to a participant rather than serving as a required object. The director herself replied. source-c040d9e0859517 source-170117f00cc224 source-fb41efc1d03fc7

concepts.title: Pronoun families and relative choices
concepts.definition: Pronoun families are grouped by their grammatical patterns and meanings. Interrogative pronouns ask for an identity, relative expressions connect a clause with an antecedent, demonstratives point, indefinites leave identity open, and reciprocal expressions present a mutual relationship.

glossary.definition: An expression to which a referring expression is linked.
glossary.example: The visitor who called links who with visitor.

glossary.definition: A construction describing a mutual relationship among participants.
glossary.example: They respect each other.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d04-m02 Pronoun families and relative choices C I gv5-topic-d04-c02 Pronoun families are grouped by their grammatical patterns and meanings. Interrogative pronouns ask for an identity, relative expressions connect a clause with an antecedent, demonstratives point, indefinites leave identity open, and reciprocal expressions present a mutual relationship. Who, what and which can ask for an identity: Who arrived? What happened? Which do you prefer? This, that, these and those can point without repeating a noun: These are ready. When a noun follows, the same forms have determiner uses: these reports. Indefinite pronouns such as someone, anything and nobody refer without naming an individual or thing. Everybody refers to people distributively but normally takes a singular present verb: Everybody knows. Each, either and neither can stand independently when the relevant set is understood. Their determiner uses were introduced on Day 3. Relative clauses give information connected with an antecedent: the driver who helped us, the form that I submitted and the office which opened yesterday. Who is used for people; which is used for things and can introduce a relative comment on a larger situation. Whose expresses a relationship and can refer to people or things: a house whose roof needs repair. That is possible in many defining relatives, but it does not replace who or which freely in every supplementary construction. Day 15 develops defining, supplementary and reduced relatives in detail; today concentrates on reference and pronoun form. Who commonly functions as either subject or object in contemporary English: Who arrived? Who did you invite?
