Whom is an object form associated especially with formal prose and directly preceding prepositions: To whom was the letter addressed? Avoid choosing whom solely because a verb or preposition occurs nearby. In Who do you think will lead the group?, who is the subject of will lead, not the object of think. Identify the pronoun’s role inside its own clause. A formal object-relative construction can use whom, while standard object who should not be rejected without a specified register requirement. Each other and one another ordinarily express mutual relations among two or more participants. The inherited convention reserving each other for two and one another for more than two is not a dependable modern grammar rule; the two are normally interchangeable. They helped themselves can describe self-directed action, while they helped each other describes mutual help. Mutual reference does not always mean every member acted towards every other member; context determines the pattern. Each other is written as two words, and its genitive is each other’s. Different grammatical frameworks analyse some traditional pronoun labels differently, so this course makes the actual construction explicit. antecedent + relative clause The learner who asked the question links who to learner. plural participants + reciprocal expression The colleagues supported each other presents mutual support. Those are the files that we requested. Those has an independent demonstrative use; that connects a relative clause to files. The house whose windows were broken is being repaired. Whose relates windows to the inanimate antecedent house. Who do you believe can solve the problem? Who is subject of can solve despite the intervening do you believe. The two neighbours helped themselves. The two neighbours helped each other. Both are grammatical. The first is self-directed; the second is reciprocal. Object who is established standard English, especially outside highly formal preposition-first patterns. A formal exercise must state that it requires whom if both forms otherwise fit. The volunteers supported each others. The volunteers supported each other. The reciprocal expression does not add plural -s. Intended: ask which person will lead. Whom do you think will lead? Who do you think will lead? The interrogative is subject of will lead; it is not an object of think. antecedent An expression to which a referring expression is linked. The visitor who called links who with visitor. reciprocal A construction describing a mutual relationship among participants. They respect each other. source-5b7819d35530f4 source-59422752b96e10 source-b7519a9fb89ab0 source-54fe3d4f8cbf83

concepts.title: Reference chains, agreement and inclusive pronouns
concepts.definition: Reference is the connection between an expression and what it identifies in context. Anaphora looks back to an earlier expression, cataphora anticipates a later one, and deixis depends on the speaker’s situation. Clear pronoun choices maintain those connections across sentences.

glossary.definition: Reference linked to an earlier expression or situation.
glossary.example: Nida found a key and kept it.

glossary.definition: Reference anticipating a later identifying expression.
glossary.example: Before she left, Nida checked the door.

glossary.definition: Reference depending on the current speaker, location, time or pointing context.
glossary.example: I will put this here tomorrow.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d04-m03 Reference chains, agreement and inclusive pronouns C K P gv5-topic-d04-c04 gv5-topic-d04-c05 gv5-topic-d04-c07 gv5-topic-d04-c08 Reference is the connection between an expression and what it identifies in context. Anaphora looks back to an earlier expression, cataphora anticipates a later one, and deixis depends on the speaker’s situation. Clear pronoun choices maintain those connections across sentences. Read Mina found a wallet. She handed it to the receptionist. She refers back to Mina and it to the wallet; both are anaphoric links. A pronoun does not always replace an earlier noun: I and you identify participants in the current exchange, while this can point to an object in view. When she entered the hall, Mina noticed the broken window can use she cataphorically, with Mina supplying the later identification. The order of mention alone therefore does not decide whether a pronoun is grammatical. The reader must have enough information to establish the intended relationship. Keep reference clear when several potential antecedents appear. Aisha told Hina that she had won the prize leaves the winner uncertain without more context. Repeating a name can improve clarity even though the original sentence is grammatically possible. A pronoun can refer to a larger event or proposition: The bridge was closed. This delayed deliveries. Here this refers to the closure situation, not simply to bridge. For formal exposition, a fuller phrase such as this closure often makes the link clearer. Do not declare every such broad reference wrong, but ask whether readers can recover it reliably. Singular they is an established way to refer to an indefinite individual: Someone has left their umbrella; if anyone calls, ask them to wait. It also serves people who use they as their personal pronoun. A singular referent does not change its usual verb forms: they are, they have. You should not automatically replace singular they with he or insist that unknown people have a binary gender. Respect a person’s stated pronouns and retain clear reference. Where a sentence becomes cumbersome, pluralising the noun phrase or repeating a name may help, provided the meaning remains equivalent. Agreement is not a mechanical matching of neighbouring letters. Someone normally takes singular has, while subsequent they has its established are/have forms even when the referent is one person. British collective reference can follow a member-focused plural: The committee have finished their separate reports. A writer must make the intended construal coherent, rather than impose one universal rule about all group nouns. Themselves is widely used with singular they. Themself is also documented, but authorities differ in its status: Cambridge labels it not standard, while Merriam-Webster records it and discusses its increasing use. Institutional editorial preferences can therefore differ. This introductory lesson uses themselves as the broad default without calling every documented alternative nonexistent. Day 10 treats collective and notional agreement in detail. indefinite singular antecedent + singular they Someone has left their folder is a standard gender-neutral reference chain. ambiguous pronoun → explicit reference Repeat a name or descriptive noun when more than one antecedent is plausible. Every applicant should bring their identification. Their can refer inclusively to each individual applicant. Before he spoke, Omar checked the microphone. He can anticipate the later name Omar; this is cataphoric reference. The reservoir was contaminated. This finding prompted a new inspection. This finding makes the connection to the preceding proposition explicit. Hina told Aisha that she had been selected. Hina told Aisha, “You have been selected.” The first can be ambiguous without context; the second explicitly identifies Aisha as the selected person. The revision is suitable only if that is the intended meaning. Pronouns can identify a situation rather than one noun: She resigned. That surprised us. This is grammatical when the event reference is clear; a fuller noun phrase can improve precision. For the stated singular they referent: They is ready to begin. They are ready to begin. Singular reference does not replace the established verb form are with is. Intended: Nida won. Nida told Saba that she had won. Nida told Saba that Nida had won. Repeating the name removes the stated ambiguity; a correction must not silently choose the wrong winner. anaphora Reference linked to an earlier expression or situation. Nida found a key and kept it. cataphora Reference anticipating a later identifying expression. Before she left, Nida checked the door. deixis Reference depending on the current speaker, location, time or pointing context. I will put this here tomorrow. source-c040d9e0859517 source-8491a7a9cd1ef0 source-c8c8eb61823502 source-a240777d42125f source-287989cd31ff3a source-875cf442627771 source-9ce5998c5a5d1a

concepts.title: Dummy subjects, generic reference and local interpretation
concepts.definition: A dummy subject fills a grammatical subject position without identifying a normal participant, as it in It is raining. Generic pronouns refer to people generally. Practical binding concerns how pronouns and reflexives are linked to other expressions within grammatical structure.

glossary.definition: A subject expression filling a structural position without ordinary participant reference.
glossary.example: It is late.

glossary.definition: The structural linking of expressions such as pronouns and reflexives with potential antecedents.
glossary.example: In Leena blamed herself, herself is linked locally to Leena.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d04-m04 Dummy subjects, generic reference and local interpretation C H P gv5-topic-d04-c06 gv5-topic-d04-c09 A dummy subject fills a grammatical subject position without identifying a normal participant, as it in It is raining. Generic pronouns refer to people generally. Practical binding concerns how pronouns and reflexives are linked to other expressions within grammatical structure. In English, a neutral finite statement normally has a subject even when no ordinary actor is involved: It is raining; It is nearly noon. It is not a person causing rain or a previously mentioned object. Existential there introduces something’s existence or presence: There is a spare chair in the corridor. This there differs from locative there in Put the chair there, where it indicates a place. Grammatical descriptions differ in how they analyse the following noun phrase, but treating there as a dummy subject is useful for understanding why the sentence does not need a named actor before is. Dummy it also permits delayed content: It is useful to check the references; It is clear that the figures differ. The infinitival or that-clause supplies the important content, while it fills the initial subject slot. This arrangement is called extraposition in the relevant constructions and receives advanced treatment on Day 23. Do not assume every it is empty: I found the report. It is useful has an ordinary referring it. The form alone does not settle the interpretation; examine what it is doing in that particular sentence. Generic you, we, one and they allow different perspectives. You can learn a great deal by listening addresses people generally in many instructional contexts. One must check one’s sources is more formal and can sound detached. We can include writer and readers in a shared generalisation; unspecified they can mean a relevant institution or authority, though naming the authority may be clearer in formal reporting. Once a perspective is selected, avoid unexplained switches such as One should check your sources. Generic reference is not an excuse to invent claims about what every reader personally experiences. For ordinary reflexive objects, identify the relevant local subject: Nida said that Sana blamed herself normally links herself with Sana. Replacing herself with himself does not ordinarily allow it to refer across that finite clause to an earlier male name. These practical restrictions are often discussed under binding in syntax. They are not a complete theory of every reflexive use: emphatic forms, exempt or perspective-sensitive reflexives and picture-noun constructions can be more complex. A pronoun can also be grammatically possible yet misleading if its antecedent is unclear. Separate the structural restriction from the editorial task of making a reference chain easy to follow. it + weather/time expression It is raining fills the subject position without a referring participant. there + be + noun phrase There is a spare chair introduces the existence or presence of the chair. It is snowing outside. It is a dummy weather subject. There are three unclaimed parcels at reception. Existential there introduces parcels; careful edited agreement is plural are. Amir said that Leena blamed herself for the delay. The local subject Leena supplies the ordinary antecedent of herself. It is useful to read the instructions. The booklet arrived. It is useful. Both are grammatical. The first uses dummy it with delayed infinitival content; the second refers back to the booklet. Reflexives used for politeness or emphasis do not all follow the ordinary local-object pattern. Do not extend a beginner’s same-clause test into a claim that all other reflexive constructions are impossible. One should always check your sources. Intended: one consistent generic perspective. One should always check one’s sources. Maintain the selected generic pronoun pattern; You should always check your sources is also possible. Intended: Sana is self-critical. Amir said that Sana blamed himself. Amir said that Sana blamed herself. For the stated local reflexive meaning, herself agrees with Sana; himself does not create that intended relation. dummy subject A subject expression filling a structural position without ordinary participant reference. It is late. binding The structural linking of expressions such as pronouns and reflexives with potential antecedents. In Leena blamed herself, herself is linked locally to Leena. source-a091ce7ce11036 source-c040d9e0859517 source-170117f00cc224 source-445532eb0f5c35

concepts.title: Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms
concepts.definition: Verbs are a word class whose members organise clauses and select characteristic patterns. Lexical verbs contribute central meanings such as wait, repair and know. Auxiliaries help express grammatical meanings and constructions. Finite and non-finite describe a verb form’s grammatical status within a clause, not whether it denotes an action.

glossary.definition: A verb with grammatical functions such as forming perfect, progressive, passive, modal, interrogative or negative constructions.
glossary.example: Has is auxiliary in has arrived.

glossary.definition: Describing a verb or clause with finite grammatical status, typically supporting tense or modal distinctions and clause independence.
glossary.example: Has is finite in she has arrived.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d05-m01 Lexical verbs, auxiliaries and the principal forms D L gv5-topic-d05-c01 gv5-topic-d05-c02 gv5-topic-d05-c03 Verbs are a word class whose members organise clauses and select characteristic patterns. Lexical verbs contribute central meanings such as wait, repair and know. Auxiliaries help express grammatical meanings and constructions. Finite and non-finite describe a verb form’s grammatical status within a clause, not whether it denotes an action. Learn a lexical verb through its principal forms. Write has the plain form write, third-person singular present writes, past wrote, past participle written and -ing form writing. A regular verb normally uses the same -ed form for its past and past participle: repair, repaired, repaired. An irregular verb has an established alternative pattern, as write/wrote/written or cut/cut/cut. Identical spelling can therefore serve different grammatical roles. The clause She cut the paper contains a past form, while has cut contains a past participle selected by has. A learner’s dictionary supplies the relevant forms and pronunciation. Be, have and do are primary verbs that can function as auxiliaries or lexical verbs. Compare She has a bicycle with She has repaired a bicycle; only the second has is a perfect auxiliary. Be forms include be, am, is, are, was, were, been and being. Have has the forms have, has, had and having; do has do, does, did, done and doing. Had serves as both past and past-participle form. Core modal auxiliaries include can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would and must. They normally select a plain verb form: can swim, not can swims. Modality receives fuller semantic treatment on Day 17. In a finite verb phrase, the first verb is finite and the following forms are selected by preceding auxiliaries: has written, is writing, may have written. Non-finite forms include to-infinitives, plain infinitives, -ing forms and past participles. The form after to in to write does not carry its own person agreement. A past participle is not a past-tense verb merely because its name contains past; The work will be finished refers forward in time. Finite does not mean that a form always visibly changes for every subject: modal can has the same spelling with I and she. Inflectional form, clause status and time reference are different dimensions. A plain form occurs in several environments, including after a modal and in an imperative such as Close the door. Modern descriptions differ in how they classify certain untensed or subjunctive constructions, so a visible -s or -ed ending cannot serve as the sole test for finiteness. Regular spelling also has conditions: stopped doubles a consonant, while opened does not; consult stress and spelling conventions rather than double every final consonant. British learnt/learned and American learned illustrate legitimate form variation, not an automatic difference in grammatical correctness. lexical verb: plain / -s / past / past participle / -ing write / writes / wrote / written / writing are the five principal form categories. modal auxiliary + plain verb Can write uses a plain form after the modal. The researcher writes carefully. Writes is the third-person singular present form of the lexical verb. The researcher has written three reports. Has is finite; written is the past participle selected by perfect have. The researcher may have been working late. May is finite; have is plain after the modal, been follows perfect have, and working follows progressive be. She has a small studio. She has opened a small studio. Both are grammatical. Has is lexical possession in the first and a perfect auxiliary in the second. A form can be irregular without changing its spelling across categories: cut serves as plain, past and past participle in different structures. Context and auxiliary selection distinguish the functions. She has wrote the summary. She has written the summary. Perfect have requires the past participle, not the past-simple form wrote. He can speaks three languages. He can speak three languages. A core modal normally selects the plain form, not the third-person singular form. auxiliary A verb with grammatical functions such as forming perfect, progressive, passive, modal, interrogative or negative constructions. Has is auxiliary in has arrived. finite Describing a verb or clause with finite grammatical status, typically supporting tense or modal distinctions and clause independence. Has is finite in she has arrived. source-5532e2d7078060 source-445532eb0f5c35 source-773e3d2df84661 source-beec0c93fa3794

concepts.title: Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation
concepts.definition: A verb phrase can contain a lexical verb with one or more auxiliaries. English auxiliaries have an ordered relationship and select the form of the next verb. Do-support supplies auxiliary do where a neutral question or negative needs an auxiliary and no suitable one is already present.

glossary.definition: Use of auxiliary do in constructions such as relevant questions, negatives or emphasis.
glossary.example: Did she leave?

glossary.definition: A reversal of normal subject–auxiliary order in the relevant construction.
glossary.example: She has arrived becomes Has she arrived?

concepts.searchText: gv5-d05-m02 Verb-phrase order, do-support, questions and negation D H gv5-topic-d05-c04 gv5-topic-d05-c09 A verb phrase can contain a lexical verb with one or more auxiliaries. English auxiliaries have an ordered relationship and select the form of the next verb. Do-support supplies auxiliary do where a neutral question or negative needs an auxiliary and no suitable one is already present. Begin with an existing auxiliary. She is working becomes Is she working? and She is not working. The finite auxiliary moves before the subject in this yes–no question, and not follows that auxiliary in the negative. With a modal, the same basic pattern gives Can she swim? and She cannot swim. The lexical verb does not move to the front by itself in an ordinary present-day neutral question. Be can also invert directly when it links a subject with a description: Is she ready? Do not automatically add do simply because there is only one written verb. For an ordinary lexical verb without another auxiliary, use do, does or did: Do they work here? Does she work here? Did she work here? The lexical verb returns to its plain form because the auxiliary carries the relevant finite contrast. Negatives follow the same arrangement: They do not work here; she did not work here. Do can occur both as auxiliary and lexical verb: Do they do laboratory work? A neutral affirmative subject question ordinarily needs no added do: Who wrote the report? Object questions do use it when needed: Who did they invite? Emphatic contexts can produce different patterns. The common auxiliary order is modal, perfect have, progressive be, passive be and lexical verb. Each item selects what immediately follows: have selects a past participle; progressive be selects an -ing form; passive be selects a past participle. Thus may have been waiting is interpretable through nested selections rather than a memorised label alone. Longer combinations can be grammatical but cumbersome, so choose a simpler wording where it preserves meaning. Questions invert the first finite auxiliary only: Has she been waiting? Negation normally follows that same first auxiliary. Contractions join forms in writing and speech: is not/isn’t, do not/don’t, I am/I’m and they have/they’ve. Their suitability depends on register, audience and emphasis; formal writing does not have one universal grammatical ban on them. The spelling ’s can mean is or has, and ’d can mean had or would; the surrounding pattern resolves ambiguity where possible. Auxiliary and lexical have show regional and constructional variation, including Have you got a pen? and Do you have a pen? Neutral be normally avoids do-support in finite questions, but imperatives such as Do be careful and Don’t be late show that do and be are not universally incompatible. finite auxiliary + subject + remaining verb phrase Has she been waiting? inverts only the first finite auxiliary. do/does/did + subject + plain lexical verb Did the learners finish? uses did, leaving finish plain. Does your brother repair bicycles? Does carries the present third-person contrast; repair remains plain. The visitors have not been waiting long. Not follows finite have; been and waiting retain the selected forms. Do be patient while the file loads. Emphatic imperative do can occur with be; this is a special construction, not an ordinary neutral yes–no question. Who phoned the office? Who did the office phone? Both are grammatical. Who is subject in the first and object in the second, so the ordinary question structures differ. Do is not added mechanically to every question. A neutral subject question such as Who arrived? and a be-question such as Are they ready? already have their appropriate structures. Did she went to the archive? Did she go to the archive? Did carries the finite past contrast; the following lexical verb is plain. Does she is ready? Intended: a neutral present question. Is she ready? Ordinary finite be inverts without do-support in this question. do-support Use of auxiliary do in constructions such as relevant questions, negatives or emphasis. Did she leave? inversion A reversal of normal subject–auxiliary order in the relevant construction. She has arrived becomes Has she arrived? source-773e3d2df84661 source-beec0c93fa3794 source-5532e2d7078060 source-445532eb0f5c35 source-f36cfc25889ed4

concepts.title: Valency, objects, predicative complements and sentence patterns
concepts.definition: Verb valency concerns the participants and complement patterns associated with a verb use. Transitive uses have an object; intransitive uses do not. Linking and complex-transitive patterns contain predicative complements that describe a subject or object rather than introduce another independent participant.

glossary.definition: The argument and complement pattern associated with a lexical use, with counting conventions stated by the analysis.
glossary.example: Give can occur with giver, recipient and thing given.

glossary.definition: An expression describing or identifying a subject or object.
glossary.example: They found the room empty.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d05-m03 Valency, objects, predicative complements and sentence patterns D H L gv5-topic-d05-c05 gv5-topic-d05-c06 Verb valency concerns the participants and complement patterns associated with a verb use. Transitive uses have an object; intransitive uses do not. Linking and complex-transitive patterns contain predicative complements that describe a subject or object rather than introduce another independent participant. Compare The child laughed with The child opened the box. Laughed is intransitive here; opened is transitive and has the box as direct object. This is a grammatical pattern distinction, not simply a distinction between physical actions and states. She owns a bicycle contains a direct object even though owning is not a momentary action. Conversely, The glass broke has a subject undergoing a change without a direct object. Identify grammatical function from the structure and the particular verb use. Some verbs allow more than one pattern: She is reading and She is reading a novel are both possible. A ditransitive pattern contains two objects: The tutor gave the learner a booklet. The learner is the indirect object and a booklet the direct object. In The tutor gave a booklet to the learner, this course calls to the learner a prepositional complement rather than a second noun-phrase object. Some traditional accounts extend indirect object more broadly, so compare the stated analysis before treating a terminology difference as a grammatical fault. A linking pattern relates a subject to a description or identity: The learner seemed tired; Leena became a doctor. Tired and a doctor are predicative complements. Complex-transitive patterns add a complement describing the object: The panel considered the plan practical; They appointed Leena coordinator. The second complement is not an indirect object receiving a separate thing. Other verbs require a location complement: Put the folder on the shelf. On the shelf completes the placement pattern; merely saying Put the folder normally leaves the instruction incomplete. Complements can therefore be noun phrases, adjective phrases, prepositional phrases or clauses, depending on the verb. Optional adjuncts add circumstances: She read the report yesterday. Distinguishing optionality from the verb’s meaning requirements needs more than a single deletion test. The verb’s lexical meaning and construction jointly determine which pattern is available. Explain normally takes a content object with a to-phrase for the listener: explain the rule to me, not explain me the rule in the broad edited standard used here. Tell allows tell me the rule, illustrating a genuine lexical difference rather than a universal conversion rule between two-object and prepositional patterns. Valency counts may include the subject as an argument in linguistic descriptions; a classroom list of objects often counts something different. Day 13 develops hierarchical parsing and diagnostic tests. Avoid defining every object as a person physically receiving an action or every complement as an adjective after be. S + V; S + V + O; S + V + subject complement The guests laughed; the guests opened the gate; the guests seemed tired. S + V + indirect object + direct object; S + V + object + object complement She gave him a key; they painted the gate blue. The lecturer sent the students a reading list. The students and a reading list are the two noun-phrase objects in this use. The committee found the explanation unconvincing. Explanation is object; unconvincing is a complement describing it, not an adverb modifying found. Please put the parcel beside the desk. The placement verb selects a locative complement; beside the desk states the required destination. The tutor gave Lina a booklet. The tutor called Lina resourceful. Both are grammatical. The first has two objects; the second has an object plus a description of that object. The same lexical verb can have transitive and intransitive uses. She is eating does not become ungrammatical merely because eat can also take an object in She is eating an apple. Please explain me the procedure. Broad edited standard requested. Please explain the procedure to me. Explain and tell do not share every complement pattern. Intended: the plan was impractical. They judged the plan impractically. They judged the plan impractical. For the stated judgement about the plan, impractical is a predicative adjective describing the object. Impractically could instead describe a manner of judging in a different context, which is not the intended meaning here. valency The argument and complement pattern associated with a lexical use, with counting conventions stated by the analysis. Give can occur with giver, recipient and thing given. predicative complement An expression describing or identifying a subject or object. They found the room empty. source-22086aff3a3fbc source-d8d773260d5fa1 source-d6af2eef369812 source-15b65ce5c1b751 source-58353073c867f7

concepts.title: Alternations, dynamic meanings and states
concepts.definition: Dynamic meanings present events, activities or changes; stative meanings present situations such as knowledge or possession without an internal activity sequence. An ergative alternation relates a transitive use with an intransitive use in which the affected object becomes the subject, as The wind opened the door and The door opened. Its intransitive partner is active, rather than a passive construction.

glossary.definition: A situation construed as a state rather than an unfolding activity or event.
glossary.example: She knows the answer.

glossary.definition: A transitive/intransitive pairing in which the transitive object corresponds to the intransitive subject.
glossary.example: The heat melted the ice; the ice melted.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d05-m04 Alternations, dynamic meanings and states D L P gv5-topic-d05-c07 gv5-topic-d05-c08 Dynamic meanings present events, activities or changes; stative meanings present situations such as knowledge or possession without an internal activity sequence. An ergative alternation relates a transitive use with an intransitive use in which the affected object becomes the subject, as The wind opened the door and The door opened. Its intransitive partner is active, rather than a passive construction. A dynamic use can involve a deliberate action, such as writing a note, or an uncontrolled event, such as a branch falling. A stative use describes a situation such as knowing the answer, owning a bicycle or resembling a parent. This distinction concerns how a meaning is presented, not whether the real world changes over a lifetime. A person can own a bicycle only temporarily, but ownership can still be described as a state. Begin by interpreting the particular sentence rather than assigning an unchanging dynamic or stative label to the dictionary spelling. Several verbs have different senses with different patterns. I think the plan is useful states an opinion; I am thinking about the plan presents mental activity. She has a bicycle expresses possession; she is having lunch describes an activity. The soup tastes salty describes its perceived quality; the cook is tasting the soup describes an action. Progressive forms are more typical of dynamic uses, but the relationship is not an absolute prohibition. A speaker can present temporary behaviour with be: He is being unusually quiet. Future lessons develop the semantic choices among simple, progressive and perfect constructions. In an ergative alternation, the affected participant appears as object in one clause and subject in another: The heat melted the wax; the wax melted. The second clause is active intransitive, not passive: it has no passive be plus participle construction. The subject need not be a conscious doer, so defining every subject as the actor produces a false analysis. Not all transitive verbs permit this alternation: The courier delivered the parcel does not yield The parcel delivered with the ordinary completed-delivery meaning. Whether an alternation is available is a lexical and constructional fact to learn. Progressive stative uses can be marked by register, temporary construal or evolving convention. I’m loving the new course is common informal evaluative English; that does not license an ordinary factual I’m knowing the answer in every context. Conversely, a temporary context can make a progressive natural with a verb otherwise often labelled stative, as The repairs are costing more than expected. Ergative is also used in wider linguistic typology for case and alignment systems. The English teaching label here refers only to the illustrated causative/inchoative alternation; it does not claim that English has a general ergative case system. Day 19 revisits alternation alongside voice. causing subject + transitive verb + affected object ↔ affected subject + intransitive verb The wind opened the gate ↔ The gate opened. same spelling + different lexical sense → different aspect possibilities Think as opinion contrasts with think as ongoing consideration. The falling branch broke the window. The window broke. The affected window is object in the transitive use and subject in the intransitive use. She has two bicycles, but she is having lunch now. Possession and eating lunch are different senses of have. The repairs are costing the club more than expected. The progressive presents an ongoing developing financial consequence; a blanket stative ban would be misleading. The technician opened the door. The door opened. Both are active clauses. The second leaves the cause unstated through an intransitive alternation rather than a passive transformation. A lexical spelling does not fix one aspect class across all senses. The cook is tasting the sauce is an ordinary dynamic use even though The sauce tastes sweet describes a state. For the ordinary knowledge-state meaning: I am knowing the answer. I know the answer. The simple form is the normal neutral expression of this knowledge state. Intended ordinary delivery meaning: The parcel delivered at noon. The courier delivered the parcel at noon. Deliver does not permit this intended subject alternation merely because some change-of-state verbs do; a passive with was delivered is another possible structure. stative meaning A situation construed as a state rather than an unfolding activity or event. She knows the answer. ergative alternation A transitive/intransitive pairing in which the transitive object corresponds to the intransitive subject. The heat melted the ice; the ice melted. source-1dcf9da383e052 source-f0dab5a2a68798 source-22086aff3a3fbc source-445532eb0f5c35

concepts.title: Present simple: tense, time and a speaker’s general view
concepts.definition: The present simple is a finite present-tense construction without progressive or perfect marking. It commonly presents states, habits and generalisations; present tense does not restrict its reference to this instant.

glossary.definition: A grammatical verb distinction associated with temporal viewpoint.
glossary.example: works contrasts with worked.

glossary.definition: A way of presenting an event’s internal temporal organisation.
glossary.example: is working views activity in progress.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d06-m01 Present simple: tense, time and a speaker’s general view D E gv5-topic-d06-c01 gv5-topic-d06-c05 gv5-topic-d06-c06 gv5-topic-d06-c08 The present simple is a finite present-tense construction without progressive or perfect marking. It commonly presents states, habits and generalisations; present tense does not restrict its reference to this instant. Begin with a distinction between a form and the time you mean. In Sara checks the filters every Friday, checks is present tense, but the sentence describes a routine across many Fridays. In Sara knows the building, knows describes a state that holds now without claiming it is permanent. Use the base form with I, you, we and they: they check. With a third-person singular subject, add the appropriate ending: she checks, he watches, the pump carries water. Be has its own forms am, is and are. Have becomes has; do becomes does. Read the complete subject before choosing the form. For ordinary lexical verbs, make a negative with do not or does not followed by the base form: The sensor does not work. Make a question by placing do or does before the subject: Does the sensor work? The ending belongs to does, so does not works duplicates the marking. With be, use The sensor is not ready and Is the sensor ready?, without added do. Frequency expressions such as often and every week help communicate a habit, but they are clues to meaning, not switches that automatically force one construction. A routine can be temporary and still be presented as a routine. Present simple also supports instructions, demonstrations, commentaries and conventional summaries of texts: First you loosen the screw; the article argues for repair. These uses need not describe timeless truths. Context can even give a present form future reference, as in The inspection begins tomorrow, or past narrative reference, as in So I open the door and there is the missing parcel. Learn these as established uses of a grammatical form rather than extra inflected tenses. In formal prose, maintain a clear viewpoint, while allowing a justified change when moving from a past event to a continuing consequence. Aspect concerns how a situation is viewed internally; tense locates a grammatical viewpoint relative to a reference time. Many grammatical accounts recognise present and past as English’s two inflectional tenses, while classroom accounts often organise twelve tense-aspect patterns. These descriptions count different things and need not conflict if the terminology is explicit. Simple does not mean easy or short. A simple-present verb can occur in a highly embedded sentence. Present-tense form does not certify factual truth: The moon consists of cheese is grammatically formed but factually false. Grammatical analysis and evaluating a claim are separate tasks. subject + base/-s form A present simple affirmative with ordinary lexical verbs. does/do + subject + base?; subject + does/do not + base Question and negative forms; only the auxiliary carries present agreement. The clinic opens at eight on weekdays. Opens presents a regular schedule; clinic is third-person singular. Does this code identify the customer or the order? Does precedes this code; identify remains the base form. The report describes the leak that damaged the store last winter. Describes gives a current textual summary; damaged locates a different, past event. Both tenses are justified. Rafi repairs bicycles. Rafi is repairing a bicycle. Both grammatical: A characterises his work or habit; B presents an activity as in progress. Present forms can refer beyond present time: The workshop starts on Monday. Do not infer the event time from the verb ending alone. The machine do not start. The machine does not start. Singular machine selects does; start stays base. Is she knows the route? Does she know the route? An ordinary lexical know forms this simple-present question with does, not be. Tense A grammatical verb distinction associated with temporal viewpoint. works contrasts with worked. Aspect A way of presenting an event’s internal temporal organisation. is working views activity in progress. source-c84bd5cbd02264 source-5532e2d7078060

concepts.title: Present progressive: activity, temporary patterns and changing states
concepts.definition: The present progressive, also called present continuous, consists of present be plus an -ing form and normally presents a situation as ongoing, temporary, developing or arranged.

glossary.definition: A construction that views a situation as ongoing or developing.
glossary.example: The queue is growing.

glossary.definition: A meaning describing a state rather than an unfolding activity.
glossary.example: She knows the answer.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d06-m02 Present progressive: activity, temporary patterns and changing states D E gv5-topic-d06-c02 gv5-topic-d06-c05 gv5-topic-d06-c06 The present progressive, also called present continuous, consists of present be plus an -ing form and normally presents a situation as ongoing, temporary, developing or arranged. Build this construction with am, is or are and the -ing form: I am checking; the technician is checking; the technicians are checking. Keep both parts. The technician checking the meter is not a complete ordinary declarative clause on its own. Add not after be for a negative, and move be before the subject for a question: Is the technician checking the meter? The main activity does not need to be happening at precisely the second of speech. I am reading a long biography can remain true while you stop to eat. The relevant interval is understood from context. Compare a general description with a current arrangement: We use the upstairs room on Fridays describes a routine; We are using the upstairs room this month presents a temporary pattern. Neither form guarantees permanence or a fixed duration. Progressive constructions also describe change: The river is rising. With always, they can convey a speaker’s reaction to repeated events: She is always finding useful shortcuts can express admiration, while He is always losing receipts can express irritation. The emotional evaluation comes from the context and wording, not from a compulsory negative meaning in always. Verb meaning matters. Know and belong normally resist a progressive interpretation in their ordinary state senses: I know the password; the keys belong to Maya. Other verbs change interpretation: I think the estimate is low expresses an opinion, while I am thinking about the estimate presents mental activity. We have a small office describes possession; We are having a meeting describes an event. Avoid learning an absolute blacklist of spellings. Ask which sense is being used and whether the construction invites an activity, temporary behaviour or developing experience. A progressive viewpoint does not itself assert that an event reaches its endpoint. The team is building a bridge does not entail that a bridge will be completed. The same construction can combine with repeated events, as in The phone is ringing every few minutes: a sequence of bounded rings forms an ongoing temporary pattern. Some innovative or expressive progressive statives are established in informal use, while other combinations remain unusual. Describe them by sense, register and communicative purpose rather than assuming that every unfamiliar -ing form is either universally wrong or universally interchangeable with the simple. am/is/are + -ing Progressive affirmative. am/is/are + not + -ing; Am/Is/Are + subject + -ing? Negation and subject–auxiliary inversion. I am sorting the photographs at the moment. Am + sorting presents current activity. The library is staying open later during revision week. A repeated temporary arrangement can take progressive marking. The director is being unusually patient while we test the equipment. Being presents temporary behaviour, not a permanent identification. The soup tastes smoky. The chef is tasting the soup. Both grammatical: the first reports a perceived quality; the second presents deliberate sampling. An -ing ending is not enough to identify a progressive: Swimming helps me relax contains an -ing clause as subject, without progressive be. They are repair the roof. They are repairing the roof. Progressive be selects an -ing form. We are having three laptops in the cupboard. We have three laptops in the cupboard. The intended possession sense normally uses simple have; having a meeting has a different sense. Progressive A construction that views a situation as ongoing or developing. The queue is growing. Stative interpretation A meaning describing a state rather than an unfolding activity. She knows the answer. source-2bc25481c69832 source-f0dab5a2a68798

concepts.title: Present perfect: experience, results and time extending to now
concepts.definition: The present perfect combines present have with a past participle, connecting a prior situation with a present reference point. Its uses include experience, present results and situations continuing to now.

glossary.definition: The verb form selected by perfect have and used in other constructions.
glossary.example: written in has written.

glossary.definition: The viewpoint against which an event is temporally interpreted.
glossary.example: Now is the viewpoint in has arrived.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d06-m03 Present perfect: experience, results and time extending to now D E gv5-topic-d06-c03 gv5-topic-d06-c05 gv5-topic-d06-c07 The present perfect combines present have with a past participle, connecting a prior situation with a present reference point. Its uses include experience, present results and situations continuing to now. Use have or has followed by the past participle: I have finished; she has written; the files have arrived. Regular participles often end in -ed, but irregular ones must be learnt: written, seen, gone, taken. Make negatives with have not or has not and questions by moving have or has before the subject: Has the courier arrived? Do not add does. The construction looks back from now. We have received the parcel can announce a result relevant to a present conversation, while We received it at ten yesterday locates an event at a finished past time. For experience, present perfect places an event somewhere in a period leading up to now: I have visited that museum twice. It need not identify the exact dates. For continuing states, it can link a past beginning with now: I have known Amal for six years. For a current tally, I have checked twelve forms today counts completed checks within a relevant period treated as open. Today can also accompany simple past when the speaker treats the relevant opportunity or activity as finished. The temporal interpretation must be read from the situation, rather than assigning one automatic construction to a time word. A definite finished-past adverbial locating the same event normally conflicts with present perfect in standard usage: I have sent it yesterday should be I sent it yesterday. However, the mere presence of a date does not create an error: I have lived here since 2019 is standard, because 2019 marks the beginning of a continuing interval. A past date inside another clause can also coexist with present perfect. British English often uses present perfect with just, already and yet where American English also readily uses simple past. These are established patterns of variation, not evidence of inferior grammar. Present relevance is a useful teaching description but cannot mean that every past event whose consequences matter must take present perfect. A writer can say The factory closed in 2020, so employment is still low. Likewise, perfect marking does not always assert a completed activity: I have lived here for years can describe continued residence. Separate the event, its reference interval and the speaker’s current purpose. In a formal account, explicitly dated historical events normally take past forms, while a present assessment may use perfect to summarise the evidence accumulated so far. Changes in form should track these distinctions. have/has + past participle Present perfect; have is finite and the participle is non-finite. Have/Has + subject + past participle? A perfect question requires inversion of have, without do-support. The committee has published its decision. A present announcement looks back to completed publication. Have you ever repaired a radio? Ever asks about experience up to now, without a specified occasion. I have kept every letter she sent during her first year abroad. Have kept has a present viewpoint; sent locates the earlier letter-writing in its own past interval. We have owned this flat for ten years. We owned that flat for ten years. Both grammatical: A normally includes continued ownership; B presents a completed past ownership period. Simple past with just/already/yet is common standard American usage. Specify the editorial convention when a task contrasts regional defaults. He has wrote the address. He has written the address. Perfect have selects the past participle written. Did you have finished? Have you finished? The intended present-perfect question inverts have rather than adding did. Past participle The verb form selected by perfect have and used in other constructions. written in has written. Reference time The viewpoint against which an event is temporally interpreted. Now is the viewpoint in has arrived. source-ca6ab50c9fe853 source-c1a93519194932 source-8cf60a1688508e

concepts.title: Present perfect progressive and cumulative application
concepts.definition: The present perfect progressive consists of have/has been plus an -ing form. It presents activity over a period connected to now, including recent activity whose traces are still evident.

glossary.definition: Perfect have plus progressive be, presenting prior/continuing activity.
glossary.example: They have been discussing the design.

glossary.definition: The length of time over which a situation holds or develops.
glossary.example: for three hours

concepts.searchText: gv5-d06-m04 Present perfect progressive and cumulative application D E gv5-topic-d06-c04 gv5-topic-d06-c05 gv5-topic-d06-c07 gv5-topic-d06-c09 The present perfect progressive consists of have/has been plus an -ing form. It presents activity over a period connected to now, including recent activity whose traces are still evident. Build the form in order: have or has, then been, then the activity in its -ing form. We have been repairing the fence. For a negative, place not after have: We have not been repairing it. For a question, invert the first auxiliary: Have you been repairing it? Been is the participle of be selected by perfect have, while repairing is selected by progressive be. This order follows the grammar of the verb phrase you studied on Day 5. A long verb phrase still needs only its first auxiliary to carry present agreement. Use the construction to foreground duration or process: I have been preparing the accounts all morning. The work may continue, or it may have just stopped. If a colleague arrives to find ledgers everywhere, the same sentence can explain the present evidence without claiming that you are still working. Compare I have prepared three statements, which foregrounds a completed tally, with I have been preparing statements, which foregrounds the activity. The simple and progressive perfect can overlap: She has worked here for years and She has been working here for years can both describe current employment. Count the events and check the verb sense before choosing. A single arrival is normally expressed as The parcel has arrived, rather than has been arriving; a repeated pattern can make The parcels have been arriving all morning natural. A continuing state such as knowing a person normally uses perfect simple: I have known her since school. For duration, for introduces a length of time and since a starting point. Neither word automatically requires progressive aspect. I have been ill for a week is perfect simple with a state, not a progressive form. Apply the whole first phase while reading a present-time paragraph. Identify noun-phrase heads before selecting has or have; distinguish a determiner from a pronoun; track what it or they refers to; then analyse the auxiliary chain and intended time. This is cumulative grammatical reasoning, not a separate tense trick. In Today the volunteers are sorting books; they have already labelled two shelves, volunteers controls are, they refers back clearly, sorting has progressive marking and have labelled supplies a completed result. A learner’s ability to recognise these forms should be checked separately from the ability to produce and explain an original paragraph. have/has + been + -ing Perfect progressive links a process to the present. How long + have/has + subject + been + -ing? Question foregrounding duration when the context establishes an ongoing/recent activity. She has been practising the introduction for an hour. The focus is duration of practice connected with now. Your sleeves are dusty. Have you been cleaning the shelves? Recent activity is inferred from present traces; it need not still be occurring. The volunteers have been checking labels, and each box now has a clear destination. Have agrees with volunteers; has agrees with each box. Activity leads to a present result. I have read the report. I have been reading the report. Both grammatical: A can present completed reading; B foregrounds the activity and does not itself confirm completion. A repeated series of short events can be progressive: Customers have been arriving since nine. The construction does not require one unbroken action. She has being waiting outside. She has been waiting outside. Perfect has selects participial been, not being. I have been knowing the porter for years. I have known the porter for years. Ordinary know as acquaintance resists progressive aspect. Perfect progressive Perfect have plus progressive be, presenting prior/continuing activity. They have been discussing the design. Duration The length of time over which a situation holds or develops. for three hours source-88d14ab6136199 source-aa53e406bdc491 source-5532e2d7078060

concepts.title: Past simple: completed events, states and narrative steps
concepts.definition: The past simple uses a finite past form and commonly locates events or states within a past frame. It can describe single events, sequences, repeated activities and past states.

glossary.definition: The temporal position from which a story is told.
glossary.example: A writer recounts yesterday’s visit using past forms.

glossary.definition: A question asking for the subject itself.
glossary.example: Who rang the bell?

concepts.searchText: gv5-d07-m01 Past simple: completed events, states and narrative steps D E gv5-topic-d07-c01 gv5-topic-d07-c05 gv5-topic-d07-c08 gv5-topic-d07-c09 The past simple uses a finite past form and commonly locates events or states within a past frame. It can describe single events, sequences, repeated activities and past states. To report a completed event, use the past form: The courier knocked. Regular forms normally add -ed; irregular forms include took, wrote, brought and left. A past form need not mention its date in the same sentence if the conversation already establishes when: Who moved the box? Mina moved it. Past simple can also describe a state: The office belonged to a local charity. Do not equate past tense with physical action. In a narrative, a sequence such as She unlocked the door, entered and switched on the light normally advances the story from one event to the next. Ordinary lexical verbs use did not + base in negatives and Did + subject + base in questions: They did not return; Did they return? Did carries the tense, so did returned duplicates past marking. Be instead uses was or were and inverts directly: Was the office open? It was not open. A subject question normally lacks added did: Who opened the gate? Compare Who did you meet?, where who is the object and you is the subject. Negation, emphasis or another structure can change the auxiliary pattern, so first identify what the question is asking. Past simple can cover a long period or a repeated routine: She worked there for twenty years; We walked to school every day. The length of an event does not by itself require progressive aspect. A finished past interval normally permits simple past even if its effects continue now: The bridge closed last month, and traffic is still diverted. A present consequence does not force present perfect. Conversely, a past form may express hypothetical distance rather than past time in a later lesson’s conditional construction. Meaning comes from the whole clause and context. In historical and biographical writing, establish dates and reference frames clearly. Past forms report events; present forms can evaluate a source that is available now: The expedition left in 1912; the diary describes its first week. Such a shift is justified, not a lapse in consistency. The historic present is another established narrative choice, but a beginner should maintain one narrative viewpoint until a reason for changing it is clear. Tense consistency means coherent relationships between viewpoints, rather than banning every different tense from one paragraph or assuming that each past verb moves the narrative clock forward. subject + past form Past simple affirmative. did not + base; Did + subject + base? Ordinary lexical negatives and non-subject questions. The assistant locked the cabinet at six. Locked locates a completed event in a specified past interval. Who brought the spare battery? Who is the subject, so this affirmative subject question uses brought without did. The laboratory operated for thirty years before it closed. A long completed period can use simple past; duration does not compel progressive. Who called Nadia? Who did Nadia call? Both grammatical: who is subject in A, object in B. Word order and auxiliary choice reflect that difference. Past be has was/were rather than did be: Were the windows open? It also appears in irrealis constructions, which Day 18 develops. Did the visitors arrived? Did the visitors arrive? Use base arrive after did. The room did not be warm. The room was not warm. Ordinary past be negates directly in this intended state description. Narrative viewpoint The temporal position from which a story is told. A writer recounts yesterday’s visit using past forms. Subject question A question asking for the subject itself. Who rang the bell? source-007ab40b0b452f source-5532e2d7078060

concepts.title: Past progressive: background, overlap and an unfinished viewpoint
concepts.definition: The past progressive combines was/were with an -ing form, presenting a situation as in progress around a past reference time. It does not by itself establish completion or interruption.

glossary.definition: A situation framing the narrative’s foregrounded event.
glossary.example: It was raining when the delivery arrived.

glossary.definition: An internal view that need not assert an event’s completion.
glossary.example: was constructing the tower

concepts.searchText: gv5-d07-m02 Past progressive: background, overlap and an unfinished viewpoint D E gv5-topic-d07-c02 gv5-topic-d07-c05 gv5-topic-d07-c06 gv5-topic-d07-c08 The past progressive combines was/were with an -ing form, presenting a situation as in progress around a past reference time. It does not by itself establish completion or interruption. Use was or were + -ing: I was listening; they were listening. Add not after was/were for a negative and invert that auxiliary for a question: Were they listening? This construction lets a narrator place a reader inside an activity. At ten, the workers were loading the van says loading was in progress around ten. It does not itself tell us when the task started or finished. A past time expression is therefore compatible with progressive aspect. The slogan yesterday means simple past is too broad: Yesterday at ten, we were loading the van is grammatical. When one event occurs during another, progressive often supplies background while simple past introduces the event: I was checking the address when the taxi arrived. Calling this an interruption is convenient, but the arrival need not stop the checking. Two progressives can present overlap: While I was checking, Salma was packing. Two simple pasts can also describe concurrent completed activities: While I checked the address, Salma packed. These are different viewpoints, not competing versions where one must be an error. A question must specify the intended scene before it can demand a particular aspect. Progressive also supports temporary repeated past activity: During the renovation, we were meeting in the kitchen every morning. Compare We met in the kitchen every morning for an ordinary retrospective habit. The progressive can suggest an unfolding pattern with boundaries in the context. With always, a speaker may express an attitude to repetition: He was always volunteering for difficult jobs. Context may make this admiring rather than critical. State verbs retain sense-dependent restrictions. I knew the answer is the ordinary form for knowledge; I was thinking about the answer presents an active process. The so-called imperfective viewpoint shows an internal phase without asserting the whole event’s completion. She was crossing the road when I saw her does not guarantee that she reached the far side, though ordinary knowledge may suggest it. Do not confuse what the grammar entails with what a reader reasonably infers. Similarly, an achievement can receive a progressive reading when an event has an approach or repeated phases: The guests were arriving as the musicians tuned up. This does not make arrive an unrestricted substitute for every stative verb. Interpret the lexical meaning and the viewpoint together. was/were + -ing Past progressive affirmative. While + past progressive, past simple/progressive A common way to frame an overlapping situation, not a compulsory tense recipe. At sunrise, the team was unloading the truck. The narrator views unloading as in progress at sunrise. The radio was playing when the power failed. Was playing is background; failed marks a new event. The relation is supplied by context. Guests were arriving throughout the afternoon, while volunteers were directing them to the hall. Two overlapping repeated patterns are presented as ongoing. I wrote the email when the meeting ended. I was writing the email when the meeting ended. A normally presents writing as a complete event associated with the end; B places the meeting’s end during ongoing writing. A short event can occur in a progressive when viewed in development or repetition: A light was flashing. Duration is not a mechanical verb-type label. They was discussing the route. They were discussing the route. They selects were. Was she waited outside? Was she waiting outside? Past progressive be requires the -ing form waiting. Background A situation framing the narrative’s foregrounded event. It was raining when the delivery arrived. Imperfective viewpoint An internal view that need not assert an event’s completion. was constructing the tower source-37d1fb575c6adc source-f0dab5a2a68798

concepts.title: Past perfect and past perfect progressive: looking back from then
concepts.definition: The past perfect uses had plus a past participle to relate a prior situation to a past viewpoint. The past perfect progressive adds been + -ing to foreground a process or duration leading towards that viewpoint.

glossary.definition: A temporal relation in which one situation is earlier than a reference point.
glossary.example: The train had left before our arrival.

glossary.definition: Had been plus an -ing form, viewing earlier activity from then.
glossary.example: had been repairing

concepts.searchText: gv5-d07-m03 Past perfect and past perfect progressive: looking back from then D E gv5-topic-d07-c03 gv5-topic-d07-c04 gv5-topic-d07-c06 gv5-topic-d07-c08 gv5-topic-d07-c09 The past perfect uses had plus a past participle to relate a prior situation to a past viewpoint. The past perfect progressive adds been + -ing to foreground a process or duration leading towards that viewpoint. Imagine arriving at a workshop yesterday and finding it empty. The instructor had left tells the reader that the departure preceded your arrival. Had left is past perfect: had + the participle left. It looks back from a past viewpoint rather than directly from now. Make negatives with had not and questions with Had + subject: Had the instructor left? No separate did is needed. The reference point can appear in the same sentence, elsewhere in the story or in the shared conversation. It need not be a second event explicitly named after every perfect verb. Past perfect does more than put the earliest of two events in a special form. It can establish background information, report an earlier statement, or show that a plan changed: I had intended to stay, but the last train was leaving. Where before or after already establishes sequence, simple past may be sufficient: After she locked the room, she handed over the keys. Past perfect can still foreground completion: After she had locked the room, she handed over the keys. Do not mark every simple past before another past as wrong, or assume that past perfect cannot appear with dates. For activity leading towards a past viewpoint, use had been + -ing: We had been waiting for an hour when the caretaker arrived. The waiting may then stop or continue. It can also explain traces at a past moment: The pavement was wet because it had been raining. Rain might already have stopped. Compare had written three letters, a completed tally, with had been writing letters, an activity. With states such as knowing someone, ordinary past perfect simple is used: We had known each other for years. Since and for express starting point and duration; they do not compel progressive aspect. Analyse reference relationships before rewriting. In When the assistant arrived, the gate had closed, closing is earlier than arrival. In When the assistant arrived, the gate closed, the natural reading links closing with the arrival, though wider context can modify that interpretation. A transformation from one to the other may change the facts. Perfect marking also occurs in counterfactual constructions discussed later: If we had left earlier is an imagined past, not a historical claim that we actually left earlier. Keep time sequence, modality and the truth of a proposition distinct when interpreting a perfect form. had + past participle Prior situation viewed from a past reference point. had been + -ing Activity or duration leading up to a past viewpoint. By noon, the team had checked all the meters. The checks are completed by the past reference point noon. Had you been working there long when the building closed? Had been working asks about duration preceding the closure. The guide had promised a longer visit, but we left early because the weather worsened. The earlier promise is distinguished from the later departure; the promise does not guarantee fulfilment. She had repaired two chairs. She had been repairing chairs. A foregrounds a completed tally; B foregrounds activity and does not itself count finished chairs. Past perfect accepts definite past reference points: By 2018, the shop had closed. The restriction on present perfect with finished event times does not apply identically. Had she went home? Had she gone home? Perfect had selects the participle gone. He had been waited for an hour. He had been waiting for an hour. Progressive been selects waiting; the intended construction is active, not passive. Anteriority A temporal relation in which one situation is earlier than a reference point. The train had left before our arrival. Past perfect progressive Had been plus an -ing form, viewing earlier activity from then. had been repairing source-eecf7dafccbf50 source-b02fa179bf3088

concepts.title: Past habits, used to, habitual would and coherent reporting
concepts.definition: Used to + base describes a past habit or state contrasted with the present. Habitual would + base recalls repeated past events within an established past frame; it is distinct from other modal meanings of would.

glossary.definition: Would used for recurring past events within an established frame.
glossary.example: Every Friday he would call.

glossary.definition: Familiar through experience.
glossary.example: I am used to the noise.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d07-m04 Past habits, used to, habitual would and coherent reporting D E gv5-topic-d07-c05 gv5-topic-d07-c07 gv5-topic-d07-c08 gv5-topic-d07-c09 Used to + base describes a past habit or state contrasted with the present. Habitual would + base recalls repeated past events within an established past frame; it is distinct from other modal meanings of would. To describe an earlier routine, you can use simple past: We walked along the canal after school. Used to can explicitly contrast that routine with the present: We used to walk there, but the path is closed now. It also describes a past state: The yard used to belong to my grandparents. The form does not change with the person of the subject. In carefully edited questions and negatives, use Did you use to live here? and We did not use to live here. Spellings with used after did occur, but the uninflected use is this course’s formal editorial default. Once a past frame is established, would can recall typical events: During our summer visits, Grandfather would open the shop early and we would sweep the pavement. It need not imply a conditional promise. Ordinary continuing states usually take used to or simple past rather than habitual would: We used to own a small shop. Some repeated situations containing be can occur with habitual would when they mean something that repeatedly happened, such as On market days, the street would be crowded. The key is an established repeated-event reading, not a prohibition on the spelling be. Distinguish used to from be used to and get used to. I used to work nights describes an earlier habit. I am used to working nights means night work is familiar; to here is a preposition, so working follows it. I am getting used to working nights describes becoming accustomed. The similarity in sound conceals different structures. Avoid turning a whole story into would without first orienting the reader: outside a past frame, would can suggest a hypothetical outcome, a polite request or a future viewed from the past. Clear time framing prevents this ambiguity. When reporting history, preserve whether an event was asserted, remembered as a habit, merely planned or imagined. The phrase was going to open expresses a past intention, without proving that opening occurred. Used to normally implies a contrast with current circumstances, but it should not be used to invent a change that the evidence does not support. If a source simply records regular deliveries in 1990, simple past may be the most neutral choice. A reliable historical paragraph can combine simple past narrative, progressive background, perfect anteriority and habitual constructions when each serves a clear temporal or discourse function. used to + base; did not use to + base Past habit/state and the formal negative default. past frame + would + base A typical repeated past event, when context establishes the habitual reading. be/get used to + noun or -ing Being/becoming accustomed; not the same construction as used to + base. The station used to have a wooden roof. Used to describes a former state. When I was an apprentice, we would check the shutters every evening. The opening frame establishes habitual past events. I used to work alone, but I am now used to sharing the workshop. The first construction describes a former habit; the second describes current familiarity. She used to visit on Sundays. She would visit on Sundays during that winter. Both can describe repeated visits; used to more readily establishes the past contrast, while would relies on the supplied frame. Habitual would can describe repeated temporary states in context: On delivery days, the corridor would be full of boxes. It does not normally replace used to for an unchanging possession state. We are used to visit that library when we were children. We used to visit that library when we were children. A former habit uses used to + base, without are. She is used to work late now. She is used to working late now. In the accustomed construction, to is a preposition followed here by an -ing clause. Habitual would Would used for recurring past events within an established frame. Every Friday he would call. Accustomed Familiar through experience. I am used to the noise. source-b08f94d0abde7f source-f8ef51164863ad

concepts.title: Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints
concepts.definition: Perfect constructions relate a situation to a later reference point; progressive constructions present a situation from within its development. They can combine, and neither construction alone tells the whole story about completion or present consequences.

glossary.definition: The temporal viewpoint relative to which another situation is interpreted.
glossary.example: In By noon, we had finished, noon supplies a past reference point.

glossary.definition: The temporal character of a predicate, including whether it expresses an endpoint.
glossary.example: Write a letter supplies an endpoint more explicitly than write letters.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d08-m01 Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints D E K gv5-topic-d08-c01 gv5-topic-d08-c04 gv5-topic-d08-c09 Perfect constructions relate a situation to a later reference point; progressive constructions present a situation from within its development. They can combine, and neither construction alone tells the whole story about completion or present consequences. Compare The technician has repaired the pump with The technician has been repairing the pump. In the first, the repair is presented as an achieved event relevant now. In the second, attention falls on the activity over a recent interval. The second sentence does not by itself say whether the pump is now repaired. Form a perfect with have plus a past participle, and a progressive with be plus an -ing form. Their combination is have been repairing: been is the participle of be, and repairing carries the progressive meaning. With a past reference point, change the finite auxiliary to had. Interpret the whole expression, including the verb and its object. She has written three reports presents three completed products. She has been writing reports presents a process, perhaps repeatedly, without specifying how many were completed. A perfect simple can also describe a continuing state: We have owned this shop for years. A perfect progressive can describe an activity that has just stopped: You look exhausted; have you been carrying boxes? The visible exhaustion is evidence for recent activity; it does not prove the person is still carrying anything while the question is asked. The same contrast operates with a past viewpoint: By noon, they had repaired the roof presents the repair as achieved before noon, whereas They had been repairing the roof before the storm arrived describes earlier activity. A simple perfect does not necessarily promise a permanent result. The roof has been repaired does not rule out a new leak tomorrow. Conversely, ongoing activity can produce results without reaching an intended endpoint. Consider a wet floor after someone has been washing it. Ask separately whether an event occurred, whether its endpoint was reached, and which consequences the context makes relevant. Advanced analysis distinguishes grammatical aspect from the situation type expressed by the whole predicate. Write reports allows an open activity; write three reports supplies a countable endpoint. This interaction is sometimes called lexical aspect or situation aspect. Perfect progressive does not automatically mean a longer duration than perfect simple, nor is simple a guarantee of a short event. Both I have worked here for ten years and I have been working here for ten years can be appropriate; the latter puts greater attention on the activity or its continuing course. Translation and editing should preserve the intended viewpoint rather than mechanically substituting forms. have/has/had + past participle A perfect construction interpreted relative to now or another reference point. have/has/had + been + -ing Perfect and progressive meanings combine; completion must be inferred from the full context. The archivist has catalogued eighty letters. The stated total concerns completed cataloguing events. The archivist has been cataloguing letters all morning. The activity occupies a recent interval; the completed total is unspecified. The floor was slippery because someone had been washing it. Earlier washing explains a later past condition; washing need not still have been happening. I have read the chapter. I have been reading the chapter. Both are grammatical. The first normally presents completion of the chapter; the second highlights engagement in the activity and leaves completion open. An achievement verb can occur in a progressive when context supports repetition or an unfolding stage: The old engine has been stopping unexpectedly describes repeated stops, not one indefinitely extended instant. She has been wrote the conclusion. She has been writing the conclusion. After progressive been, use the -ing form; wrote is a past-tense form. They had been repaired the road before the rain; the intended subject is the repair crew. They had been repairing the road before the rain. The active perfect progressive requires repairing. They had repaired the road is another construction with a different presentation of completion. Reference point The temporal viewpoint relative to which another situation is interpreted. In By noon, we had finished, noon supplies a past reference point. Situation aspect The temporal character of a predicate, including whether it expresses an endpoint. Write a letter supplies an endpoint more explicitly than write letters. source-88d14ab6136199 source-a79546fdace5e0 source-ca6ab50c9fe853

concepts.title: States, actions, temporary interpretations and repetition
concepts.definition: Stative and dynamic describe interpretations of predicates. A stative reading presents a condition or relationship; a dynamic reading presents activity or change. Many verbs support more than one reading, and progressive compatibility depends on that reading and its context.

glossary.definition: A reading that presents a condition, perception, possession or relationship rather than an unfolding action.
glossary.example: Own the flat describes possession.

glossary.definition: A reading that presents action, development or change.
glossary.example: The surveyor is measuring the flat describes an activity.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d08-m02 States, actions, temporary interpretations and repetition D E K gv5-topic-d08-c02 gv5-topic-d08-c03 Stative and dynamic describe interpretations of predicates. A stative reading presents a condition or relationship; a dynamic reading presents activity or change. Many verbs support more than one reading, and progressive compatibility depends on that reading and its context.
