Use the simple form for ordinary possession, knowledge or belief: I have two sisters; We know the address; I believe the explanation. These describe conditions rather than actions unfolding before us. Merely adding at the moment does not make every state naturally progressive: I know the answer at the moment is ordinary English. The term stative is a useful tendency, not a permanent prohibition attached to a spelling. Compare We have a small kitchen, describing possession, with We are having lunch, describing an event. The verb is the same word, but its meaning and pattern change. Several familiar contrasts illustrate the importance of interpretation. I think the figures are wrong expresses an opinion; I am thinking about the figures describes a process of consideration. The soup tastes salty reports a perception; The cook is tasting the soup describes deliberate sampling. He is polite presents a characteristic; He is being unusually polite describes behaviour in the current situation. Progressive be is normally about conduct or a temporary presentation, not ordinary identity: She is being a dentist is not the normal way to state her profession. Read the complements and the situation before selecting a form. Some predicates permit more flexibility than a short classroom list suggests. I feel tired and I am feeling tired can both describe a current condition, with the progressive making its present or temporary character more prominent. Informal I am loving this concert presents enjoyment as an immediate experience; it is marked by context and register rather than automatically ungrammatical. Repeated brief events can also receive progressive interpretation: Someone has been tapping on the window. A progressive with always can express an evaluative view of repeated behaviour, as in He is always interrupting, without making annoyance an obligatory part of the grammar. Temporary does not define progressive, and permanent does not define simple. We are currently living with relatives can be progressive without a promise that the arrangement will soon end; I live with relatives is a neutral characterisation, even when the arrangement is temporary. A speaker chooses how to package the situation. Duration is another independent property: I have known her for thirty years is lengthy but normally simple. Where a creative advertisement or a special discourse uses a normally stative verb progressively, identify the intended interpretation and register. Do not extend that exceptional use to every context, and do not reject it solely because a memorised list says never. simple have + noun phrase Possession or another stative relationship, according to the noun and context. be + having/thinking/tasting + complement A dynamic interpretation such as experiencing, considering or deliberately sampling. The parcel weighs two kilograms. Weighs expresses a measured property; simple is ordinary. The assistant is weighing the parcel. Weighing describes an action performed on the parcel. I have been thinking about your suggestion, although I still think it needs revision. Thinking is a process; think expresses the opinion reached or held. Mina is helpful. Mina is being helpful. Both are grammatical: a characterisation contrasts with behaviour in the relevant situation. Some expressions allow simple and progressive state-like readings: I feel better and I am feeling better are both established. A learner should explain the viewpoint rather than force a universal ban. I am knowing the password, in an ordinary statement of current knowledge. I know the password. Ordinary know in this sense is stative and normally uses a simple construction. The owner is having three warehouses, meaning possession. The owner has three warehouses. Possession normally takes simple have. Having may be progressive in event meanings such as having a meeting. Stative interpretation A reading that presents a condition, perception, possession or relationship rather than an unfolding action. Own the flat describes possession. Dynamic interpretation A reading that presents action, development or change. The surveyor is measuring the flat describes an activity. source-f0dab5a2a68798 source-88d14ab6136199

concepts.title: Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints
concepts.definition: For normally introduces a duration, since a starting point in temporal uses, by a latest time or deadline, and until the endpoint of a continuing situation. These meanings guide interpretation but do not select one tense mechanically.

glossary.definition: The length of time for which a situation holds or an event continues.
glossary.example: For forty minutes expresses duration.

glossary.definition: The latest time allowed for an action or result.
glossary.example: Submit by noon gives a deadline.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d08-m03 Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints D E K gv5-topic-d08-c06 gv5-topic-d08-c07 For normally introduces a duration, since a starting point in temporal uses, by a latest time or deadline, and until the endpoint of a continuing situation. These meanings guide interpretation but do not select one tense mechanically. A duration answers How long? Use for with a measured interval: for twenty minutes, for a decade, for several weeks. A temporal starting point answers From when? Use since with a point or a clause locating that point: since Tuesday; since the office moved. Compare We have waited for an hour and We have waited since nine. Both can describe waiting that began earlier and continues now. Do not replace for with since merely because the sentence contains a perfect construction. The complement after the preposition determines which expression accurately represents the intended interval. For works with past, present and future reference: We waited for an hour yesterday; We have waited for an hour; We will stay for an hour. Since often combines with perfect constructions when measuring from an earlier point to a later viewpoint, but it is not exclusively a present-perfect signal. By 2022, she had worked here for five years is a past-perfect account, and She had been unwell since Monday measures to a past reference point. Since can also mean because: Since the gate was locked, we used another entrance gives a reason, not the beginning of a duration. By sets a latest acceptable or relevant time: Send the signed form by Friday means no later than Friday. Until presents continuation to an endpoint: Keep the original until Friday means retain it through the relevant interval. Negation changes the relationship: She did not sign until Friday locates the eventual signing no earlier than Friday in the ordinary reading. Compare She had signed by Friday, which presents signing as achieved at or before that point. These are not stylistic substitutes. Preserve the intended deadline, continuation or delay when correcting a sentence, and do not change a promise into a mere prediction. The temporal expression and the verb viewpoint contribute separate information. By six, I will have finished explicitly looks back from a future boundary; I will finish by six can communicate the same deadline without a perfect form. A finished date is compatible with past perfect when another past viewpoint is established: At the review in May, we discovered that the permit had expired in March. The finished-time restriction on ordinary present perfect does not ban past perfect with dates. Until and by can also have non-temporal uses, and temporal clauses require their own analysis. Describe the particular construction rather than converting a useful contrast into an unrestricted word-substitution rule. for + duration; since + starting point Measure an interval or locate its beginning. by + deadline; continuing situation + until + endpoint Distinguish completion no later than a time from continuation up to a time. The exhibition remained open until six. Remaining open continues to the stated endpoint. The driver must return the vehicle by six. The return is due no later than the deadline. By last winter, the family had lived there for a decade. A past viewpoint licenses a past perfect with a duration; no present continuation is asserted. We will work until Friday. We will finish by Friday. Both are grammatical. Work continues to the endpoint in A; completion occurs no later than the deadline in B. Since is not always temporal: Since you have the key, please open the cabinet means because. Its presence does not itself require a perfect construction in every clause. The queue has stretched outside since two hours. The queue has stretched outside for two hours. Two hours is a duration, not a starting point. The customer has waited for Monday; intended meaning: the waiting began on Monday. The customer has waited since Monday. Use since to identify the intended starting point. Wait for Monday has a different meaning: await that day. Duration The length of time for which a situation holds or an event continues. For forty minutes expresses duration. Deadline The latest time allowed for an action or result. Submit by noon gives a deadline. source-aa53e406bdc491 source-ef3e812f3fb26c source-44c9bc31ab8158 source-eecf7dafccbf50

concepts.title: Already, yet, just, lately and recently in context
concepts.definition: Time adverbs help locate events and convey expectations. Their meaning, position and compatibility with a construction must be interpreted together; they are not automatic tense selectors.

glossary.definition: An adverb that contributes information about time or temporal relationships.
glossary.example: Recently locates an event in a recent period.

glossary.definition: The portion of an expression over which a word’s meaning operates.
glossary.example: Just in I just need help can limit what is needed rather than locate the need in time.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d08-m04 Already, yet, just, lately and recently in context D E K gv5-topic-d08-c05 gv5-topic-d08-c08 Time adverbs help locate events and convey expectations. Their meaning, position and compatibility with a construction must be interpreted together; they are not automatic tense selectors. Already commonly presents a situation as existing or achieved by a relevant point, often earlier than expected: The bus has already left. Yet in a question asks whether an expected event has happened by now: Has the bus left yet? In a negative, The bus has not left yet indicates that departure has not happened up to the reference point and commonly remains expected. Just can mean a very short time ago: The bus has just left. These adverbs add interpretation to the clause; the verb form still needs to fit the broader temporal setting. Position changes emphasis and can affect naturalness. Already and recent-event just commonly follow the first auxiliary: We have already checked the locks; We had just finished. Already can also appear at the end: Have you finished already? often expresses surprise. Yet commonly appears at the end of a question or negative statement. It also has other established uses: a yet more difficult problem means a still more difficult one, while The result is promising yet uncertain uses yet as a coordinator. Identify the use before applying a rule learned for temporal questions. Lately normally refers to a recent interval, especially with states, repeated events or continuing activity: I have been sleeping badly lately. Recently can do that too, but also readily locates a single completed past event: We inspected the lift recently. A precise finished time such as last Tuesday normally selects a past construction for the event: We inspected it last Tuesday. British English frequently uses present perfect for recent events with just, already and yet; American English also commonly uses simple past in such contexts: Did you send it yet? This is an established regional alternative, not evidence of carelessness. Adverbs carry scope and pragmatic expectations as well as clock time. Just may mean only, exactly, or emphatic merely, so I just need a signature need not describe a very recent need. Already does not require perfect aspect: We already know the answer is simple present. Special contexts permit negated already, for example a question challenging a presupposition, so not usually is more accurate than never. An assessment must give sufficient context when two tense-aspect forms or adverb positions remain defensible. Where the task asks for the most natural expression in a stated register, explain that criterion rather than marking every less frequent alternative as structurally impossible. have + already/just + past participle Common position for already and recent-event just with a perfect auxiliary. question/negative clause + yet Common temporal use concerning an expected event up to the relevant point. The catering team has already prepared the room. Already indicates completion by now, perhaps earlier than expected. Has the repair team tested the alarm yet? Yet asks whether the expected test has occurred up to now. The manager recently visited the site, but maintenance has been irregular lately. Recently locates one visit; lately frames a recent interval of maintenance. I have just called the laboratory. I just called the laboratory. Both can report a recent call. The perfect is frequent in British English; simple past is also an established American English choice when no finished date is stated. These words have other senses and constructions: yet can mean nevertheless or still in combinations, and just can mean only. Analyse the actual use instead of applying a tense rule to the spelling alone. She has already sent the application yet, meaning it is complete. She has already sent the application. Ordinary affirmative completion uses already; temporal yet does not naturally add this meaning at the end. They have just wrote to the supplier. They have just written to the supplier. The perfect auxiliary requires written; just does not alter the required verb form. Temporal adverb An adverb that contributes information about time or temporal relationships. Recently locates an event in a recent period. Scope The portion of an expression over which a word’s meaning operates. Just in I just need help can limit what is needed rather than locate the need in time. source-35b08d956b9e9f source-b95713ca5526fb source-af1f4261eb75b1 source-37be5609b5c953 source-9761ab1edb0e5f source-8cf60a1688508e

concepts.title: Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment
concepts.definition: English uses several constructions to refer to future time. Will and shall are modal auxiliaries, while be going to combines a form of be with going to and a plain-form verb. Their meanings overlap but their use depends on the speaker’s purpose and viewpoint.

glossary.definition: Interpretation concerning a time later than the relevant viewpoint.
glossary.example: The ferry leaves tomorrow uses a present form for future reference.

glossary.definition: The degree to which a speaker undertakes or supports a proposition or action.
glossary.example: I promise I will help makes a commitment.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d09-m01 Will, shall and be going to: prediction, intention and commitment D E gv5-topic-d09-c01 gv5-topic-d09-c02 gv5-topic-d09-c05 English uses several constructions to refer to future time. Will and shall are modal auxiliaries, while be going to combines a form of be with going to and a plain-form verb. Their meanings overlap but their use depends on the speaker’s purpose and viewpoint. Use will with the base form: The driver will return. Add not for a negative, The driver will not return, and put will before the subject for a question, Will the driver return? The contraction will not becomes won’t. A promise, prediction, offer and decision can all use will: I will return your call; The river will rise; I will carry that bag; I will take the early train. The word future identifies the intended time, not a guarantee that a prediction is factually certain. Identify what the speaker is doing as well as when the event is expected. Be going to commonly highlights an intention already held or evidence visible now: We are going to replace the roof; Those loose tiles are going to fall. Its finite be agrees with the subject: I am, she is, they are. Make negatives and questions with be: They are not going to move; Are they going to move? Going to need not describe physical travel. Compare They are going to the clinic, where to the clinic is a destination phrase, with They are going to inspect the clinic, where inspect belongs to the intended action. Keep these different structures separate. Will and going to often both fit the same future event, with a different conversational emphasis. I will call her can make a decision or commitment; I am going to call her can state a prior intention. A context may favour one without making the other structurally impossible. Shall with I and we remains possible for formal future reference, especially in British English, though will is more widespread. Shall I open the window? offers action or asks what the speaker should do; Shall we begin? proposes joint action. These questions have a modal purpose, not merely an announcement of future time. Future expressions interact with modality: they present expectations, intentions and commitments from the speaker’s current standpoint. A spontaneous decision is a useful context for teaching will, not a test proving that will can never describe an earlier plan. Likewise, visible evidence favours going to without banning will from evidence-based predictions. Informal gonna represents a reduced pronunciation of going to in the intended-action construction; it is unsuitable as a default spelling in formal reports. A careful transformation preserves the communicative force: changing I promise I will help into I may help weakens commitment, even though both clauses are grammatically formed. will/shall + base form Modal future reference; interpretation may include prediction, willingness, decision or commitment. am/is/are + going to + base form Common intention or evidence-based prediction construction. I will send the receipt tonight. Will can express the speaker’s commitment to a future action. The panels are going to fall if the supports move again. The prediction is presented in relation to an existing dangerous condition. Shall we discuss the draft before lunch? This is a proposal about joint action, an established British use of shall. I will ask the curator. I am going to ask the curator. Both are grammatical. The first may announce a decision or promise; the second commonly foregrounds an intention already held. The form going to can describe destination rather than intention: We are going to Lahore contains a destination phrase. Do not analyse every occurrence as a future auxiliary construction. She will to send the figures. She will send the figures. Core modal will selects a base form without infinitival to. They is going to review the application. They are going to review the application. Finite be agrees with plural they; going to does not replace agreement. Future reference Interpretation concerning a time later than the relevant viewpoint. The ferry leaves tomorrow uses a present form for future reference. Commitment The degree to which a speaker undertakes or supports a proposition or action. I promise I will help makes a commitment. source-e48023284fa4ed source-60a104cf8211b4

concepts.title: Present forms for arrangements, timetables and future facts
concepts.definition: Present-tense forms can have future reference. Present progressive commonly presents an arrangement, while present simple commonly presents a timetable, fixed schedule or future fact. These uses rely on context and do not create new verb endings.

glossary.definition: A plan presented as settled or organised in the relevant context.
glossary.example: I am seeing the dentist tomorrow presents an appointment.

glossary.definition: A use of present simple to report a scheduled event.
glossary.example: The museum reopens on Tuesday.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d09-m02 Present forms for arrangements, timetables and future facts D E gv5-topic-d09-c03 Present-tense forms can have future reference. Present progressive commonly presents an arrangement, while present simple commonly presents a timetable, fixed schedule or future fact. These uses rely on context and do not create new verb endings. Consider The interview starts at nine tomorrow. Starts is present tense, but tomorrow places the event in the future. A timetable, programme or scheduled event commonly uses present simple: The coach departs at six; The term ends in July. Negative and question formation stays the same as for present simple: The coach does not stop here; When does the coach leave? Be also keeps its ordinary present forms: The ceremony is on Friday. A future time expression helps the reader recognise the intended reference; without one, the surrounding conversation may supply it. Present progressive commonly presents an arrangement: I am meeting the surveyor at ten; We are moving next month. An arrangement can involve other people, a booking, or the speaker’s own settled plan; another person need not appear in every sentence. Build it with finite be and an -ing form, and form questions and negatives with be. Compare Are you meeting the surveyor? and You are not meeting the surveyor today. The construction presents the action as planned or arranged from the present viewpoint. It does not assert that the future is immune to cancellation or disruption. A single event can be described as schedule or arrangement: The delegation leaves on Thursday and The delegation is leaving on Thursday may both be natural. The first can report its programme, while the second draws attention to an arrangement in progress. An objective item should not ask for the only correct form when both readings are available. Present progressive is not the ordinary neutral choice for a bare speculative prediction such as a distant weather guess; will or going to normally serves that purpose. Context may support marked conversational uses, so explain the default rather than invent an absolute prohibition. Form and temporal interpretation are distinct levels of analysis. A present-tense schedule can concern one future occasion, not an eternal habit: The eclipse begins at 14:10 tomorrow. Present simple also occurs in subordinate time clauses such as when the train arrives, a structure studied in the final module of this day. Do not confuse that syntactic pattern with a main-clause timetable merely because both verbs look present. When editing, preserve the source of certainty: The timetable says the train leaves at six explicitly attributes the schedule; I expect the train will leave at six expresses an expectation. Both are grammatical but make different claims. present simple + future context Commonly presents a schedule, fixed programme or future fact. am/is/are + -ing + future context Commonly presents a current arrangement for a later event. The examination begins at nine on Monday. Present begins reports an official schedule with future reference. We are interviewing two applicants tomorrow. The progressive presents an arrangement already established. The timetable says the last bus departs at 22:15, but we are leaving earlier. A stated schedule and a personal arrangement coexist without requiring identical constructions. The team flies to Muscat on Tuesday. The team is flying to Muscat on Tuesday. Both are grammatical in suitable contexts: programme or schedule versus current arrangement. Present simple can refer to a unique future fact, not only a repeated timetable: Her birthday falls on a Sunday next year. Do not require repetition where the context supplies a fixed future occurrence. What time the train does leave tomorrow? What time does the train leave tomorrow? A direct present-simple question places does before the subject. We are meet the architect tomorrow. We are meeting the architect tomorrow. A progressive arrangement requires the -ing form after are. Arrangement A plan presented as settled or organised in the relevant context. I am seeing the dentist tomorrow presents an appointment. Timetable use A use of present simple to report a scheduled event. The museum reopens on Tuesday. source-fd380d90a9dc1a source-5ca26d5f6101ad

concepts.title: Future progressive, perfect and perfect progressive
concepts.definition: Future-oriented auxiliary combinations can present an activity in progress at a later point, a situation viewed from that later point, or the duration of earlier activity up to it. The construction and the temporal context must both be considered.

glossary.definition: A conventional label for will/shall have plus past participle with a common later-retrospective interpretation.
glossary.example: By dusk, we will have arrived.

glossary.definition: A will/shall be + -ing construction commonly used for activity at a future point.
glossary.example: At dusk, we will be travelling.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d09-m03 Future progressive, perfect and perfect progressive D E gv5-topic-d09-c04 Future-oriented auxiliary combinations can present an activity in progress at a later point, a situation viewed from that later point, or the duration of earlier activity up to it. The construction and the temporal context must both be considered. Future progressive uses will be plus an -ing form: At ten tomorrow, I will be interviewing applicants. It places the reader within an activity expected to be in progress at that point. Negate the finite modal, I will not be interviewing, and invert it in a question, Will you be interviewing? Do not change be to is after will: a modal selects the base form. This construction can also present an expected course of events, as in I will be passing the pharmacy, so I can collect the prescription. The intended time is supplied by the context. Future perfect uses will have plus a past participle: By ten, I will have interviewed three applicants. It looks back from a future boundary and presents what will then be completed or true. A state can also extend to that boundary: By June, she will have known him for ten years. Future perfect progressive uses will have been plus -ing: By ten, I will have been interviewing for two hours. It draws attention to activity and its duration up to the future viewpoint. It does not necessarily state that the activity stops at that boundary. Compare completed quantity with continuing course: By Friday, we will have inspected six bridges reports a completed total; By Friday, we will have been inspecting bridges for a week highlights the period of activity. Neither construction alone guarantees the whole project is finished unless the project’s limits are stated. With some predicates, both future perfect simple and progressive are defensible: In May, I will have worked here for five years and I will have been working here for five years can describe the same employment period. A question must specify the desired construction or intended focus if it is to have a unique answer. The so-called future perfect is a combination of modal will and perfect have; its conventional label describes a common temporal interpretation. A deadline does not automatically make it obligatory: We will finish by Friday is ordinary English beside We will have finished by Friday. The latter explicitly adopts a later retrospective viewpoint. Progressive restrictions also remain sensitive to meaning: will have known is the ordinary form for a continuing knowledge state, while will have been considering describes a process. Avoid mechanically generating all possible auxiliaries for every verb. A formally elaborate sequence can be semantically awkward even when the component endings appear in the correct order. will + be + -ing An activity viewed as in progress at a future point. will + have + past participle A retrospective view from a future point. will + have + been + -ing Activity and its duration leading up to a future viewpoint. At this time tomorrow, the committee will be hearing evidence. The future point lies within the projected hearing activity. By the end of tomorrow, the committee will have heard six witnesses. The future perfect presents a completed count by the boundary. By noon, the volunteers will have been working for four hours. The perfect progressive foregrounds duration without necessarily ending the work at noon. We will finish the audit by Friday. We will have finished the audit by Friday. Both are grammatical promises or predictions in context. The second explicitly views completion retrospectively from the future boundary. Some duration predicates allow either simple or progressive perfect forms with overlapping reference: will have lived and will have been living can both measure a period up to a future point. A duration phrase does not alone select one uniquely. At eleven, they will are discussing the report. At eleven, they will be discussing the report. After will, use base be, not are. By July, she will have wrote three chapters. By July, she will have written three chapters. Perfect have selects the past participle written, not past-tense wrote. Future perfect A conventional label for will/shall have plus past participle with a common later-retrospective interpretation. By dusk, we will have arrived. Future progressive A will/shall be + -ing construction commonly used for activity at a future point. At dusk, we will be travelling. source-1a60bd11a38c5f source-265ff20b9cb0da source-8c254b0b44ea03 source-88d14ab6136199

concepts.title: Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints
concepts.definition: Future reference is relative to a viewpoint. A past narrator can describe an event that was still future then. Time and condition clauses follow their own patterns, and reporting may shift a viewpoint without requiring every verb to become the same tense.

glossary.definition: A change to a past-oriented form when reporting from a past viewpoint.
glossary.example: Will return can be reported as would return.

glossary.definition: A later situation presented from an earlier past viewpoint.
glossary.example: She knew she would leave the next morning.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d09-m04 Future in the past, time clauses and consistent viewpoints D E gv5-topic-d09-c06 gv5-topic-d09-c07 gv5-topic-d09-c08 Future reference is relative to a viewpoint. A past narrator can describe an event that was still future then. Time and condition clauses follow their own patterns, and reporting may shift a viewpoint without requiring every verb to become the same tense. Future in the past describes a later situation viewed from an earlier past point: On Monday, she said she would return on Tuesday. Would is the usual backshifted counterpart of will in this reporting pattern. Past forms of other future expressions are also available: She was going to return; She was leaving the next day. The construction does not by itself establish that the planned return happened. Add the outcome if it matters: She was going to return, but the storm cancelled the ferry. Identify the earlier viewpoint before deciding what a later expression means. In ordinary future time clauses, use a present form rather than future will: I will call when the meeting ends; We will leave after she has signed the register. Present perfect in the time clause can emphasise prior completion. The main clause can still contain will. Similar teaching patterns occur with open conditions: If the weather improves, we will leave. This guidance concerns a particular subordinate use; it is not a ban on will after the spelling when or if. Distinguish a clause locating an event from an embedded question asking what time an event will occur. Compare I will phone when the train arrives with I do not know when the train will arrive. The first when-clause supplies the time of phoning; the second is an embedded interrogative complement expressing an unknown arrival time. Will is appropriate in that embedded question. In an if-clause, will may express willingness or insistence rather than simple future location: If you will hold the ladder, I can carry the tools. This means if you are willing to hold it. A later lesson develops the full range of conditional meanings. Do not remove a modal mechanically when it carries such an independent meaning. Backshift is common after past reporting verbs, but reporting also considers whether a statement remains true or a plan remains future at report time. She said the office opens at nine can retain a currently valid schedule; She said the office opened at nine adopts a past reporting viewpoint without necessarily asserting that the schedule changed. Choose and explain the viewpoint. Temporal consistency is coherence, not uniform tense: Yesterday I learned that the exhibition opens next month contains a past discovery and a future schedule. Time and place words also depend on the reporting context. Use explicit dates when a transformation would otherwise make tomorrow, next week or the following day ambiguous. past reporting verb + would + base form A common future-in-the-past reporting pattern. main future clause + when/after/until + present form Common future time-clause pattern; not the pattern of every clause introduced by the same word. The witness said she would send the photographs the next day. Would presents sending as future from the earlier statement. We will publish the report after the auditors have checked the figures. The present perfect time clause presents checking as prior to publication. I cannot tell you when the report will appear. The when-clause is an embedded question, so future will is appropriate. I will wait when she arrives. I wonder when she will arrive. Both are grammatical. The first clause locates waiting; the second expresses an unknown arrival time. Will can occur in a conditional clause with willingness: If you will sign here, we can proceed. Explain its modal meaning instead of teaching never use will after if. I will contact you when the ordinary scheduled meeting will end. I will contact you when the ordinary scheduled meeting ends. For this intended future time-clause reading, present ends is the neutral pattern. She said she would to bring the original documents. She said she would bring the original documents. Modal would takes the base form without to. Backshift A change to a past-oriented form when reporting from a past viewpoint. Will return can be reported as would return. Future in the past A later situation presented from an earlier past viewpoint. She knew she would leave the next morning. source-901e6631c7d82a source-9fcbdb35005527 source-89176b529bbc02 source-ef3e812f3fb26c

concepts.title: Person, number and the structure of the subject
concepts.definition: Subject–verb agreement is the correspondence between a subject’s grammatical person and number and the finite verb forms that show those distinctions. Agreement depends on structure and interpretation, not simply the nearest visible noun.

glossary.definition: The subject expression whose person and number determine a relevant finite verb form.
glossary.example: The form of have in The files have arrived is controlled by files.

glossary.definition: Reference other than to the speaker as I/we or the addressee as you.
glossary.example: She and the committee are third-person expressions.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d10-m01 Person, number and the structure of the subject B D P gv5-topic-d10-c01 gv5-topic-d10-c02 Subject–verb agreement is the correspondence between a subject’s grammatical person and number and the finite verb forms that show those distinctions. Agreement depends on structure and interpretation, not simply the nearest visible noun. Compare The guard checks the door and The guards check the door. In present simple, an ordinary lexical verb normally adds -s with a third-person singular subject. I and you use the base form even when referring to one person: I check; you check. Be has am, is and are in the present and was and were in the past. Have has has with a third-person singular subject. Most other past-tense verbs do not change for number: the guard checked and the guards checked. Agreement therefore does not mean adding an ending to every verb in every sentence. Find the complete subject and its head, the central noun in an ordinary noun phrase. In The condition of the external walls is worrying, condition is the head; walls occurs inside a modifying of-phrase. A relative clause or parenthetical phrase also does not normally replace that head as agreement controller: The folder that contains the photographs is missing. When auxiliaries occur, the finite auxiliary carries the relevant agreement: The folders have been moved. Do not alter moved to make it plural. Subject identification is a structural analysis; merely crossing out every prepositional phrase can remove information needed to interpret the sentence. Coordination with and normally creates a plural subject: The clerk and the porter are waiting. An accompanying phrase such as together with, as well as or along with is not ordinary subject coordination: The clerk, together with two porters, is waiting. If two descriptions identify a single individual, the subject may be interpreted as singular: The founder and treasurer is one person in this organisation. If the founder and the treasurer are different people, use plural agreement. Articles and context help identify the intended reference; do not decide identity from a memorised surface formula alone. The familiar head-noun rule is a reliable starting point for ordinary noun phrases, not an exhaustive theory of English agreement. Quantificational constructions, collectives and notional readings require further analysis in later modules. Distinguish genuine coordination from a phrase merely mentioning another person. Also distinguish the subject from an object or predicative complement: The main difficulty is the missing records does not make records the subject of is in this ordinary clause. Where the number or identity of coordinated referents is unclear, rewriting to make that identity explicit is often better than defending an ambiguous choice by rule recital. third-person singular subject + present verb in -s A common present-simple agreement pattern; be and some verbs have special forms. head noun + modifying phrase + finite verb In an ordinary noun phrase, the modifier does not replace the head as agreement controller. The colour of the curtains has faded. Singular colour controls has; curtains is inside the of-phrase. The inspectors have been reviewing the photographs. Plural inspectors controls finite have; the other forms do not acquire plural endings. The director, as well as two advisers, is attending. As well as introduces an accompanying phrase rather than a second coordinated subject. The designer and the builder are different people. The designer and builder is available; in this project both roles are performed by the same person. Both can be grammatical with the explicitly different reference. Agreement follows the intended subject organisation and identity. Most lexical past-tense forms do not distinguish singular and plural: The driver arrived and The drivers arrived. Do not manufacture a plural past ending. The schedule of public hearings are available. The schedule of public hearings is available. Singular schedule is the ordinary subject head. The manager, along with two assistants, have signed the letter. The manager, along with two assistants, has signed the letter. The accompanying phrase does not ordinarily make the singular subject plural. Agreement controller The subject expression whose person and number determine a relevant finite verb form. The form of have in The files have arrived is controlled by files. Third person Reference other than to the speaker as I/we or the addressee as you. She and the committee are third-person expressions. source-287989cd31ff3a source-dee460d0260d9b source-5532e2d7078060

concepts.title: Collectives, indefinite pronouns and competing agreement cues
concepts.definition: English agreement can reflect grammatical form, the meaning of a group, or proximity in particular coordinated patterns. Collective nouns and quantifying pronouns require qualified guidance about reference, register and established regional variation.

glossary.definition: Agreement influenced by the interpreted number or organisation of the referent.
glossary.example: Three years is a long time treats the period as one measure.

glossary.definition: An unintended agreement choice influenced by a nearby noun that is not the ordinary controller.
glossary.example: In The quality of the copies are poor, plural copies attracts are away from singular quality.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d10-m02 Collectives, indefinite pronouns and competing agreement cues B D P gv5-topic-d10-c03 gv5-topic-d10-c04 gv5-topic-d10-c10 English agreement can reflect grammatical form, the meaning of a group, or proximity in particular coordinated patterns. Collective nouns and quantifying pronouns require qualified guidance about reference, register and established regional variation. A collective noun names a group: team, government, committee, family. In British English, singular agreement commonly presents the group as a unit, while plural agreement can present its members: The committee has issued its report; The committee have changed their minds. American English more often uses singular agreement with these ordinary group nouns, especially when acting as one unit. This is a broad convention rather than a claim that every collective has identical behaviour in all varieties. Police ordinarily takes plural agreement: The police are investigating. Do not transfer a rule for committee blindly to police. Indefinite pronouns and determiners form different patterns. Everyone, somebody, nobody and each ordinarily take singular finite agreement: Everyone is ready; Each of the rooms has a window. Both, few, many and several are plural in their ordinary countable uses. Singular they can refer back to a grammatically singular person expression without changing its verb: Everyone has their own ticket. All, some and most depend on what is quantified: Some of the water is contaminated; Some of the wells are contaminated. None can also support singular or plural interpretation, particularly when referring to a countable set. Neither of and either of commonly take singular agreement in careful formal prose: Neither of the plans is suitable. Plural agreement occurs in established conversational usage, especially when a plural noun phrase is close to the verb; a register-sensitive exercise should identify its target convention. With subjects joined by or or nor, a common editing convention makes the verb agree with the nearer coordinated part: Neither the director nor the assistants are available; Neither the assistants nor the director is available. Recast awkward combinations, particularly those mixing person, rather than assuming proximity alone makes every possible sequence elegant or uncontroversial. Notional agreement follows an interpretation of number rather than surface form alone. Proximity agreement follows a nearby eligible expression in constructions where that convention is established. These should not be confused with accidental agreement attraction, as in The cost of the repairs are high in ordinary formal prose. Collective pronouns should make the intended unit-versus-members reference clear across the passage, though a writer may deliberately shift perspective when context supports it. None of is especially unsuitable for an absolute always-singular rule: authoritative usage accounts describe both singular and plural verbs. State the desired register and interpretation when a task depends on the choice. collective noun + singular/plural verb Possible unit/member contrast, particularly in British English; conventions vary by noun and variety. each/everyone + singular verb; both/several + plural verb Ordinary agreement of these specific quantifying expressions. Everyone has their own locker. Everyone takes singular has; singular their provides inclusive personal reference. The committee have not agreed among themselves. British plural agreement foregrounds the members’ differing views. Neither the secretary nor the assistants are free. Plural are follows the common nearer-subject convention, with assistants nearest. The team is improving its public image. The team are arguing among themselves. Both are established in British English. The first treats the team as a unit; the second foregrounds members. None of the candidates is available and None of the candidates are available both occur in standard usage; guidance differs in its preferred register. A trustworthy answer key must not reject one without an explicitly justified criterion. Each of the windows have a safety lock. Each of the windows has a safety lock. Each is the singular quantifying subject. The police is questioning the witnesses, in ordinary standard usage. The police are questioning the witnesses. Police ordinarily has plural agreement, unlike many singular-form collective nouns. Notional agreement Agreement influenced by the interpreted number or organisation of the referent. Three years is a long time treats the period as one measure. Agreement attraction An unintended agreement choice influenced by a nearby noun that is not the ordinary controller. In The quality of the copies are poor, plural copies attracts are away from singular quality. source-fa438d9714f33f source-5e8743788d0639 source-8cf60a1688508e source-b558c0e9b89f1a source-a49c734e279b1a source-6d5d2fbb856026 source-dee460d0260d9b

concepts.title: Relative clauses, inversion and existential constructions
concepts.definition: Each clause has its own agreement relationships. Relative-clause verbs follow the intended antecedent, and inversion can place a subject after an auxiliary or verb. Existential there introduces an additional construction whose formal agreement commonly follows its postverbal noun phrase.

glossary.definition: The expression to which a referring item, such as a relative pronoun, is related.
glossary.example: Drivers is the antecedent of who in drivers who work nights.

glossary.definition: A construction introducing the existence or presence of a situation or entity, often with dummy there.
glossary.example: There are two exits introduces the exits.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d10-m03 Relative clauses, inversion and existential constructions B D P gv5-topic-d10-c05 gv5-topic-d10-c06 Each clause has its own agreement relationships. Relative-clause verbs follow the intended antecedent, and inversion can place a subject after an auxiliary or verb. Existential there introduces an additional construction whose formal agreement commonly follows its postverbal noun phrase. In The drivers who work nights receive an allowance, the relative pronoun who refers to plural drivers, so its clause uses work. The main clause also has plural drivers as its subject. In The driver who works nights receives an allowance, both relevant subjects are singular. Analyse the clauses separately; the verb of one clause does not mechanically control the other. A longer subject can contain a plural antecedent inside a singular outer phrase: One of the drivers who work nights receives an allowance. Outer one controls receives, while drivers supplies the usual antecedent for who work nights. Expressions such as one of those people who usually select a relative clause describing the plural group: She is one of those people who notice everything. A relative attached specifically to the individual one has a different interpretation and may take a singular verb. The only one of the drivers who has a permit normally singles out the one permitted individual. Do not decide all relative attachments from the presence of the word only alone. Where the intended scope is important, make it explicit: She is the only driver who has a permit; among the permitted drivers, she is the only one available. In questions, the subject often follows a finite auxiliary: Are the documents ready? Does the document contain a signature? In locative inversion, the subject can follow the lexical verb: On the shelf were three sealed boxes. Find boxes before selecting were. Existential There is a problem and There are several problems conventionally match the form of be to the postverbal noun phrase in careful formal writing. Contracted There’s several problems is widespread in conversation; revise it to There are several problems for the stated formal convention without presenting all conversational occurrences as evidence of ignorance. Grammatical frameworks differ in analysing existential there: many modern accounts treat it as a dummy subject, while traditional teaching calls the following noun phrase the real subject. Both descriptions can support the same practical formal-agreement guidance if terminology is made explicit. Not every word after a verb is a subject: compare On the desk lies the report with The clerk filed the report. Negative inversion also leaves agreement with the actual subject: Never have the records been so clear. Parsing requires clause structure and reference, not an instruction to choose whichever noun is closest to the finite verb. antecedent + who/which/that + agreeing finite verb Relative-clause agreement reflects the intended antecedent. There is + singular noun phrase; There are + plural noun phrase Common careful formal pattern in existential be-constructions. One of the books that explain the method is missing. Books controls explain in the relative; one controls main-clause is. Near the entrance stand two noticeboards. Plural noticeboards follows stand and is its subject. There are three reasons why the proposal needs revision. The plural postverbal noun phrase selects are in this formal existential construction. The only driver who has a permit is waiting. One of the drivers who have permits is waiting. Both are grammatical with different relative-clause antecedents: driver versus drivers. The main waiting subject is singular in each. Informal contracted there’s commonly introduces plural associates. For formal prose, use the agreed full form; distinguish register-sensitive editing from a universal ban on attested conversational grammar. One of the students who lives on this corridor are absent; intended meaning: several students live on the corridor, one is absent. One of the students who live on this corridor is absent. The stated context makes students the relative antecedent and one the main agreement controller. Beside the printer was two unopened boxes. Beside the printer were two unopened boxes. Plural boxes is the postverbal subject in the locative inversion. Antecedent The expression to which a referring item, such as a relative pronoun, is related. Drivers is the antecedent of who in drivers who work nights. Existential construction A construction introducing the existence or presence of a situation or entity, often with dummy there. There are two exits introduces the exits. source-b04555eae72042 source-dee460d0260d9b source-f36cfc25889ed4 source-43b3913aec1e91

concepts.title: Quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking forms
concepts.definition: Agreement with a quantity depends on what is measured or counted and how it is construed. The spelling of a noun, a percentage or a numerical expression does not by itself establish the number required in every use.

glossary.definition: A grammatical singular/plural distinction that is not always predictable from real-world quantity or spelling.
glossary.example: News has singular agreement despite final -s.

glossary.definition: A construction whose purpose is to express an amount or number of referents.
glossary.example: A number of complaints means several complaints.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d10-m04 Quantities, measures, titles and plural-looking forms B D P gv5-topic-d10-c07 gv5-topic-d10-c08 gv5-topic-d10-c09 Agreement with a quantity depends on what is measured or counted and how it is construed. The spelling of a noun, a percentage or a numerical expression does not by itself establish the number required in every use. Some nouns look plural but take singular agreement in their ordinary meanings: The news is encouraging; Mathematics is compulsory. Other nouns normally take plural agreement: The trousers are wet; The scissors are blunt. A pair of scissors is different because pair is singular: This pair of scissors is blunt. Series has the same spelling in singular and plural: This series is useful; These two series are useful. Use determiners, meaning and a learner’s dictionary where the form alone is misleading. Do not add an invented singular police or a plural news merely to make the ending match a simplified pattern. Fractions and percentages commonly follow the number interpretation of the of-complement: Half of the water is gone; Half of the bottles are empty; Twenty per cent of the applicants were absent. A percentage without an explicit complement still requires context: Twenty per cent is a substantial share treats the proportion as one amount. If the complement is a collective, its own possible unit/member readings can matter. A number of applications have arrived is a conventional plural quantifying construction; The number of applications has risen treats number as the quantity being discussed. These are different structures, not contradictory examples of the same rule. A measure phrase can denote one amount: Ten kilometres is too far to walk today; Three years is a long wait. Plural agreement remains natural when separate units or their passage are in view: Three years have passed. A title naming one work commonly receives singular agreement despite plural words inside it: Great Expectations is a novel. This does not make every plural proper name singular in every variety; team and organisation names may follow collective conventions. Mathematical statements also have conventional forms, such as Two plus two is four, but do not infer a universal rule for every coordinated numerical expression. Meaning can change the number behaviour of the same spelling. Statistics is difficult can name a discipline; The statistics are misleading refers to numerical figures. Politics can name an academic topic or a person’s views, with differing agreement: Her politics are well known. Such contrasts illustrate why grammatical number, semantic quantity and lexical convention must be distinguished. A rigid instruction to make the verb agree with the nearest noun fails with The number of files is increasing; an unrestricted head-noun slogan also needs qualification for quantifying A number of files are missing. Analyse the construction, then state which meaning and editorial convention support the chosen verb. fraction/percentage + of + mass/plural count noun Agreement commonly follows the relevant mass or count interpretation. a number of + plural noun + plural verb; the number of + plural noun + singular verb Conventional contrast between quantifying several items and discussing their number. Half of the evidence is missing. Evidence is a mass noun here, so the fraction has singular agreement. Half of the witnesses are waiting outside. The fraction ranges over plural people, giving plural agreement. The number of reports has doubled, although a number of reports are still incomplete. The first subject concerns a figure; the second quantifies several reports. Statistics is part of the syllabus. The statistics are based on last year’s survey. Both are grammatical: the discipline differs from a set of figures. A period can be construed as one measure or as separate years whose passage is asserted: Three years is a long time and Three years have passed are both ordinary. Do not impose singular agreement on every expression containing a measurement. The news are more encouraging this week. The news is more encouraging this week. News ordinarily takes singular agreement despite its ending. This series of seminars are intended for new staff. This series of seminars is intended for new staff. This identifies a singular series; seminars is inside its modifier. Grammatical number A grammatical singular/plural distinction that is not always predictable from real-world quantity or spelling. News has singular agreement despite final -s. Quantificational construction A construction whose purpose is to express an amount or number of referents. A number of complaints means several complaints. source-dee460d0260d9b source-5e8743788d0639 source-e7e8a77edf2a6f source-0a1520eb3317af source-3e42fea943d431

concepts.title: Adjective classes, positions and ordered description
concepts.definition: An adjective is a word class with characteristic modifying and predicative uses; no single meaning or suffix identifies every member.

glossary.definition: Modifying a noun from within its noun phrase.
glossary.example: a careful editor

glossary.definition: A complement that characterises a subject or object.
glossary.example: The editor seems careful.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d11-m01 Adjective classes, positions and ordered description F K gv5-topic-d11-c01 gv5-topic-d11-c02 An adjective is a word class with characteristic modifying and predicative uses; no single meaning or suffix identifies every member. Start with a small contrast: a quiet room and the room is quiet. In the first, quiet is an attributive modifier inside a noun phrase. In the second, it is a predicative complement after a linking verb. Both describe the room, but they occupy different structures. An adjective phrase may contain only its head adjective or additional words: very quiet, unusually quiet for this building. A noun used before another noun remains a noun in many modern analyses: stone in a stone wall names material but need not become an adjective merely because it modifies wall. Adjectives express many kinds of meaning: evaluative excellent, descriptive narrow, relational medical and participial exhausted or convincing. Participial adjectives resemble verb participles; the surrounding construction helps identify their use. The exhausted nurse needed rest describes a state, while the long shift had exhausted the nurse describes an event with a verbal object. Attributive adjective order reflects meaning: an attractive small wooden desk is neutral, with opinion before size before material. This is a preference shaped by meaning and grouping, not a mechanical requirement to fill nine slots before every noun. Some adjectives favour particular positions. Asleep normally follows a linking verb: the child is asleep, rather than an asleep child. Mere normally precedes its noun: a mere suggestion. Available can occur before or after the noun with small differences of information structure: available rooms and the rooms available tonight. Complements also affect placement: a room suitable for interviews is more natural than a suitable for interviews room. Adjectives ending in -ed often describe the affected experiencer, and -ing forms often describe a cause, but bored/boring is a lexical pattern to learn rather than a universal translation rule. Postpositive means positioned after the head noun within its phrase, not necessarily a separate clause complement. Something useful has postpositive useful; the proposal is useful has a predicative complement. Coordination and adjective grouping affect punctuation: a clear, practical explanation permits two independent evaluations, whereas a dark green folder contains a colour unit. Order can change deliberately when a writer contrasts wooden rather than metal or old rather than new. Relational adjectives may acquire evaluative readings: a very political decision concerns degree of political motivation, although the same adjective can classify a subject without degree. Analyse the actual sense and structure together. determiner + adjective phrase + noun A common attributive pattern: an unusually quiet room. subject + linking verb + adjective phrase A predicative description: the room became quiet. The soup is hot. Hot is an adjective functioning as subject complement, not an object. They reserved a small circular table. Size precedes shape in a neutral description. The documents available after the hearing included a revised timetable. Available after the hearing postmodifies documents within the subject noun phrase. The students were bored. The lecture was boring. Both are grammatical: bored describes the affected students; boring characterises what causes boredom. Position is lexical: asleep is normally predicative, while mere is normally attributive. An adjective's figurative or evaluative sense may be gradable even when its classifying sense is not. an asleep passenger a sleeping passenger / a passenger who is asleep Asleep normally does not occur attributively before a noun. The audience was very boring by the lecture. The audience was very bored by the lecture. The intended affected-experiencer reading needs bored; boring would describe an audience that caused boredom. attributive Modifying a noun from within its noun phrase. a careful editor predicative complement A complement that characterises a subject or object. The editor seems careful. source-605aba8561eab2 source-58353073c867f7 source-1a30fc7f658cdc

concepts.title: Degree, comparison and sense-dependent gradability
concepts.definition: Degree constructions locate a quality on a scale or compare it with a contextual standard; the scale depends on the adjective's sense.

glossary.definition: A modifier that lowers the degree asserted.
glossary.example: slightly warmer

glossary.definition: The contextual group within which a superlative is assessed.
glossary.example: the cheapest of these three tickets

concepts.searchText: gv5-d11-m02 Degree, comparison and sense-dependent gradability F K gv5-topic-d11-c03 gv5-topic-d11-c04 gv5-topic-d11-c05 gv5-topic-d11-c09 Degree constructions locate a quality on a scale or compare it with a contextual standard; the scale depends on the adjective's sense. A gradable adjective can describe different amounts of a quality: fairly warm, very warm, warmer. A comparative relates two values or groups; a superlative identifies an extreme within a comparison set. Form is partly lexical. Short adjectives commonly take -er and -est, with spelling adjustments such as large/larger and happy/happier. Many longer adjectives use more and most. Good/better/best and bad/worse/worst are irregular. Do not add more to an already comparative form for an ordinary comparison: more colder duplicates the degree marking. Check a dictionary when a two-syllable adjective allows competing forms. Comparisons require a recoverable standard: this route is shorter than the coastal route. As ... as expresses equality against a standard; not as ... as denies that equality. A comparative clause may be reduced because repeated material is understood: the office is quieter than it was yesterday. When comparing quantities associated with different places, make the intended objects clear: the district's budget is smaller than the city's, rather than a budget being smaller than a city. A clause can itself supply an amount: our revenue is less than what the branch collected. Matching surface word classes is not a universal requirement. Intensifiers increase a degree, while downtoners reduce it: extremely helpful, rather difficult, slightly cheaper. Their compatibility differs: much cheaper, not normally very cheaper; absolutely impossible, rather than an ordinary scale reading of very impossible. Some adjectives have an endpoint meaning, such as complete meaning having all parts, but a related sense may allow comparison: a more complete account can mean one covering more information. Unique meaning the only example of its kind resists degree logically; unique meaning unusual can be graded in established usage. In precise formal work, choose a wording that makes the intended sense explicit. Comparison involves grammar and interpretation. One of the better applications selects from a relatively strong group; one of the best applications makes a stronger ranking claim. Neither pattern requires the other. The better of two is the traditional formal default, while the best of two is common in informal standard usage. Comparative complements may be phrases or clauses, and than me is an ordinary alternative to the explicit than I am when meaning permits it. A sentence such as Kim likes Noor more than Ali is ambiguous between people liked and people doing the liking; repeating a verb or object resolves the comparison rather than merely changing a pronoun form. more/less + adjective + than + standard Compare a quality using a recoverable standard. as + adjective + as + standard Express equality, with not as ... as expressing a lower degree. This path is narrower than the track beside the canal. Narrower marks one comparison; than introduces its standard. Her explanation was much clearer than mine. Much modifies a comparative; mine stands for my explanation. The revised estimate is higher than we expected it to be. The standard is supplied by a finite comparative clause with understood degree. one of the better answers one of the best answers Both grammatical: the second makes the stronger superlative claim. Formal prose often prefers the better of two; informal standard usage also has the best of two. Gradability belongs to a sense in context. A more complete account need not claim that a fully complete object becomes more than complete. This version is more clearer. This version is clearer. Ordinary comparison takes one comparative marker. The cost of the plan is lower than the other town. The cost of the plan is lower than that of the other town. The intended comparison is cost with cost, not cost with a town. downtoner A modifier that lowers the degree asserted. slightly warmer comparison set The contextual group within which a superlative is assessed. the cheapest of these three tickets source-8ddf38a0fd2628 source-930d01e686ac67 source-c9e3872504dda3

concepts.title: Adverb forms, phrases, placement and local scope
concepts.definition: An adverb phrase is headed by an adverb; it may modify an event, an adjective, another adverb, or a larger unit, depending on its use.

glossary.definition: A grammatical function expressing a circumstance or relation; several phrase types can fill it.
glossary.example: at dawn in We left at dawn

glossary.definition: The material over which a modifier or operator is interpreted.
glossary.example: not deliberately versus deliberately not

concepts.searchText: gv5-d11-m03 Adverb forms, phrases, placement and local scope F K gv5-topic-d11-c06 gv5-topic-d11-c07 An adverb phrase is headed by an adverb; it may modify an event, an adjective, another adverb, or a larger unit, depending on its use. Many manner adverbs have an adjective plus -ly form: careful becomes carefully. The ending is a useful clue, not a definition. Fast, hard and late can be adverbs without -ly; friendly and costly are commonly adjectives. Ask what construction the word participates in. She spoke calmly describes the speaking, whereas she seemed calm characterises the subject through a linking verb. A linking verb can also take a noun phrase or other complement, so this contrast should not become a claim that every word after be must be an adjective. The whole clause determines the relation. Adverbs can express manner, place, time, frequency and degree, among other meanings. An adverb phrase may contain its own modifier: very slowly, quite unexpectedly. Adverbials are functions, not a single word class: at noon is a prepositional phrase functioning as a time adjunct, while yesterday can do similar work as an adverb. Neutral frequency adverbs often precede a lexical verb, follow main-verb be, or follow the first auxiliary: she usually walks; she is usually early; she has usually arrived by nine. These are common placements, not the only grammatical possibilities in every context. Some related forms have separate meanings. Hard means with effort or force, but hardly means almost not. Late concerns a time later than expected; lately means recently. Near concerns closeness; nearly means almost. Well commonly describes successful performance, while good is an adjective; well can also be a predicative adjective meaning healthy. Placement may change interpretation or information focus. They deliberately did not reply describes a deliberate decision not to reply; they did not deliberately reply can deny intention while leaving open whether a reply occurred. Do not diagnose scope from the nearest word alone. Distinguish an adverb's lexical category from its clause-level function and semantic scope. An adverb can modify a verb phrase while taking a broader proposition as its interpretive domain. Fronting, parenthetical position and stress create marked readings: repeatedly she had asked for a meeting foregrounds recurrence, while she had repeatedly asked is more neutral. A long object may make an intervening manner adverb acceptable even when a short-object version sounds awkward. Analyse acceptability in context rather than replacing every unconventional position automatically. When revising, state the intended frequency, manner or scope first, then choose an order that expresses it clearly. subject + frequency adverb + lexical verb A common neutral position: she often travels. subject + first auxiliary + frequency adverb + remaining verb phrase A common neutral position: she has often travelled. The train arrived late. Late is an adverb here; no -ly ending is needed. The train has rarely arrived before sunrise. Rarely follows the first auxiliary and expresses frequency. They did not deliberately omit the appendix. Negation can deny deliberate intention; it does not by itself prove whether the omission occurred. The apprentice worked hard. The apprentice hardly worked. Both grammatical, with nearly opposite implications about effort or activity. Well can be an adjective meaning healthy: I feel well today. Frequency and manner adverbs have neutral positions, but emphasis and constituent length permit alternatives. She answered the question confident. She answered the question confidently. For the intended manner of answering, the ordinary form is confidently. He worked hardly all afternoon, completing every repair. He worked hard all afternoon, completing every repair. Hardly means almost not and conflicts with the intended effort reading. adverbial A grammatical function expressing a circumstance or relation; several phrase types can fill it. at dawn in We left at dawn scope The material over which a modifier or operator is interpreted. not deliberately versus deliberately not source-58353073c867f7 source-8ddf38a0fd2628 source-886c8cf34966b2 source-e2ea6705d28178 source-ca2d512f202f95

concepts.title: Focus, sentence adverbials and responsible interpretation
concepts.definition: A focusing adverb highlights alternatives; a sentence adverbial comments on a whole proposition, its likelihood, or the speaker's relation to it.

glossary.definition: An adverb relating a highlighted element to contextual alternatives.
glossary.example: Only the treasurer replied.

glossary.definition: An expression commenting on certainty, evaluation or the speaker's perspective.
glossary.example: Probably, the journey will take an hour.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d11-m04 Focus, sentence adverbials and responsible interpretation F K gv5-topic-d11-c08 A focusing adverb highlights alternatives; a sentence adverbial comments on a whole proposition, its likelihood, or the speaker's relation to it. Only, even and also guide a listener toward relevant alternatives. Only Leena signed says that no other relevant person signed. Leena signed only the form contrasts that object with other things she might have signed. Even Leena signed presents her participation as surprising against an expectation. These meanings depend on a context: surprising to whom, and compared with which alternatives? When a question offers two plausible positions without supplying that context, more than one answer may be grammatical. Your task as a writer is to make the intended comparison easy to recover, not to treat every other reading as impossible. Only often occupies normal mid-position even when its focus is later: Leena only signed two forms can mean that two was the limit. Moving it nearer the focus can improve precision in an ambiguous written context, but adjacency is not a universal syntax rule. Also can add a new action by the same person, another participant in the same action, or another related fact. A preceding sentence usually determines which reading is relevant. In deliberate editing, write the intended alternative in a margin note, then check whether a reader has enough context to find that interpretation. Sentence adverbials express stance or organise discourse: probably, fortunately, frankly and therefore do different jobs. Probably qualifies certainty; fortunately evaluates an event; frankly comments on the manner of speaking; therefore presents a conclusion. Compare Fortunately, the files survived with The files were stored fortunately, where end placement makes a manner interpretation awkward. Parenthetical commas often help separate a comment from the proposition, but punctuation follows structure and intended reading. Conjunctive adverbs do not independently license joining two full clauses by a comma: the server failed; therefore, the session ended is a standard written pattern. Scope can interact with negation, quantification and presupposed alternatives. Not all applicants replied denies universal response; all applicants did not reply may be interpreted in more than one way, so an explicit none or some did not is clearer. Even presupposes a scale of expectation in many uses but does not tell us a measurable probability. An evaluative adverb can comment on an entire event without describing how an agent acted: surprisingly, the silent room was useful does not mean anyone acted surprisingly. Advanced analysis should identify these distinctions without pretending that every conversational inference is encoded as a rigid grammatical rule. only + focused subject + predicate Exclude relevant alternative subjects. sentence adverbial, + clause A frequent pattern for an explicit comment on the proposition. Only Farah checked the totals. The exclusion concerns other relevant checkers. Farah also checked the totals after verifying the dates. The context makes also add a second checking activity. The totals were probably wrong; nevertheless, the estimate remained useful for planning. Probably qualifies confidence in the first claim; nevertheless marks concession between claims. Only Hana emailed the chart. Hana emailed only the chart. Different grammatical focuses: sender versus object; neither is an error. Mid-position only can focus later material. Context and stress help identify its scope. A sentence adverbial may be mobile, but mobility does not make every punctuation pattern equivalent. The signal failed, therefore the recording stopped. The signal failed; therefore, the recording stopped. In standard edited prose the two independent clauses need a licensed boundary. He is very taller than the others. He is much taller than the others. Much, rather than ordinary degree very, modifies the comparative taller. focusing adverb An adverb relating a highlighted element to contextual alternatives. Only the treasurer replied. stance adverbial An expression commenting on certainty, evaluation or the speaker's perspective. Probably, the journey will take an hour. source-5c48dc3ab4712a source-886c8cf34966b2 source-701ec209075aec

concepts.title: Time, space and abstract relationships
concepts.definition: A preposition commonly heads a phrase expressing a relationship; spatial meanings often extend to time, cause, means and other abstract relations.

glossary.definition: The starting place or origin of a relation.
glossary.example: from Multan

glossary.definition: The latest time by which completion is required.
glossary.example: by noon

concepts.searchText: gv5-d12-m01 Time, space and abstract relationships G L gv5-topic-d12-c01 gv5-topic-d12-c02 A preposition commonly heads a phrase expressing a relationship; spatial meanings often extend to time, cause, means and other abstract relations. Begin with visible relations: a folder on the desk, a letter in the folder, a visitor at the gate. In often presents containment, on often presents contact with a surface, and at can locate an activity or point. These are useful meaning patterns, not a size-based rule that decides every case. A person may be at the office as a workplace or in the office as an interior. Direction contrasts with location: the child is in the garden, but runs into the garden. From identifies a source or starting point, while towards gives a direction without guaranteeing arrival. Time expressions have conventional patterns: at noon, on Tuesday, in October and in the evening. On Tuesday morning includes a named day and therefore differs from in the morning. At night is a conventional expression; during the night selects an interval. Since gives a starting point, for a duration, by a deadline and until an endpoint for continuation. I will send it by Friday promises completion no later than Friday; I will stay until Friday describes a continuing stay. These choices interact with tense and aspect, so a time word cannot substitute for understanding the event. Abstract uses include cause because of the delay, purpose for the examination, means by train, instrument with a key and relationship between two proposals. The same preposition can express different meanings, and alternative constructions may make related claims. Between is not restricted to exactly two: negotiations between the five named departments presents separate participants, whereas disagreement among the staff presents a group setting. By and with differ when an agent and an instrument are expressed: the cabinet was opened by the caretaker with a spare key. Learning the entire relation is more reliable than translating one preposition in isolation. Spatial perspectives permit legitimate alternatives: a bird in a tree and an apple on a tree select different relationships, not different sized locations. Abstract prepositions can be productive rather than arbitrary: under pressure and beyond the budget extend spatial schemas. Nevertheless, idiomatic selection limits prediction, and region or institutional convention may affect at the weekend versus on the weekend. Give the intended time span, route or relation before declaring an alternative wrong. In cumulative review, separate an aspect error from a preposition error: has lived here since March requires an appropriate verb phrase as well as since, and a past residence ending before now needs a different temporal frame. by + deadline Completion occurs no later than the stated time. until + endpoint A state or activity continues up to a boundary. The parcel travelled from Quetta to Sukkur. From identifies source and to identifies destination. The office will remain open until six. Until marks the endpoint of a continuing state. The agreement between the four laboratories covers shared equipment. Between presents distinguishable participants; four does not make it ungrammatical. Please finish by Thursday.
