Please remain until Thursday. Different event relations: deadline for completion versus endpoint of continuation. At the weekend is a common British pattern; on the weekend is established American usage. Between can relate more than two individually identified participants. The meeting starts in Monday. The meeting starts on Monday. A named day takes on in this ordinary temporal construction. She has worked here since three years. She has worked here for three years. Three years expresses duration; since normally introduces a starting point. source The starting place or origin of a relation. from Multan deadline The latest time by which completion is required. by noon source-70e3bfdac01616 source-ca6ab50c9fe853

concepts.title: Prepositional phrases, complements and stranding
concepts.definition: A prepositional phrase contains a preposition as head and, commonly, a complement; the complete phrase can perform several grammatical functions.

glossary.definition: Leaving a preposition apart from its fronted or understood complement.
glossary.example: the chair I sat on

glossary.definition: Moving a preposition together with its dependent phrase.
glossary.example: the chair on which I sat

concepts.searchText: gv5-d12-m02 Prepositional phrases, complements and stranding G L gv5-topic-d12-c03 gv5-topic-d12-c04 A prepositional phrase contains a preposition as head and, commonly, a complement; the complete phrase can perform several grammatical functions. In beside the window, beside is the preposition and the window is its noun-phrase complement. The whole phrase can describe a noun, as in the desk beside the window, or locate an event, as in she waited beside the window. Pronouns normally use their object form after a preposition: with her, between you and me. The complement need not be one isolated word. A complex noun phrase such as the narrow window at the end of the hall remains a single complement of beside even though it contains another prepositional phrase. Common complements include noun phrases, pronouns and -ing clauses: about the delay, with us, without checking the figures. Prepositions can also take other kinds of complement in particular patterns: from there has a place expression; until after the interview contains another prepositional phrase; surprised at what she wrote has a wh-clause. The familiar instruction use -ing after a preposition is useful when choosing an ordinary non-finite verbal complement, but it should not be expanded into the false claim that every complement is a gerund or that clauses can never follow a preposition. In a question or relative construction, a preposition may remain at the end while its complement is understood earlier: Which bench did you sit on? This is preposition stranding and is normal standard English. On which bench did you sit? moves the preposition together with the question phrase, a pattern often called pied-piping. It is more formal and can sound natural in legal or academic contexts. Selection matters: we cannot freely separate parts of every idiom, and some fronted patterns are very unnatural. Where both versions are established, choose according to register and clarity rather than a blanket ban on sentence-final prepositions. Function and category remain distinct. In the proposal on transport, the prepositional phrase postmodifies a noun; in interested in transport, it complements an adjective; in rely on transport, it belongs to the verb's lexical pattern. Modern grammatical frameworks differ in their classification of before in before lunch and before she left: some keep a broader preposition category, while many teaching grammars call the finite-clause use a conjunction. This course names the framework where it matters and always identifies the complement and function. A change of label must not turn an otherwise acceptable construction into an alleged error. preposition + noun phrase / -ing clause / licensed wh-clause The complement type depends on the preposition and construction. wh-phrase ... preposition / preposition + wh-phrase ... Stranding and pied-piping are alternative question patterns where licensed. The folder beside the printer is empty. Beside the printer postmodifies folder; beside is its head. We left without checking the figures. Without takes an -ing clause as complement. The question on which the panel disagreed concerned funding. On which is a fronted prepositional phrase inside the relative clause. Which file are you referring to? To which file are you referring? Both standard: the second is more formal; neither is wrong merely because of preposition placement. Prepositions license several complement types; at what she wrote is a genuine wh-clause complement. Frameworks may call before she left a subordinating conjunction pattern or a preposition with a clause complement; the label must be stated consistently. We spoke between you and I. We spoke between you and me. In the intended prepositional coordination, use the ordinary object case me. She left without to sign the receipt. She left without signing the receipt. Without in this non-finite complement pattern takes an -ing clause, not a to-infinitive. stranding Leaving a preposition apart from its fronted or understood complement. the chair I sat on pied-piping Moving a preposition together with its dependent phrase. the chair on which I sat source-84ae307be3e618 source-70e3bfdac01616

concepts.title: Lexical selection, fixed combinations and meaning
concepts.definition: Lexical selection is the requirement or preference of a particular word for a complement pattern, including a specific preposition where its meaning requires one.

glossary.definition: A word's constraints or preferences concerning its complements.
glossary.example: depend on support

glossary.definition: The marker introducing a to-infinitive rather than a preposition.
glossary.example: hope to finish

concepts.searchText: gv5-d12-m03 Lexical selection, fixed combinations and meaning G L gv5-topic-d12-c05 gv5-topic-d12-c08 Lexical selection is the requirement or preference of a particular word for a complement pattern, including a specific preposition where its meaning requires one. Some verb patterns are straightforward only after the whole expression is learned: depend on a colleague, listen to a recording, discuss a problem. Discuss takes a direct object in the ordinary meaning illustrated here; listen introduces the thing heard with to. Do not infer that one pattern applies to every synonym. Explain a problem to someone differs from tell someone about a problem. A useful dictionary entry records the word's sense, the types of complement it permits, and examples of the actual construction. Keep a pattern notebook using complete short sentences, not an undifferentiated list of supposedly interchangeable prepositions. Adjectives and nouns select patterns too: interested in a subject, responsible for a decision, an increase in costs and a solution to a problem. Some words allow alternatives with overlapping meanings or different emphases; a dictionary, not a simplistic single-partner slogan, should resolve a doubtful case. Insist on a receipt and insist that the receipt be issued are both grammatical. The first contains a prepositional complement; the second contains a content clause. Insist does not always need on. Likewise, enter the room and enter into an agreement use different senses and should not be collapsed into one prohibition. The spelling to belongs to different constructions. In hope to leave, it marks an infinitive. In look forward to leaving, it is a preposition within a lexical pattern and takes an -ing complement. Be used to describes accustomedness and differs from used to for a past habit: she is used to cycling versus she used to cycle. No visual shortcut based solely on the word to can decide the structure. Look at the governing expression and the intended meaning. A correct form may still make the wrong claim: used to work does not by itself say that work continues now. Lexical grammar overlaps vocabulary, syntax and register. Different from is an appropriate British editorial default; different than is established in American English, while different to occurs especially in British speech. Formal preference does not justify scoring a standard regional alternative as universally wrong. In review, explain the selected sense and its complement, then compare a close alternative. This is particularly useful when a first language distributes relations differently, including for many Urdu-speaking learners, but no learner should be presumed to make the same error because of background. Record personal evidence from actual writing and practice, and revisit patterns that genuinely cause difficulty. insist on + noun phrase / -ing clause Demand or maintain something in an on-pattern. insist that + content clause State insistence through a proposition or mandative clause. We discussed the revised timetable. Discuss takes the timetable directly in the intended sense. Rida insisted that the minutes were accurate. The content clause expresses the proposition she maintained; no on is needed. The team is used to working remotely but used to meet in person. Accustomedness takes -ing; the past-habit construction takes a base infinitive. She is used to working late. She used to work late. Both standard, with accustomedness versus past-habit meaning. Insist also takes content clauses, so insist always takes on is false. A verb's other sense can permit another pattern: enter a hall versus enter into negotiations. They discussed about the new rota. They discussed the new rota. In the ordinary discuss-a-topic pattern the topic is a direct object. We look forward to meet your team. We look forward to meeting your team. The lexical expression look forward to takes an -ing complement here. lexical selection A word's constraints or preferences concerning its complements. depend on support infinitival to The marker introducing a to-infinitive rather than a preposition. hope to finish source-70e3bfdac01616 source-84ae307be3e618 source-ccfbea5f751a50

concepts.title: Particles, multi-word verbs and cumulative review
concepts.definition: Multi-word verbs combine a verb with a particle, preposition or both; their object-placement patterns reveal important differences.

glossary.definition: A small word in a multi-word verb with its own placement behaviour.
glossary.example: off in switch it off

glossary.definition: A lexical combination containing a verb, particle and preposition.
glossary.example: put up with noise

concepts.searchText: gv5-d12-m04 Particles, multi-word verbs and cumulative review G L gv5-topic-d12-c06 gv5-topic-d12-c07 gv5-topic-d12-c09 Multi-word verbs combine a verb with a particle, preposition or both; their object-placement patterns reveal important differences. In turn off the lamp, off is a particle in a phrasal verb. With this separable pattern, an ordinary noun object can precede or follow the particle: turn the lamp off and turn off the lamp. A personal-pronoun object normally comes between: turn it off. This placement is not available with look after a child: after introduces its complement, so look the child after is not the ordinary care-for construction. Learn whether a particular expression is transitive or intransitive as well as whether it separates; the bus broke down needs no object, whereas someone may break down a calculation into parts. Traditional teaching often calls all multi-word expressions phrasal verbs, but a narrower classification distinguishes three patterns. A phrasal verb has a particle, such as give up; a prepositional verb has a selected preposition, such as rely on; a phrasal-prepositional verb has both, such as put up with. In put up with the noise, the noun complement follows with. The whole expression means tolerate, but its meaning is not obtained by translating each word separately. Dictionaries vary in their labels, so check the actual object placement shown by their examples rather than treating a broad label as a complete rule. Formality belongs to individual expressions and contexts. Carry out an investigation and account for an increase are entirely at home in formal writing, although put off may be less formal than postpone. A single-word substitute must preserve meaning: give up a habit, give up a seat and give up hope do not all invite the same replacement. Longer noun objects often favour position after a particle because it is easier to process the verb sequence before a heavy phrase. Personal-pronoun placement remains the useful elementary diagnostic for many separable particle verbs, but idiomatic restrictions still require lexical checking. The cumulative tasks revisit past narrative sequence, perfect/progressive meanings, future reference, agreement and degree from Days 7–11. Separate first-encounter recognition from an immediate retry: seeing the same item again can measure recall of that item without demonstrating transfer to a new sentence. For each error, name the underlying distinction before choosing a review lesson. A perfect-aspect error in has been waiting since noon should link to aspect and temporal reference, not merely be counted as a generic preposition mistake. Open-response explanations and short corrections supply production evidence through self-review; a displayed model is an aid to analysis, not an independent automated grade. separable verb + noun + particle / verb + particle + noun Both positions occur with an ordinary noun object where the lexical pattern permits. separable verb + personal pronoun + particle Ordinary placement: turn it off, not turn off it. Please turn the reading lamp off. The noun object precedes the separable particle. Please turn it off before leaving. The personal pronoun appears between verb and particle. We could not put up with the noise from the generator. Put up with is phrasal-prepositional; the complement follows with. look up the number / look the number up look after the child / not normally look the child after Different lexical patterns, not a free choice of where every small word can move. Some phrasal verbs are intransitive: the generator broke down. A formally acceptable multi-word verb need not be replaced by a single word merely to look academic. Please turn off it. Please turn it off. A personal-pronoun object normally precedes the separable particle. She looked the visitor after. She looked after the visitor. After is a selected preposition in the intended care-for meaning, not a freely movable particle. particle A small word in a multi-word verb with its own placement behaviour. off in switch it off phrasal-prepositional verb A lexical combination containing a verb, particle and preposition. put up with noise source-dc50449ecddf62 source-70e3bfdac01616

concepts.title: Heads and the central phrase classes
concepts.definition: A phrase is a grammatical unit organised around a head, the element that determines its category and much of its distribution. A phrase may consist of one word or contain several nested units.

glossary.definition: The structural class determined by a phrase’s head.
glossary.example: beside the gate is a prepositional phrase

glossary.definition: A narrow grouping of a main verb and its auxiliaries.
glossary.example: might have arrived

concepts.searchText: gv5-d13-m01 Heads and the central phrase classes H gv5-topic-d13-c01 gv5-topic-d13-c02 A phrase is a grammatical unit organised around a head, the element that determines its category and much of its distribution. A phrase may consist of one word or contain several nested units. In a familiar noun phrase such as the narrow bridge, bridge is the head. The and narrow depend on that noun, while the complete noun phrase can be used as subject in The narrow bridge needs repairs. The head does not mean the first word or the longest word. It names the organising element. The five phrase classes developed here are noun phrase, verb phrase, adjective phrase, adverb phrase and prepositional phrase. Find the head first, then ask what other material belongs with it. A one-word expression can still occupy a phrase position: in They laughed, they is a noun phrase headed by a pronoun in this course's analysis. A noun phrase is headed by a noun or pronoun; an adjective phrase by an adjective; an adverb phrase by an adverb; and a prepositional phrase by a preposition. Extremely proud of her class is an adjective phrase headed by proud. Very carefully is an adverb phrase headed by carefully. Beside the noticeboard is a prepositional phrase headed by beside, containing the noun phrase the noticeboard as complement. Those labels describe form. A prepositional phrase can function as a modifier inside a noun phrase or as an adjunct in a clause, without changing its phrase category. For verb phrases, state the convention being used. The narrow pedagogical convention groups a lexical verb with its auxiliaries: may have been waiting. It excludes an object or location phrase from that particular verb group. A broader syntactic convention includes the lexical verb and its complements inside a VP: read the proposal. Both conventions occur in reputable grammars. This course uses narrow verb group when describing auxiliary order and labels a broader VP explicitly when it includes complements. Do not decide that an analysis is wrong merely because its author has chosen the other stated convention. A phrase has an external function and internal relations. The entire adjective phrase very proud of her work can be a subject complement, while of her work is an internal complement of proud and very is a degree modifier. A category label does not encode all those functions. Likewise, noun phrases are not restricted to subjects or objects: the following day can function as a time adjunct. A prepositional phrase can also supply a predicative complement, as in the keys are under the mat. These distributions show why adverbial is a function term in this course rather than a universal synonym for adverb phrase. noun phrase: determiner + modifiers + noun head + post-head material Optional dependents combine around a noun head. narrow verb group: modal + perfect have + progressive be + passive be + lexical verb Only the selected auxiliary meanings occur; each determines the next verb form. Those three unusually steep steps need a handrail. Steps heads the subject noun phrase; unusually steep is an embedded adjective phrase. The technician may have been waiting outside. May have been waiting is the narrow verb group; outside gives additional location information. The child seemed surprisingly confident about the interview. Surprisingly confident about the interview is an adjective phrase functioning as subject complement. We left after lunch. The discussion after lunch was brief. After lunch is a prepositional phrase in both, but it is a clause adjunct in the first and a noun-phrase modifier in the second. Narrow and broad VP conventions differ; a labelled analysis must make its convention clear. A noun phrase may contain only a pronoun, as in She arrived, and an adjective phrase may contain only its adjective head. Classification: “at the harbour” is an adverb phrase because it answers where. At the harbour is a prepositional phrase; it may function as a place adjunct. A semantic question suggests function but does not determine phrase class. Classification: the head of “very useful” is very. Useful is the adjective head; very is its degree modifier. The head determines the phrase category rather than merely occupying first position. phrase category The structural class determined by a phrase’s head. beside the gate is a prepositional phrase verb group A narrow grouping of a main verb and its auxiliaries. might have arrived source-58353073c867f7 source-49ac929acd7fe5 source-a26f490947be2a source-3cb399907c285d source-7fbbabb6fbc6f9 source-84ae307be3e618

concepts.title: Determiners, modifiers and selected complements
concepts.definition: A dependent is material associated with a phrase's head. Determiners help establish reference or quantity; modifiers add description; complements are licensed by the head's particular grammatical pattern.

glossary.definition: Modification occurring before the head.
glossary.example: a carefully revised draft

glossary.definition: Modification occurring after the head.
glossary.example: the draft beside the printer

glossary.definition: The compatibility of a construction with a particular word’s grammatical patterns.
glossary.example: depend on assistance

concepts.searchText: gv5-d13-m02 Determiners, modifiers and selected complements H gv5-topic-d13-c02 gv5-topic-d13-c03 A dependent is material associated with a phrase's head. Determiners help establish reference or quantity; modifiers add description; complements are licensed by the head's particular grammatical pattern. Look inside a noun phrase before treating every word before its verb as one undifferentiated subject. In these two detailed reports on drainage, these is a determiner, two gives a number, detailed modifies reports, and reports is the noun head. On drainage follows the head and gives its topic. A premodifier occurs before a head; a postmodifier occurs after it. These position labels do not name word classes. A noun can premodify another noun, as in drainage report, while an adjective phrase can appear after a noun, as in the reports available today. A complement is related to a head's lexical pattern, not simply anything standing after it. Proud commonly licenses of her achievement, depend licenses on the grant, and a decision can have an infinitival complement such as to postpone the launch. A modifier adds a description such as the report on the top shelf. Context and grammatical framework can affect the boundary between noun complements and modifiers. For teaching, ask whether the following expression specifies something selected by the head's meaning, such as the content of a claim, or adds an independent property, such as the place of a printed copy. Complements are not invariably obligatory. She has already eaten omits the food, although eat also licenses an object in she ate a sandwich. Conversely, the ordinary placing sense of put requires a location or destination expression: she put the tray on the table, rather than she put the tray with no recoverable continuation. Adjunct omission is often a useful first check, but optionality alone is not a complete definition of complement. The same phrase can receive different analyses after different heads: in the library is an optional place adjunct after read but supplies the required location after put the book. Structure constrains placement. An adjective with a substantial complement commonly follows its noun: students eager to volunteer. Packing the whole sequence before the noun as eager to volunteer students is not the neutral attributive pattern. Modification can also be layered: the very small office near the stairs contains a degree modifier inside the adjective phrase and a location modifier after the noun. A genitive such as the editor's draft can fill a determining role; the apostrophe does not make editor's an adjective by itself. Keep the analyses of grammatical form, internal function and position distinct, especially when comparing school terminology with a more detailed grammar. premodifier + head + postmodifier Position is described relative to the head being modified. head + licensed complement The head’s lexical pattern determines which kinds of complement are possible. A detailed report on coastal erosion arrived yesterday. Report heads the noun phrase; detailed precedes it and on coastal erosion specifies its topic. The students eager to volunteer met after class. The complete adjective phrase eager to volunteer follows students. She placed the signed form inside the envelope. The location completes the placing pattern; its importance comes from the verb’s valency, not from being last. She read the book in the library. She put the book in the library. The same location phrase adds optional circumstances after read but completes the ordinary placing pattern after put. A licensed complement can be omitted in a suitable lexical pattern: she has eaten is complete. Complement and modifier distinctions may be gradient or framework-dependent, especially inside noun phrases; explain the evidence rather than pretending position settles the issue. They are proud for their daughter’s progress. They are proud of their daughter’s progress. The ordinary adjective-complement pattern is proud of in this meaning. We met a ready to depart group. We met a group ready to depart. The full adjective phrase with its infinitival complement normally follows the noun in this construction. premodification Modification occurring before the head. a carefully revised draft postmodification Modification occurring after the head. the draft beside the printer lexical licensing The compatibility of a construction with a particular word’s grammatical patterns. depend on assistance source-49ac929acd7fe5 source-d6af2eef369812 source-63b41bcf84b05f source-3cb399907c285d

concepts.title: Embedding, coordination and structural hierarchy
concepts.definition: A hierarchical analysis groups words into units within larger units. Embedding places one unit inside another; coordination links units at a comparable structural level.

glossary.definition: Inclusion of one grammatical unit inside another.
glossary.example: the box [under the desk]

glossary.definition: The structural connection of a modifier to the expression it modifies.
glossary.example: with a torch may modify searching or identify a person

concepts.searchText: gv5-d13-m03 Embedding, coordination and structural hierarchy H gv5-topic-d13-c04 gv5-topic-d13-c05 A hierarchical analysis groups words into units within larger units. Embedding places one unit inside another; coordination links units at a comparable structural level. In the cover of the book, the whole expression is a noun phrase headed by cover. Inside it, of the book is a prepositional phrase, and the book is a smaller noun phrase within that phrase. This is embedding. It does not mean that all three units perform the same job. The larger noun phrase may be the subject of a clause, while the smaller one is complement of of. Brackets help you preserve these levels: [NP the cover [PP of [NP the book]]]. Read the structure from the outside inward, then check that every bracket has a matching closing bracket. Coordination links expressions using and, or and related coordinators. The carefully revised draft and the original report coordinates two noun phrases. A phrase can contain coordination internally: the red and blue folders coordinates two adjective modifiers, while the red folders and the blue folders coordinates full noun phrases. These are different structures even if a suitable context lets them refer to the same collection. Shared material can be understood rather than repeated. The editor reviewed and corrected the draft coordinates predicates sharing a subject and object; merely counting occurrences of and does not tell you how many main clauses there are. Hierarchy explains attachment ambiguity. The researcher photographed the student with the telescope may describe an instrument used for photographing or identify a student carrying a telescope. One analysis attaches with the telescope to the event; another places it inside the object noun phrase. Both readings follow from available structural relations, not from a defective word ending. If the intended meaning matters, revise explicitly: using a telescope, the researcher photographed the student; or the researcher photographed the student who was carrying a telescope. An interpretation should be supported by context rather than imposed because it was the first one you imagined. Coordination often links expressions of the same category, but matching category labels is not an absolute condition in every construction. She is a doctor and very experienced can coordinate predicates with different internal categories because both characterise the same subject. Such examples require care with shared grammatical functions. Coordination tests are therefore evidence for constituency, not a proof that any two strings joined by and are interchangeable phrases. In a complete parse, state the relation between each unit and its parent. That approach prevents the common error of treating a noun embedded in an of-phrase as the head governing agreement for the whole subject. [NP determiner + head [PP preposition [NP complement]]] A larger noun phrase can contain a prepositional phrase with its own noun phrase. [NP ...] and [NP ...] Coordination can join full noun phrases at the same structural level. The manager of the two clinics has resigned. Manager heads the complete subject; clinics is embedded as complement of of. The red and green indicators were flashing. Red and green coordinate within a larger noun phrase headed by indicators. The lawyer interviewed the witness with an interpreter. The final phrase can describe assistance during the interview; context is needed to exclude other attachments. the cover of [the revised report] [the cover of the report] and [the revised appendix] The first shows embedding within one noun phrase; the second shows coordination of two noun phrases. Different categories can sometimes coordinate when their functions are compatible; identical word-class labels are not an unrestricted universal requirement. A repeated subject or object may be understood through sharing or ellipsis; analyse the chosen construction before counting clauses. The director of the three museums have replied. The director of the three museums has replied. The larger subject noun phrase is headed by singular director. The analyst compared the budget with the school, meaning the school’s budget. The analyst compared the budget with the school’s budget. Make the intended parallel entities explicit rather than comparing a budget with an institution. embedding Inclusion of one grammatical unit inside another. the box [under the desk] attachment The structural connection of a modifier to the expression it modifies. with a torch may modify searching or identify a person source-58353073c867f7 source-49ac929acd7fe5 source-d6af2eef369812 source-1ceaeffe194685

concepts.title: Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing
concepts.definition: A constituent is a unit within a grammatical structure. Diagnostics such as substitution, movement and answering a focused question can provide evidence about units, but no one diagnostic is decisive in every context.

glossary.definition: A unit that forms part of a larger grammatical structure.
glossary.example: the revised timetable in We checked the revised timetable

glossary.definition: A test that supplies evidence for an analysis.
glossary.example: Replacing a subject noun phrase with they

concepts.searchText: gv5-d13-m04 Constituency diagnostics and practical parsing H gv5-topic-d13-c06 gv5-topic-d13-c07 A constituent is a unit within a grammatical structure. Diagnostics such as substitution, movement and answering a focused question can provide evidence about units, but no one diagnostic is decisive in every context. Start a parse by finding the finite verb group and the major clause elements, then analyse the phrases inside those elements. In the new assistant filed three invoices, the new assistant is the subject noun phrase and three invoices is the object noun phrase. Replacing the subject with she gives she filed three invoices. This substitution supports the grouping of those subject words. It does not mean that the original phrase was a pronoun or that the replacement has preserved every detail. A diagnostic changes the sentence in order to test one structural possibility. Use more than one check. Ask who filed three invoices; the new assistant forms a natural answer. In the right context, fronting a unit may also be possible: three invoices, the assistant filed before lunch. This marked order supplies evidence for the object grouping, but it is less neutral than the original and may need a contrastive context. Coordination can give further evidence, as in the new assistant and the office manager filed the invoices. A failure under one test can result from meaning, information structure or register rather than proving that the tested string is not a constituent. Bracket only what the analysis supports. In a very experienced teacher from Multan, very modifies experienced within an adjective phrase, while from Multan postmodifies teacher in one natural reading. Bracketing [very experienced teacher] as a single adjective phrase misidentifies teacher, the noun head. Likewise, a group of adjacent words may cross a boundary: in she sent the student a note, student a is not a natural constituent merely because the words are neighbours. Avoid constructing a parse solely from translation or a question such as what, which can elicit several kinds of answer. Substitution tests have restrictions. One can replace some noun-phrase material but does not reproduce every nominal pattern, and it may refer to a different kind of entity from a longer expression. A movement test can change scope or require a special discourse setting. Coordination also has exceptional patterns and shared dependents. Record a tentative analysis when evidence conflicts, then compare a reputable grammar using the same framework. A practical final analysis should name each relevant category, its head and its function in the next larger unit. That is more informative than assigning a label to every individual word while leaving the sentence's larger organisation unexplained. identify unit → test substitution → check context → compare another diagnostic A sequence of evidence is stronger than a single mechanical trick. [clause [subject NP] [verb group] [object NP] [optional adjunct]] A readable first-pass parse can show major relations before every internal detail is added. The revised handbook arrived. → It arrived. Pronoun substitution supports treating the revised handbook as a subject noun phrase. She spoke very quietly. → How did she speak? Very quietly. The manner answer supports the adverb-phrase grouping; quietly is its head. We stored the material in the room beside the lift. Analyse the room beside the lift as an embedded noun phrase within the in-phrase, rather than treating all location words as one unstructured list. the very experienced teacher the teacher is very experienced The adjective phrase very experienced is internal to the noun phrase in the first and a subject complement in the second. A meaningful answer fragment can identify a phrase in conversation without being a complete formal sentence. Failure under movement, substitution or coordination alone does not settle every constituency question; contextual and lexical restrictions matter. Parse: “[AP very experienced teacher]”. Parse: “[NP [AP very experienced] teacher]”. Teacher is a noun head, so the whole phrase is a noun phrase. The explanation seems quite clearly to the beginners. The explanation seems quite clear to the beginners. The intended subject description takes an adjective phrase headed by clear, not a manner adverb headed by clearly. constituent A unit that forms part of a larger grammatical structure. the revised timetable in We checked the revised timetable diagnostic A test that supplies evidence for an analysis. Replacing a subject noun phrase with they source-58353073c867f7 source-49ac929acd7fe5 source-1ceaeffe194685 source-d6af2eef369812

concepts.title: Main, subordinate, finite and non-finite clauses
concepts.definition: A clause is a grammatical unit organised around a verb. Main clauses supply a principal message; subordinate clauses function within a larger structure. Finite and non-finite distinguish verb forms and clause construction, not whether an event is real.

glossary.definition: A clause containing a finite verb or auxiliary.
glossary.example: whether she has arrived

glossary.definition: A clause headed by a non-finite verb form without independent tense inflection.
glossary.example: for Sam to arrive early

glossary.definition: A relation in which a clause is dependent within a larger construction.
glossary.example: because the road was closed

concepts.searchText: gv5-d14-m01 Main, subordinate, finite and non-finite clauses H I gv5-topic-d14-c01 gv5-topic-d14-c02 A clause is a grammatical unit organised around a verb. Main clauses supply a principal message; subordinate clauses function within a larger structure. Finite and non-finite distinguish verb forms and clause construction, not whether an event is real. The train stopped is a main declarative clause. In the train stopped because a signal failed, because a signal failed is a subordinate reason clause associated with the main event. The first clause can form an independent neutral statement; the because-clause normally relies on a larger construction in formal connected prose. A clause is not simply any group of words that happens to contain a noun and a verb spelling. Identify the grammatical organisation of the group and its relation to the larger sentence. A phrase can contain a clause, as in the promise that she would return. A finite clause contains a finite verb or auxiliary, as in she returns, she returned and she may return. The modal may is finite even though it does not display a person contrast such as returns versus return. A non-finite clause is headed by an infinitival or participial form without independent tense inflection: to return soon, returning home, or signed yesterday in the noun phrase the documents signed yesterday. A non-finite clause can still express time relative to context. In she hoped to return next week, next week gives time reference, while to return remains non-finite. Non-finite clauses often leave their subject understood: she hopes to return normally makes her the intended returner. Some have an expressed subject: for the visitors to arrive early would be convenient. The clause for the visitors to arrive early serves as the subject of would be convenient, despite lacking independent tense. Finite clauses may also function as subjects, objects or other complements. Whether the grant will continue remains unclear has a finite interrogative clause as its subject. The whole sentence is declarative; the embedded subject clause does not use direct-question inversion. The main/subordinate distinction is not identical to the finite/non-finite distinction. Many subordinate clauses are finite, while other subordinate clauses are non-finite. Imperatives deserve separate attention because their ordinary main verb is a plain form and their subject is usually unexpressed: take your seat. Different grammatical frameworks discuss their finiteness differently; this course identifies the imperative construction rather than inferring that take your seat is an ungrammatical fragment. Supplementary non-finite clauses such as weather permitting have their own internal structure. The practical question is how the clause is licensed and interpreted in the complete construction, not whether it mechanically contains a written subject plus an overt tense ending. main clause + because + finite subordinate clause The subordinate clause supplies a reason for the principal message. for + expressed subject + to-infinitive clause A non-finite clause can contain its own expressed subject. The meeting ended because the chair was ill. Ended and was are finite; the because-clause is subordinate. To postpone the decision would be unwise. The to-infinitival clause functions as subject of the main predicate. Whether the figures have changed remains uncertain. A finite embedded question functions as the subject; the complete sentence is declarative. She knows that the office is closed. She hopes to leave early. Both contain a subordinate complement; the first has a finite content clause, while the second has a non-finite infinitival clause. A grammatical imperative normally has an unexpressed subject: please wait is not a fragment simply because you is absent. A non-finite clause may have an explicit subject, as in for the guests to leave, and may contain temporal expressions without acquiring independent tense. Whether has the result changed remains unclear. Whether the result has changed remains unclear. The embedded interrogative subject takes ordinary statement order rather than direct-question inversion. Because the printer failed. The assistant used another machine. Because the printer failed, the assistant used another machine. Join the reason clause to its main clause in ordinary formal prose. finite clause A clause containing a finite verb or auxiliary. whether she has arrived non-finite clause A clause headed by a non-finite verb form without independent tense inflection. for Sam to arrive early subordination A relation in which a clause is dependent within a larger construction. because the road was closed source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5 source-445532eb0f5c35 source-a70db92421dbc9 source-1ceaeffe194685

concepts.title: Clause forms and communicative purposes
concepts.definition: Clause form describes grammatical construction, such as declarative or interrogative. Communicative function describes what a speaker uses it to do, such as state, ask, request or exclaim; the two do not correspond one to one.

glossary.definition: A clause form characteristically used for questions.
glossary.example: Did the meeting finish?

glossary.definition: The action performed through an expression in context.
glossary.example: Could you wait? can function as a request

glossary.definition: A grammatical construction characteristically expressing a striking degree or quality.
glossary.example: What a quiet room this is!

concepts.searchText: gv5-d14-m02 Clause forms and communicative purposes H I gv5-topic-d14-c03 gv5-topic-d14-c04 Clause form describes grammatical construction, such as declarative or interrogative. Communicative function describes what a speaker uses it to do, such as state, ask, request or exclaim; the two do not correspond one to one. A declarative clause commonly places a subject before its verb: the workshop begins at ten. An interrogative clause commonly asks a question: does the workshop begin at ten? An imperative commonly directs action: begin the workshop at ten. An exclamative commonly expresses a reaction to a striking degree or quality: how quickly the workshop ended! These are useful central patterns, not interchangeable labels for punctuation marks. A full stop does not turn a question-shaped clause into a declarative, and an exclamation mark alone does not make a structure an exclamative clause. Interrogatives include yes-no and wh-patterns. Does Amina teach here? is a yes-no interrogative. Where does Amina teach? asks for a place. Who teaches here? asks about the subject and does not need do-support or an extra subject after the verb. An embedded question normally has different order: I wonder where Amina teaches. The complete clause I wonder ... is declarative, although one part is an interrogative complement. Pay attention to the boundary at which each form label applies rather than treating a sentence containing any wh-word as one direct question. Form and purpose can diverge. Could you close the window? is interrogative in form but often functions as a polite request. You will submit the form today can function as an instruction, prediction or reminder depending on situation and intonation. Imperatives can offer advice, invitations or permissions as well as commands: have another biscuit. A declarative with rising intonation may seek confirmation in conversation, but the absence of inversion remains part of its grammatical form. Describe the form and the likely use separately instead of replacing grammatical analysis with a guess about the speaker's attitude. The central what- and how-exclamative patterns have their own order: what an unusual design this is; how carefully she explained it. A question can also express surprise: wasn't that remarkable? It remains interrogative in construction even when it performs an exclamatory function. In formal writing, punctuation should reflect the complete utterance and its intended force. An indirect question embedded in a statement usually ends with a full stop, while can you tell me where the office is? ends with a question mark because the complete construction is a direct interrogative. These distinctions become essential in reporting speech and in distinguishing an embedded question from a faulty inversion. auxiliary + subject + lexical verb A central yes-no interrogative pattern: does she agree? what + noun phrase + subject + verb / how + adjective or adverb + subject + verb Central exclamative patterns; their word order differs from a neutral direct question. The door is open. A declarative commonly used as a statement, but it could also hint that someone should close the door. Who authorised the payment? A subject wh-question uses authorised directly without adding did. Could you tell me where the archive is? The complete sentence is interrogative, while the embedded question where the archive is has no inversion. How quickly did she finish? How quickly she finished! The first is a direct interrogative; the second is a how-exclamative with subject before verb. A subject wh-question such as who left? does not use the same auxiliary-subject inversion as who did she meet? Communicative force depends on context: a polite interrogative can request action without being an imperative in grammatical form. I wonder where is the station. I wonder where the station is. The interrogative complement is embedded inside a declarative construction. How beautiful is this courtyard!, intended as a neutral how-exclamative. How beautiful this courtyard is! The central how-exclamative pattern places the subject before the verb; an inverted version would require a different interrogative interpretation. interrogative A clause form characteristically used for questions. Did the meeting finish? communicative function The action performed through an expression in context. Could you wait? can function as a request exclamative A grammatical construction characteristically expressing a striking degree or quality. What a quiet room this is! source-ef9d400d1dbaab source-1ceaeffe194685 source-89176b529bbc02

concepts.title: Simple, coordinated and subordinate architecture
concepts.definition: Sentence architecture describes how clauses combine. In the finite-clause classroom classification used here, a simple sentence has one main finite clause, a compound sentence coordinates main clauses, and a complex sentence includes finite subordination.

glossary.definition: Under the stated convention, a sentence with main-clause coordination and finite subordination.
glossary.example: The office closed because the lift failed, and visitors returned later.

glossary.definition: A clause expressing content selected by a head such as a verb or noun.
glossary.example: that the figures are reliable in I believe that the figures are reliable

concepts.searchText: gv5-d14-m03 Simple, coordinated and subordinate architecture H I gv5-topic-d14-c05 gv5-topic-d14-c06 Sentence architecture describes how clauses combine. In the finite-clause classroom classification used here, a simple sentence has one main finite clause, a compound sentence coordinates main clauses, and a complex sentence includes finite subordination. A simple sentence can still be long: the patient researcher in the upstairs office checked all the entries carefully. Its length does not create another main clause. A compound sentence joins main clauses, as in the researcher checked the entries, and her colleague verified the totals. A complex sentence includes a subordinate finite clause: the researcher checked the entries because several totals looked unusual. A compound-complex sentence has at least two coordinated main finite clauses and at least one subordinate finite clause. These labels offer a useful first map, but they do not replace a detailed analysis of every embedded unit. State the counting convention when non-finite clauses are present. For the classroom labels in this lesson, the researcher hopes to finish today has one main finite clause and an infinitival complement. We describe that full structure rather than pretending that to finish today contains no clause. Some grammatical accounts use complex more broadly to include non-finite subordination. A different count based on an explicit convention need not be an error. What matters for accurate editing is that you recognise the complement relationship and the understood subject, even if a school exercise uses a narrower label. Coordination can occur below clause level. Amina opened and checked the package coordinates predicates sharing a subject and object; it does not automatically display two separately expressed main clauses. In Amina opened the package and Bilal checked the contents, the two subjects help reveal full clause coordination. Subordinate clauses can fill selected complement positions: she believes that the claim is mistaken. Others serve as adjuncts expressing reason, condition or time: she left when the discussion ended. A clause modifying a noun, such as the claim that the witness repeated, has a different internal relation from the content clause in the claim that the witness was mistaken. Subordination establishes grammatical dependency without determining every logical inference. Although the road was wet, the driver continued presents a concession, but grammar alone does not tell us whether continuing was wise. Coordination with and can suggest sequence, addition or other relations from context. Avoid assuming that any two grammatical clauses can be joined without changing the message. When transforming a complex sentence into two independent sentences, preserve the reason, condition or qualification through explicit wording if it is important. Similarly, an embedded complement can contain further subordination: she said that she would leave if the meeting ran late. A layered parse shows the conditional clause inside the reported content rather than attaching it automatically to said. main finite clause + coordinator + main finite clause Full main-clause coordination under the classroom convention. main clause containing [content clause containing [adjunct clause]] Subordination can be nested within another subordinate clause. The technician opened and cleaned the scanner. The sentence coordinates predicates with shared arguments; and does not by itself prove two full main clauses. The technician opened the scanner, and the assistant photographed its interior. Two separately expressed main clauses form compound architecture. The technician said that the scanner would work if the sensor was replaced. The reported content includes a conditional clause; brackets can make that embedding explicit. The clerk knows that the form is missing. The form that the clerk needs is missing. The first that-clause gives content selected by knows; the second modifies form through a relative relation. Some descriptions count non-finite subordination when calling a sentence complex; use the specified convention and still identify the non-finite clause. A sentence with several coordinated verbs is not automatically a compound sentence with several fully independent clauses. The workshop ended because the tutor was ill, and therefore because was a coordinator. Because introduces a subordinate reason clause; and is a coordinator in the larger wording. Classify connectors by their actual construction, not by the fact that both connect ideas. The assistant said that would return after lunch. The assistant said that she would return after lunch. The finite content clause needs its subject in this intended reading; that does not fill the subject position here. compound-complex sentence Under the stated convention, a sentence with main-clause coordination and finite subordination. The office closed because the lift failed, and visitors returned later. content clause A clause expressing content selected by a head such as a verb or noun. that the figures are reliable in I believe that the figures are reliable source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5 source-1ceaeffe194685 source-ef9d400d1dbaab source-d6af2eef369812 source-701ec209075aec

concepts.title: Clause boundaries and accessible visual parsing
concepts.definition: A sentence-boundary error occurs when written clauses are left without the relationship or punctuation their intended construction needs. A bracketed parse can reveal missing main clauses, fused clauses and comma splices.

glossary.definition: Independent clauses placed together without a suitable boundary.
glossary.example: The bell rang the doors opened.

glossary.definition: Independent clauses joined by a comma alone where formal prose needs another boundary or grammatical link.
glossary.example: The bell rang, the doors opened.

glossary.definition: An expression lacking the structure expected of a complete sentence in its writing context.
glossary.example: Although the office was closed.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d14-m04 Clause boundaries and accessible visual parsing H I gv5-topic-d14-c07 gv5-topic-d14-c08 A sentence-boundary error occurs when written clauses are left without the relationship or punctuation their intended construction needs. A bracketed parse can reveal missing main clauses, fused clauses and comma splices. For ordinary formal paragraphs, a subordinate reason clause alone usually leaves the sentence unfinished: because the road was blocked. Adding a main clause completes the intended relationship: because the road was blocked, the delivery arrived late. A fragment may instead lack a main predicate, as in the report beside the printer. That noun phrase is perfectly useful as a label or answer fragment, but it is not a full neutral declarative sentence about what the report did or was. Context decides whether fragmentary wording is a defect or a deliberate feature of a heading, conversation or literary style. Two independent clauses placed together without a suitable boundary form a fused sentence: the lights failed the audience waited. Joining them only with a comma creates a comma splice: the lights failed, the audience waited. Some teaching uses run-on as a broad label for both; this course names the specific error whenever possible. Repairs include a full stop, a semicolon, a coordinator with appropriate punctuation, or subordination that preserves the intended relation. A colon can also join a complete first clause to a second clause that explains or specifies it. Do not use a connector merely because it produces grammatical punctuation; its meaning must fit. A linking adverb does not behave like a coordinating conjunction. The lights failed; however, the audience waited is a grammatical contrast between independent clauses. However does not itself license joining those clauses with a comma alone. Commas around supplementary clauses and introductory material follow additional conventions developed fully in Day 24. A comma before and between short closely connected main clauses can be a style choice; the essential point here is not to separate a subject from its predicate or create a boundary that contradicts the intended structure. Use textual brackets as a visual parsing method that is also readable by assistive technology. In [MAIN the courier waited [SUBORDINATE because the office was closed]], the inner clause supplies a reason within the main construction. More detailed brackets can identify [SUBJECT NP the courier] and [VERB GROUP waited]. A parse is a representation of an analysis, not a substitute for explaining it. If a sentence seems awkward, locate the finite clauses, identify any non-finite complements, label the connectors and then inspect the boundaries. This sequence avoids a common editing error: fixing a perceived comma problem while leaving the actual missing main clause or mistaken logical relationship untouched. [MAIN ... [SUBORDINATE because ...]] A readable nesting shows that the reason clause is dependent in the whole construction. independent clause ; however, independent clause A semicolon or full stop supplies the boundary; however signals a logical contrast. The path was flooded. We took the bridge. Two independent sentences have an explicit full-stop boundary. The path was flooded, so we took the bridge. So coordinates two clauses while expressing the resulting action. [MAIN We took the bridge [SUBORDINATE because the path was flooded]]. The bracketed parse shows the reason clause as subordinate to the main message. Although the deadline had passed. The office accepted the form. Although the deadline had passed, the office accepted the form. The first is fragmentary as ordinary connected formal prose; the second joins the concession clause to its main clause. Fragments are normal in headings and many conversational answers; the requirement for full sentences concerns the specified writing context. Run-on has broad and narrow teaching uses. Naming fused sentence or comma splice avoids a terminology-based false disagreement. The forms arrived, we checked them. The forms arrived; we checked them. A comma alone does not supply the intended formal boundary between independent clauses. The proposal was expensive, however it was approved. The proposal was expensive; however, it was approved. However is a linking adverb here; the independent clauses need their own licensed boundary. fused sentence Independent clauses placed together without a suitable boundary. The bell rang the doors opened. comma splice Independent clauses joined by a comma alone where formal prose needs another boundary or grammatical link. The bell rang, the doors opened. sentence fragment An expression lacking the structure expected of a complete sentence in its writing context. Although the office was closed. source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5 source-1ceaeffe194685 source-93f2b5c2495752 source-701ec209075aec

concepts.title: Defining and supplementary relative information
concepts.definition: A relative clause connects to an antecedent through a grammatical relation within the clause. Integrated or defining relatives help identify or delimit a referent; supplementary or non-defining relatives add a separate associated comment.

glossary.definition: The expression to which a relative or referring expression is related.
glossary.example: the author in the author who spoke

glossary.definition: A relative clause presented as a separate comment about an identified referent or situation.
glossary.example: The author, who arrived late, apologised.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d15-m01 Defining and supplementary relative information I gv5-topic-d15-c01 gv5-topic-d15-c02 A relative clause connects to an antecedent through a grammatical relation within the clause. Integrated or defining relatives help identify or delimit a referent; supplementary or non-defining relatives add a separate associated comment. In the students who arrived early found seats, who arrived early helps identify the relevant students. The relative clause is integrated into the noun phrase, so ordinary written presentation does not enclose it in commas. In the students, who arrived early, found seats, the relative is a supplementary comment about the already identified students. The punctuation signals a different organisation of information, not simply a longer pause. Whether the speaker has one brother or several, or one class or several, cannot be inferred reliably from a noun phrase in isolation without its discourse context. Who commonly relates to people; which commonly relates to things and can also introduce a comment about a whole preceding proposition. Whose marks a genitive relation and can refer to people or other entities: the school whose roof collapsed. Whom is an object form favoured in formal styles, especially after a fronted preposition. Object who is ordinary standard usage in many contexts, as in the colleague who we met. That introduces integrated relatives about people or things in established usage; it does not introduce the ordinary comma-marked supplementary pattern in edited standard English. Restrictive which is grammatical in British English: the route which passes the lake. Many American editorial guides prefer that for such integrated relatives, but that preference is not a universal grammatical ban on which. A relative preposition can remain at the end of a clause or move before an appropriate relative pronoun: the proposal which we agreed on; the proposal on which we agreed. That does not normally follow a fronted preposition in this construction. A whole-clause supplementary relative uses which: the train was cancelled, which delayed the meeting. Here which refers to the cancellation situation, not simply to the noun train. Relative pronouns have a function inside their clause. In the student who wrote the letter, who is subject of wrote. In the student whom the tutor praised, whom is object of praised while the tutor is the expressed subject. Avoid choosing case by the pronoun's distance from the main verb. Traditional accounts call relative that a pronoun; many modern analyses treat it as a subordinator with an associated gap. This course accepts either terminology when it is applied consistently and the missing subject or object relation is identified. Also distinguish supplement from a claim that information is unimportant: a non-defining relative can contain information central to the writer's purpose. noun + integrated relative clause The relative contributes to identifying or delimiting the noun’s referent. identified noun phrase, supplementary relative, main predicate The comma pair marks a separate associated comment. The visitors who had booked online entered first. The integrated relative restricts the relevant set to online bookers. Dr Malik, whose research concerns wetlands, joined the panel. Whose links Dr Malik to the research in a supplementary relative. The server stopped during registration, which prevented several applicants from finishing. Which refers to the preceding event or situation as a whole. My cousins who live nearby visit often. My cousins, who live nearby, visit often. The first identifies the nearby cousins within a contextually relevant set; the second treats the living-nearby information as a supplement about the identified cousins. Restrictive which is established British usage; an American house-style preference for that should be labelled as style. Whose can have a non-human antecedent: a building whose entrance faces the square. Object who is common standard usage; whom remains useful in formal constructions and after fronted prepositions. The hall, that was renovated last year, reopened. The hall, which was renovated last year, reopened. The ordinary supplementary relative uses which rather than that. The officer to that we wrote has replied. The officer to whom we wrote has replied. A fronted preposition takes the appropriate relative pronoun, not relative that. antecedent The expression to which a relative or referring expression is related. the author in the author who spoke supplementary relative A relative clause presented as a separate comment about an identified referent or situation. The author, who arrived late, apologised. source-e3ac7fb8fbb2e1 source-5b7819d35530f4 source-028ce099d2bb32 source-70e3bfdac01616

concepts.title: Contact clauses and non-finite relatives
concepts.definition: A contact relative omits an overt relative marker in an integrated construction where omission is licensed. Non-finite relatives use infinitival or participial structure rather than a full finite relative clause.

glossary.definition: An integrated relative clause with no overt relative marker where omission is licensed.
glossary.example: the story I read

glossary.definition: A relative-like postmodifier with infinitival or participial structure.
glossary.example: the documents signed yesterday

concepts.searchText: gv5-d15-m02 Contact clauses and non-finite relatives I gv5-topic-d15-c03 A contact relative omits an overt relative marker in an integrated construction where omission is licensed. Non-finite relatives use infinitival or participial structure rather than a full finite relative clause. In the article that I recommended, that corresponds to the object of recommended. Because the relative is integrated and already contains its subject I, the marker can be omitted: the article I recommended. This is often called a contact or zero relative. It is not simply any relative clause with a word deleted. In the article that changed my view, that corresponds to the subject of changed. Omitting it would remove the subject relation needed by the intended ordinary finite relative, producing the article changed my view as a main-clause pattern rather than the same modifying structure. A contact relative can leave a preposition stranded: the issue we spoke about. It does not license deleting the pronoun from an ordinary supplementary relative: the editor, whom I met yesterday, has replied. Relative adverbs also allow several patterns. The place where we met, the place at which we met and the place we met can each be grammatical with the appropriate sense. The day we met is a familiar integrated temporal relative. Learn the whole construction instead of assuming that every zero relative contains the same kind of missing object. Participial relatives include the people waiting outside and the papers received yesterday. Waiting outside gives a non-finite active description; received yesterday normally gives a passive interpretation. Expanding the first as who are waiting and the second as which were received can clarify their relationships, but a reduced construction is not always produced by mechanically deleting who and be. A finite relative may locate a completed event or express modality that a participial version does not preserve. The author who wrote the letter need not mean the same as the author writing the letter. Preserve the intended time and relation when choosing a shorter structure. Infinitival relatives also have distinct patterns. The next person to speak supplies a subject interpretation for the understood speaker, while a book to read has an understood reader and an object relation to book. For Noor to read can identify that reader explicitly in a book for Noor to read. Expressions traditionally called reduced relatives overlap with participial adjective and postmodifier analyses. A retired teacher contains an attributive participial adjective in a common analysis; it need not be explained by deleting a visible relative-clause sequence. Use the non-finite form because its grammar and meaning fit the context, not because every finite relative is assumed to have one equivalent shorter form. antecedent + subject + finite verb + object gap An integrated object relative may omit its overt marker: the book I borrowed. noun + -ing / past-participial / infinitival clause Non-finite postmodification has different voice, subject and temporal interpretations. The memo we circulated yesterday contains a correction. The integrated object relative has an expressed subject we and no overt marker. The passengers waiting by the exit boarded first. The -ing clause identifies passengers engaged in waiting at the relevant time. The first applicant to finish the task will receive feedback today. The infinitival relative associates the applicant with the subject role of finish. the scientist who discovered the material the scientist examining the material Both are grammatical descriptions but refer to different activities and potentially different times; shortening must preserve the intended information. An ordinary integrated finite subject relative normally retains its marker: the student who arrived, rather than omitting who within the same construction. Contact relatives are not the ordinary pattern for comma-marked supplementary information. Participial and infinitival relatives do not preserve every tense, aspect or modal distinction of a possible finite version. The volunteer arrived early received a badge, intending a single noun phrase followed by received. The volunteer who arrived early received a badge. The intended finite subject relative needs an overt marker. The files, I requested yesterday, have arrived, intending a supplementary relative. The files, which I requested yesterday, have arrived. The ordinary supplementary relative retains which; an integrated version can instead omit both commas and marker. contact relative An integrated relative clause with no overt relative marker where omission is licensed. the story I read non-finite relative A relative-like postmodifier with infinitival or participial structure. the documents signed yesterday source-e3ac7fb8fbb2e1 source-a70db92421dbc9 source-5b7819d35530f4 source-70e3bfdac01616

concepts.title: Content, nominal and embedded interrogative structures
concepts.definition: A content clause expresses a proposition, question or other content associated with a selecting word. Traditional nominal-clause labels describe some external functions; they do not mean that the internal clause has become a noun word.

glossary.definition: A clause expressing content associated with a selecting verb, noun or adjective.
glossary.example: that the result is final in We believe that the result is final

glossary.definition: An expression combining an antecedent-like meaning with a relative relation.
glossary.example: what she wrote meaning the thing that she wrote

glossary.definition: An interrogative clause functioning within a larger construction.
glossary.example: where she went in I wonder where she went

concepts.searchText: gv5-d15-m03 Content, nominal and embedded interrogative structures I gv5-topic-d15-c04 gv5-topic-d15-c05 gv5-topic-d15-c06 A content clause expresses a proposition, question or other content associated with a selecting word. Traditional nominal-clause labels describe some external functions; they do not mean that the internal clause has become a noun word. In she believes that the timetable is wrong, the that-clause supplies what she believes. It is a content complement of believes. Similar clauses can follow nouns and adjectives: the claim that the timetable is wrong; certain that the timetable is wrong. That introduces the clause but does not serve as its subject or object. Compare the claim that she repeated: here the relative clause has an object relation missing after repeated, linked to claim. In the claim that the timetable is wrong, the subordinate clause is internally complete and states the content of the claim. Embedded questions express a question within another construction: I wonder whether the hall is open; she asked why the hall had closed. They normally use subject-before-verb order rather than direct-question inversion. Subject questions remain recognisable: I know who sent the message has who as subject of sent. Whether and if can introduce many embedded yes-no questions, but they are not interchangeable in every construction. Before a to-infinitive, use whether: she cannot decide whether to apply. The question clause whether the hall is open can also function as a subject; for formal clarity, whether is the normal choice in that position. Wh-expressions have more than one analysis. I wonder what she wrote presents an embedded question about the identity of her writing. I kept what she wrote can mean I kept the thing that she wrote; this is a fused-relative expression, with what combining an antecedent-like meaning and a relative relation. Many modern accounts analyse the whole fused relative as a noun phrase containing a relative clause; traditional accounts often group it with nominal clauses. State the intended interpretation and grammatical function instead of assuming that every what-clause is an indirect question. Context can also leave a genuine ambiguity between question-like content and reference to a thing. Infinitival complements express selected relationships too. She hopes to finish normally makes she the understood finisher; she wants the assistant to finish expresses the subordinate subject. An extraposed pattern moves a heavy subject clause into a later position: that the hall is open is useful becomes it is useful that the hall is open. The it in that construction does not refer to a previously named hall; it fills the ordinary subject position. Not all verbs license the same complement types or allow the same alternations. Compare suggest that she apply or suggest applying with tell her to apply. Advanced transformation therefore begins with the selecting word's pattern, the subordinate subject and the original degree of certainty or obligation. verb/adjective/noun + that + finite content clause The subordinate clause gives associated content; introductory that is not its subject or object. whether + to-infinitive An embedded alternative can be expressed non-finitely: whether to leave. The report confirms that the water is safe. The internally complete that-clause states what the report confirms. I cannot remember where I stored the invoice. The embedded question keeps subject I before stored. What the witnesses described was difficult to verify. A natural reading treats what the witnesses described as the things or account described, functioning as the sentence subject. the claim that the board rejected the claim that the board had resigned The first is relative, with a missing object after rejected; the second supplies the content of the claim and is internally complete. That is often omitted after some reporting and mental-process verbs, but omission depends on the construction and clarity; it is not a compulsory deletion rule. Whether is used before a to-infinitive; if to apply does not form the corresponding standard embedded-question pattern. A what-expression may be an embedded question or a fused relative, depending on interpretation and the selecting construction. She asked where was the register. She asked where the register was. An embedded question normally has subject-before-verb order. They suggested me to postpone the launch. They suggested that I postpone the launch. Suggest does not license the intended personal-object + to-infinitive pattern; a mandative clause preserves the recommendation. content clause A clause expressing content associated with a selecting verb, noun or adjective. that the result is final in We believe that the result is final fused relative An expression combining an antecedent-like meaning with a relative relation. what she wrote meaning the thing that she wrote embedded question An interrogative clause functioning within a larger construction. where she went in I wonder where she went source-1ceaeffe194685 source-d6af2eef369812 source-89176b529bbc02 source-ccfbea5f751a50 source-a70db92421dbc9

concepts.title: Adverbial clauses and semantic relationships
concepts.definition: An adverbial or adjunct clause adds a circumstance or logical relationship to another situation, including time, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession, manner or comparison.

glossary.definition: A clause functioning as an adjunct expressing a circumstance or logical relation.
glossary.example: when the meeting ended in We left when the meeting ended

glossary.definition: A relation presenting a potential obstacle or contrary expectation alongside the main situation.
glossary.example: although the route was longer

glossary.definition: A clause expressing an intended outcome or goal.
glossary.example: so that we could finish

concepts.searchText: gv5-d15-m04 Adverbial clauses and semantic relationships I gv5-topic-d15-c07 gv5-topic-d15-c08 gv5-topic-d15-c09 An adverbial or adjunct clause adds a circumstance or logical relationship to another situation, including time, reason, purpose, result, condition, concession, manner or comparison. Choose an adjunct clause by the relation you intend. We left when the rain stopped locates an event in time. We left because the room was closing gives a reason. We left early so that we could catch the train expresses purpose. The room was so crowded that we could not enter expresses a result associated with the degree of crowding. These constructions do different jobs even when all describe connected events. A cause reported by the writer is not automatically a proven scientific cause; grammatical linkage expresses the relationship being asserted in that particular account. Time clauses can use when, while, before, after, until and once. Their tense choices depend on reference and meaning rather than a universal requirement to repeat the main clause's tense. In the office will open when the repairs are complete, present form refers to future time in the subordinate clause. Reason can be expressed with because, since or as, but since and as also have other senses. Make a relation explicit if ambiguity matters. Because of the cancellation is a prepositional phrase with a noun-phrase complement in the traditional account; because the service was cancelled is a finite reason clause. Concession presents a circumstance against which the main event is unexpected: although the route was longer, we chose it. Condition sets a situation relevant to the main proposition: if the permit arrives, we can begin. Unless often expresses a negative condition, but replacing every if-not construction mechanically can change scope or emphasis. Manner and comparison can use as, as if, as though and than in their appropriate patterns: arrange the folders as the instructions show; she spoke as if she knew the answer; the task took longer than we expected. The hypothetical interpretation of as if is developed further in Day 18. A clause's function should not be inferred from its opening word alone. As the bell rang can express timing, while as the hall was already full may be understood as a reason in context. So that can express an intended purpose or an actual consequence, depending on context, modality and the rest of the wording. Non-finite purpose clauses such as to avoid a delay normally share an understood subject with the main clause in the relevant construction; for a different participant, name that subject or choose a finite clause. Some modern grammars classify many traditional subordinating conjunctions as prepositions taking clause complements. This terminology difference does not remove the temporal, causal or conditional relation that learners must interpret and preserve in writing. main clause + so that + subject + can/could + verb A common finite purpose pattern; context determines whether it describes an intention. so + adjective/adverb + that + result clause A result construction associates degree with a consequent situation. We paused while the technician tested the microphone. The while-clause locates the pause during a simultaneous activity. The adviser repeated the address so that the visitors could write it down. The finite purpose clause has its own subject the visitors, distinct from the adviser. Although the evidence was limited, the report reached a firm conclusion. The concession presents a potential obstacle to the main action without asserting that the conclusion was justified. She lowered her voice because the baby was asleep.
