She lowered her voice so that the baby could sleep. Both grammatical: the first supplies a reason involving an existing state; the second expresses a purpose concerning a possible result. Since and as have more than one meaning; context, not spelling alone, identifies a time, cause or manner relation. A purpose clause with an understood subject must connect to the intended participant: to inspect the roof, the engineer climbed the ladder. Different grammatical frameworks classify clause-introducing words differently; the pedagogical function labels remain useful if the framework is stated. Because of the office had closed, we returned home. Because the office had closed, we returned home. The full finite clause takes because rather than because of in this construction. To collect the documents, the door was opened by the assistant, intending that the assistant collected them. To collect the documents, the assistant opened the door. Make the intended collector the main subject for this purpose construction. adverbial clause A clause functioning as an adjunct expressing a circumstance or logical relation. when the meeting ended in We left when the meeting ended concession A relation presenting a potential obstacle or contrary expectation alongside the main situation. although the route was longer purpose clause A clause expressing an intended outcome or goal. so that we could finish source-701ec209075aec source-1ceaeffe194685 source-a70db92421dbc9 source-89176b529bbc02 source-70e3bfdac01616

concepts.title: Coordination and subordination: what is connected
concepts.definition: Coordination places units alongside one another at the same structural level; subordination makes one clause dependent within a larger structure.

glossary.definition: A relation joining units at the same structural level.
glossary.example: forms and receipts

glossary.definition: A relation in which one clause is dependent within a larger structure.
glossary.example: We waited because the road flooded.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d16-m01 Coordination and subordination: what is connected H M gv5-topic-d16-c01 gv5-topic-d16-c02 Coordination places units alongside one another at the same structural level; subordination makes one clause dependent within a larger structure. Start by finding the units being joined. In tea and coffee, and joins two nouns. In unusually calm and very patient, it joins two adjective phrases. In The alarm sounded and the staff left, it joins clauses. A clause normally contains a predicate; the second clause may repeat a subject or share material with the first. Subordination is different: because the alarm sounded gives a reason inside a larger sentence. Neither arrangement is inherently more sophisticated; choose the structure that represents the intended relation. Coordinators include and, or and but; traditional school lists also include for, nor, so and yet. Their distributions are not identical. And can combine many kinds of unit, while causal for is mainly a clause connector in relatively formal writing. A subordinator such as although or if introduces a dependent clause. A sentence may contain both: Although the alarm sounded, the staff waited and the manager checked the corridor. First identify the outer concession, then the coordination inside the main part. Shared material avoids unnecessary repetition: The librarian checked and stamped the forms shares a subject and an object across coordinated predicates. Repetition is sometimes useful for emphasis or disambiguation. Coordination does not demand that every item have the same spelling or length. Even different phrase categories can perform compatible functions: The room was quiet and without windows coordinates an adjective phrase and a prepositional phrase as predicative descriptions. The editing question is whether each item fits the surrounding construction and the intended meaning. Grammatical frameworks differ over the membership of the conjunction category and the analysis of clause-linking so or temporal after. The course uses familiar school labels while keeping category separate from function. Brackets reveal hierarchy: [Mina checked the register] and [Omar locked the door] has two coordinated clauses; Mina [checked the register and locked the door] has coordinated predicates. These descriptions explain structure without requiring a claim that every coordinated unit is an independent sentence. A repeated subject, a finite verb and the wider context help decide the analysis. X and Y Both units contribute at the same structural level. although + clause, main clause The main assertion holds despite a contrasting circumstance. The workshop supplies paper and ink. Two noun heads form the direct-object coordination. The workshop was inexpensive but exceptionally useful. But coordinates two predicative adjective phrases. Although the hall was small, the speakers arrived early and the audience stayed. One subordinate concession precedes two coordinated main clauses. The hall closed because the ceiling was unsafe. The hall closed, and the ceiling was unsafe. Both grammatical: because asserts a reason; and alone does not specify that causal relation. Unlike categories can coordinate when their functions are compatible: calm and in control are both predicative descriptions. Surface uniformity is a useful style preference, not an exceptionless syntax law. The scheme combines training and to employ graduates. The scheme combines training and employment for graduates. The second unit must fit as a complement of combines; a bare to-infinitival goal does not fit this intended list. Although the road flooded. The bus continued. Although the road flooded, the bus continued. In this intended single concession, the dependent clause needs integration with the main assertion. coordination A relation joining units at the same structural level. forms and receipts subordination A relation in which one clause is dependent within a larger structure. We waited because the road flooded. source-701ec209075aec source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5

concepts.title: Correlative patterns, agreement and balanced alternatives
concepts.definition: Correlative expressions distribute a relationship across two positions, such as both … and or either … or; their placement identifies what is being paired.

glossary.definition: An expression with related markers in two positions.
glossary.example: either tea or coffee

glossary.definition: The part of a meaning over which an expression operates.
glossary.example: Not both passed allows one to pass.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d16-m02 Correlative patterns, agreement and balanced alternatives H M gv5-topic-d16-c03 gv5-topic-d16-c04 Correlative expressions distribute a relationship across two positions, such as both … and or either … or; their placement identifies what is being paired. Both the receptionist and the technician attended includes two people. Either the receptionist or the technician will attend presents alternatives. Neither attended excludes both in that context. Not only adds emphasis to an inclusion: The visit was not only useful but also inexpensive. Place the first marker before the first intended unit, then make sure that the second unit can complete the same surrounding construction. Read the whole meaning before editing, because moving either or not only can change which alternatives are being offered. A subject coordinated with and normally takes plural agreement: Both the map and the timetable are useful. A single package or conventional combination can instead receive singular notional agreement: Bread and butter is all that is available. With either … or and neither … nor, mixed singular and plural subjects create variation and possible awkwardness. Agreement with the nearer subject is a common editorial solution: Either the assistant or the supervisors are attending. Recasting often gives a clearer result than treating proximity as a universal linguistic law. Fronted not only normally triggers subject–auxiliary inversion when it introduces a clause: Not only did the team finish early, but it also documented the process. Within a predicate no such inversion is needed: The team not only finished early but also documented the process. Also is optional in some not only … but constructions. Correlative markers do not make every imperfectly symmetrical sentence ungrammatical; what matters first is whether the coordinated units fit the same syntactic position and whether the contrast is intelligible. Negation and scope require careful reading. Neither the manager nor the deputy signed says that each failed to sign; Not both signed excludes joint success but allows one signature. Either in an ordinary choice often suggests one alternative rather than both, but inclusive or is possible where context allows it. An instruction should say whether multiple selections are permitted. In formal editing, preserve these logical differences rather than replacing all negative or alternative expressions mechanically. Grammatical agreement, logical inclusion and stylistic balance are related questions that should be diagnosed separately. both X and Y Includes both coordinated alternatives. not both X and Y Denies their joint inclusion; it does not necessarily exclude each separately. Both the labels and the seals are missing. Plural coordination takes are. Either the supervisor or the two assistants are available. The nearer plural encourages are; recasting avoids mixed-number awkwardness. Not only has the archive expanded, but its catalogue has also become searchable. Fronting licenses has before the subject; the second clause states an additional improvement. Neither application was approved. Not both applications were approved. Both grammatical; the first excludes approval of either, the second allows one approval. Some conventional and-coordinations describe one unit and take singular agreement. If mixed-number or-coordination sounds strained, use two clauses rather than force a contested agreement choice. Not only the team did finish early, but it also checked every form. Not only did the team finish early, but it also checked every form. Fronted clause-level not only triggers auxiliary inversion. Both the labels and the seal is missing. Both the labels and the seal are missing. The intended subject includes separate items joined by and. correlative An expression with related markers in two positions. either tea or coffee scope The part of a meaning over which an expression operates. Not both passed allows one to pass. source-701ec209075aec source-8db1cebfd15ccb source-287989cd31ff3a

concepts.title: Logic: addition, contrast, concession and qualification
concepts.definition: A logical connector signals the relationship a writer intends between propositions; grammatical form alone does not prove that the relationship is factually justified.

glossary.definition: A relation in which an assertion holds despite a contrary expectation.
glossary.example: Although tired, she continued.

glossary.definition: A limitation on the conditions or strength of a claim.
glossary.example: The estimate is reliable if the records are complete.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d16-m03 Logic: addition, contrast, concession and qualification H M gv5-topic-d16-c05 gv5-topic-d16-c06 A logical connector signals the relationship a writer intends between propositions; grammatical form alone does not prove that the relationship is factually justified. Addition presents another relevant point: The room is accessible; moreover, it has hearing assistance. Contrast presents a difference: The morning group worked online, whereas the evening group met in person. Concession goes further: Although the room was small, everyone found a seat presents the second fact as holding against an expectation raised by the first. Qualification limits a claim: The method is useful, provided that the samples are representative. Read the underlying claims first, then select a relationship that the evidence supports. Because introduces a reason; so can introduce a result; so that commonly introduces purpose or result depending on context. We moved the display so that visitors could see it states an intended goal. We moved it, so visitors could see it more directly presents the resulting consequence. Before, after and then organise sequence without necessarily asserting causation. Or offers an alternative, while otherwise can introduce the consequence of rejecting an option: Submit the form today; otherwise, processing will be delayed. Each relationship needs enough context to distinguish it from plausible alternatives. Unless normally means if not in an exceptive condition, but replacing it mechanically can disturb scope. Do not enter unless authorised means authorisation is necessary for entry; it does not promise that every authorised person will enter. While can mark time or contrast; since can mark time or reason. A reader may need a less ambiguous connector when both readings are plausible. Moreover adds information but does not itself turn it into proof. Therefore presents an inference whose validity must be assessed independently of the grammar. Discourse relations can be implicit: The road flooded. The delivery was late leaves a causal connection available without explicitly asserting it. Choosing because commits the writer more strongly to that explanation. Likewise a contrast is not automatically a concession; two different timetables need not violate anyone's expectation. Advanced revision should ask whose expectation a concessive clause invokes, what a qualification excludes and whether an apparent inference reverses cause and effect. These questions connect grammar to pragmatic interpretation while preserving a distinction between a well-formed sentence and a sound argument. because + reason clause Presents the reason for the associated assertion. so that + finite clause Often states an intended purpose; context can support a result reading. We chose the ground floor because the lift was unavailable. The subordinate clause supplies the stated reason. The lift was unavailable; nevertheless, all visitors reached the exhibition. Nevertheless marks a result contrary to a likely expectation. The trial is promising, although its small sample limits the conclusion. The concession qualifies the positive assessment rather than cancelling it. The alarm sounded before the doors opened. The alarm sounded because the doors opened. Both grammatical: the first orders events; the second makes a causal assertion. A connector can have several senses: since Monday marks a starting point, whereas since nobody objected can introduce a reason. Analyse the complement and context together. The alarm sounded, therefore we should ignore it. [intended consequence: evacuate] The alarm sounded; therefore, we should evacuate. The original contradicts the stated practical inference; punctuation also needs a clause boundary. We installed a ramp so as visitors could enter. We installed a ramp so that visitors could enter. A finite clause with visitors requires so that, not the infinitival expression so as to. concession A relation in which an assertion holds despite a contrary expectation. Although tired, she continued. qualification A limitation on the conditions or strength of a claim. The estimate is reliable if the records are complete. source-701ec209075aec

concepts.title: Connector classes and punctuation in use
concepts.definition: A conjunction links syntactic units; a linking adverb or discourse marker signals a relationship without necessarily supplying the grammatical clause boundary.

glossary.definition: An adverb that signals a discourse relation between propositions.
glossary.example: The road closed; consequently, we turned back.

glossary.definition: An expression that helps organise discourse or signal a relation between contributions; it need not join clauses syntactically.
glossary.example: However can signal contrast between two punctuated sentences.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d16-m04 Connector classes and punctuation in use H M gv5-topic-d16-c07 A conjunction links syntactic units; a linking adverb or discourse marker signals a relationship without necessarily supplying the grammatical clause boundary. Compare Although it rained, the match continued with Despite the rain, the match continued. Although introduces a finite clause; despite takes a noun phrase here. However behaves differently: It rained; however, the match continued. In this formal written pattern the semicolon separates the independent clauses, while however signals concession. A full stop is equally possible. Do not decide punctuation merely by where you pause aloud. First decide whether there are two independent clauses, a main clause plus dependent material, or a phrase within one clause. The neutral pattern for two independent clauses joined by a coordinator is often a comma before and, but or so. Very short clauses may omit it, and complex clauses may justify stronger separation under an editorial style. An introductory subordinate clause usually ends with a comma. A following reason clause often needs no comma, but punctuation may distinguish supplementary reasoning or remove ambiguity. However can move inside a clause: The match, however, continued. Because cannot move in the same way while retaining the same clause structure. A word's traditional class can differ between constructions. Before lunch is prepositional; before we ate is traditionally subordinating. Contemporary grammars may analyse before as a preposition in both, with different complement types. This is a difference in framework, not an error in the sentence. Notwithstanding also has a less common formal conjunction use with a finite clause, alongside its prepositional use. Do not reject a construction simply because a beginner table lists only its most frequent pattern. Check the actual lexical entry and the intended register. Discourse markers such as well, anyway and in fact organise conversation or an argument as well as local logical relations. Their presence cannot repair a run-on: The queue grew however the gate stayed shut still needs punctuation in edited prose. Conversely a sentence beginning with And or But is not automatically ungrammatical; its appropriateness depends on continuity and editorial style. A reliable diagnosis identifies the missing boundary, the connector's role and any genuine semantic inconsistency. It does not count the number of linking words and infer a fault without examining their scope. independent clause; however, independent clause Two assertions plus an explicit contrast. because of + noun phrase A reason expressed through a prepositional phrase. The bus was late because of a diversion. Because of takes the noun phrase a diversion. The bus was late because the road was closed. Because introduces a finite reason clause. The report was short. It was, however, fully documented. A sentence boundary separates the assertions; paired commas mark medial however. Despite the delay, the hearing continued. Although the hearing was delayed, it continued. Both grammatical; the prepositional and clausal complements have different internal structures. Some punctuation choices depend on style and clause length. Sentence-initial And/But and formal conjunctive notwithstanding are legitimate; do not label them universally incorrect. Despite of the delay, the hearing continued. Despite the delay, the hearing continued. The standard expression is despite, or alternatively in spite of. The hall filled, however the doors remained open. The hall filled; however, the doors remained open. However does not by itself license this comma splice in edited prose. conjunctive adverb An adverb that signals a discourse relation between propositions. The road closed; consequently, we turned back. discourse marker An expression that helps organise discourse or signal a relation between contributions; it need not join clauses syntactically. However can signal contrast between two punctuated sentences. source-701ec209075aec source-93f2b5c2495752

concepts.title: Core modals, marginal forms and substitutes
concepts.definition: Core modal auxiliaries are a small class including can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should and must; related expressions share some, but not all, of their grammatical behaviour.

glossary.definition: An auxiliary expressing meanings such as possibility, obligation or willingness.
glossary.example: They may arrive.

glossary.definition: A label for an expression with some modal properties and some ordinary verb properties.
glossary.example: Do we need to wait?

concepts.searchText: gv5-d17-m01 Core modals, marginal forms and substitutes D K gv5-topic-d17-c04 Core modal auxiliaries are a small class including can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should and must; related expressions share some, but not all, of their grammatical behaviour. A core modal comes before the base form of the next verb: can swim, might leave, must be. It has no third-person singular -s: She can swim, not she cans swim. Form a negative directly with not and a question by moving the modal before the subject: She cannot attend; Can she attend? Ordinary do-support is unnecessary. The next verb can itself be an auxiliary: may have arrived, should be working. These simple structural facts apply even when the whole verb phrase expresses a complicated time relationship. Core modals lack ordinary infinitival and participial forms. To express ability after want, use want to be able to, not want to can. For a past obligation, had to often supplies a form that must lacks. Ought to contains to, while need and dare have both modal-like and lexical patterns. Compare Need we leave? with Do we need to leave? The former is relatively formal and more characteristic of British usage. Names such as semi-modal and marginal modal vary between grammars; learn the actual pattern rather than assuming all related expressions behave identically. Have to, be able to, be supposed to and be allowed to use ordinary auxiliary and tense machinery: Does she have to leave? She has been able to work. They can follow a core modal: She may have to leave. Two core modals do not normally appear together in the edited international standard taught here; use might be able to rather than might can. Some regional English varieties permit multiple modals. Describing that variation does not make the form appropriate for every written context, nor does the course default make the regional construction meaningless. Modal form and temporal meaning are not a simple present/past table. Could can describe earlier ability, present tentative possibility or a polite request; would can describe reported future reference, willingness or a hypothetical result. A core modal may stand alone when its complement is recoverable: Can she attend? She can. This is ellipsis, not an incomplete sentence. When analysing a modal chain, identify the finite modal first, then each following auxiliary and its required verb form. This prevents incorrect forms such as should has gone or must to leave without making an inaccurate claim that every word following a modal is a lexical infinitive. modal + base form The base form can be a lexical verb or an auxiliary. modal + subject + base form? Canonical interrogative order without do-support. Nida can swim. Can has no -s with the singular subject. Does Nida have to swim today? Have to uses do-support here; it is not a core modal. Nida might have been swimming when the call arrived. Might precedes perfect have, participial been and progressive swimming. Need we print the agenda? Do we need to print the agenda? Both grammatical: modal-like need is more formal; lexical need takes to and do-support. Related expressions need individual patterns: ought to includes to, but core should takes a base form. Recoverable complements may be omitted: Yes, she can. She cans attend tomorrow. She can attend tomorrow. Core can has no third-person -s. Do you must leave? Must you leave? A core modal forms the question through inversion, not do-support. modal auxiliary An auxiliary expressing meanings such as possibility, obligation or willingness. They may arrive. semi-modal A label for an expression with some modal properties and some ordinary verb properties. Do we need to wait? source-10e4340e83d799 source-32e349b2ed28e5 source-7bb68e7575962d

concepts.title: Ability, permission, necessity and inference
concepts.definition: Modal meaning includes judgments about what is possible or likely and attitudes towards what people are able, permitted, required or willing to do.

glossary.definition: An inference based on evidence or assumptions.
glossary.example: She must be home; her car is outside.

glossary.definition: A requirement that an action not occur.
glossary.example: Visitors must not touch the exhibits.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d17-m02 Ability, permission, necessity and inference D K gv5-topic-d17-c01 gv5-topic-d17-c02 gv5-topic-d17-c03 Modal meaning includes judgments about what is possible or likely and attitudes towards what people are able, permitted, required or willing to do. Use can for present ability in a suitable context: Farah can read the script. Can or may can grant permission, with may often more formal. Must can impose a strong obligation; must not can prohibit. Do not confuse prohibition with absence of obligation: You must not enter excludes entry; You do not have to enter permits a choice. Should commonly gives advice or expresses an expected outcome. The same words can serve different purposes, so a label should explain the sentence in context rather than become a permanent dictionary tag. Could often describes general past ability: At ten, she could swim well. For a specific successful event, managed to or was able to is often clearer: Despite the current, she managed to reach the bank. However could occurs naturally in many negative, perception and mental-activity contexts: I could hear the bell. Will can express prediction, willingness, insistence or a promise. Would commonly softens a request: Would you close the door? The interrogative asks about willingness on its surface but usually functions as a request, not a test of physical ability. Deductive must presents a conclusion drawn from evidence: The lights are on; someone must be inside. Deductive cannot rejects a possibility: She cannot be inside; the room was sealed before she arrived. This is different from cannot as prohibition or inability. May not is particularly scope-sensitive: The office may not open means opening is uncertain, whereas You may not enter in an official notice normally denies permission. Should can express expectation as well as advice: The parcel should arrive today. A speaker's confidence is affected by evidence and the type of statement, so a universal numerical ranking is misleading. Necessity and possibility are interpreted relative to assumptions, rules, abilities or evidence. In deontic necessity, the relevant background includes regulations; in epistemic necessity, it includes what the speaker believes the evidence establishes. Neither use automatically guarantees compliance or factual truth. The student must attend does not assert attendance, and The student must be attending is a strong inference that may prove mistaken. Advanced interpretation therefore separates the modal's type from the truth of its complement. A precise explanation says what the speaker commits to and what remains open, rather than replacing a modal with an unconditional assertion. must not + verb Commonly prohibits the action. do not have to + verb Expresses lack of necessity; it does not by itself prohibit. You may use the side entrance. In this permission context, may authorises entry. The courier should arrive before noon. Should states an expectation rather than an obligation imposed on the speaker. The laboratory must be empty: its lights are off and the staff have left. Must presents an evidence-based inference, not an order to empty the room. You must not submit a duplicate. You do not have to submit a duplicate. Both grammatical: prohibition versus absence of obligation. Could is not excluded from every specific past event: I could hear the warning is natural. Distinguish the meaning and lexical context before replacing it. The rules say entry is optional: You must not enter. The rules say entry is optional: You do not have to enter. The original wording prohibits rather than permits an optional action. I want to can interpret this chart. I want to be able to interpret this chart. Ability after an infinitival complement requires a substitute for core can. deduction An inference based on evidence or assumptions. She must be home; her car is outside. prohibition A requirement that an action not occur. Visitors must not touch the exhibits. source-10e4340e83d799 source-32e349b2ed28e5

concepts.title: Modal perfects: evidence, regret and unnecessary actions
concepts.definition: A modal-perfect construction combines a modal with have and a past participle, often locating a situation before the current or another reference point while retaining the modal meaning.

glossary.definition: A modal followed by have plus a past participle.
glossary.example: The parcel may have arrived.

glossary.definition: A usual interpretation that context can cancel without contradiction.
glossary.example: We did not need to pay, but paid anyway.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d17-m03 Modal perfects: evidence, regret and unnecessary actions D K gv5-topic-d17-c05 gv5-topic-d17-c06 gv5-topic-d17-c07 A modal-perfect construction combines a modal with have and a past participle, often locating a situation before the current or another reference point while retaining the modal meaning. Begin with the form: modal + have + past participle. Must have left draws an inference about a departure; might have left leaves it possible; should have left often evaluates an earlier obligation or sensible action. Have stays in its base form even after a singular subject: she might have gone. The lexical participle must be correct: could have written, not could have wrote. These forms are not all reports of completed facts. Modal meaning determines whether an event is inferred, merely possible, desired or counterfactual. She must have missed the train presents a strong inference. She might have missed it does not assert that she did. She should have checked the timetable often criticises an omission, but should have can also express expectation: The train should have arrived by now, although I have not checked. Could have describes an unrealised opportunity in one context and a possible explanation in another. I could have called, but chose not to is different from That noise could have been the printer. Always identify the time and the intended modal reading before paraphrasing. Need not have + participle normally says an action happened but was unnecessary: I need not have printed the agenda; everyone had a digital copy. Did not need to states lack of necessity; it does not logically settle whether the action happened. We did not need to print it, but we did is coherent. In everyday conversation, did not need to often suggests that the action was omitted, but that inference can be cancelled. A reliable assessment must supply the event facts instead of treating a common implication as a universal rule. The perfect can locate an event before a future reference point: By Friday, the laboratory must have completed the audit can be a requirement with a deadline, rather than a past deduction. Negation also changes modal scope: cannot have left denies the possibility of an earlier departure; might not have left presents the possibility of non-departure. Should not have sent the file usually evaluates sending negatively and commonly implies it happened, but expectation contexts can alter the interpretation. Avoid deriving truth or falsity solely from the modal-perfect shape; test the interpretation against the surrounding discourse. must have + participle Commonly an inference about an earlier situation; context can supply a deadline requirement. need not have + participle An action is treated as having occurred unnecessarily. The gate is locked; the caretaker must have left. An inference concerns an earlier departure. We need not have paid for delivery; collection was free. The payment is presented as having happened unnecessarily. By the next inspection, the contractor must have repaired the roof. The perfect locates required completion before a future deadline. I need not have printed it. I did not need to print it, but I did. Both present unnecessary printing as actual; the second makes actuality explicit because did not need to alone leaves it open. Did not need to often suggests non-performance, but the suggestion is defeasible. Should have may express expectation rather than criticism; do not mark those readings as errors. She might has taken the key. She might have taken the key. Have remains base form after a modal. He should have wrote yesterday. He should have written yesterday. Perfect have requires the past participle written. modal perfect A modal followed by have plus a past participle. The parcel may have arrived. defeasible inference A usual interpretation that context can cancel without contradiction. We did not need to pay, but paid anyway. source-10e4340e83d799 source-7bb68e7575962d source-32e349b2ed28e5

concepts.title: Epistemic and deontic meaning, hedging and commitment
concepts.definition: Epistemic modality concerns the status of a proposition as possible, probable or necessary given evidence; deontic modality concerns permission, requirements and related norms.

glossary.definition: Concerning the assessment of knowledge or evidence.
glossary.example: The lights are on; she must be there.

glossary.definition: Concerning permission, obligation or norms.
glossary.example: You must wear a badge.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d17-m04 Epistemic and deontic meaning, hedging and commitment D K gv5-topic-d17-c08 gv5-topic-d17-c09 Epistemic modality concerns the status of a proposition as possible, probable or necessary given evidence; deontic modality concerns permission, requirements and related norms. Compare The visitor must be in the lobby with The visitor must sign the register. The first is usually an inference; the second is usually a requirement. These labels help explain why the same auxiliary has different paraphrases. Academic and professional writing often needs a calibrated degree of commitment. The results suggest that the treatment may help makes a limited claim. The treatment helps states the conclusion more directly. A hedge is useful when it reflects uncertainty or a restricted evidential basis, not when it merely makes a sentence longer. Hedging can use modals, adverbs and lexical verbs: may, might, possibly, probably, appear and suggest. These expressions interact with context rather than assign fixed percentages. Probably is stronger than possibly in ordinary neutral use, but a whole sentence's force also depends on its evidence and qualifications. The proposal may reduce delays in small offices limits both certainty and domain. Removing in small offices broadens the claim even if may stays. In revision, track the population, time, conditions and strength of the original assertion as well as its verb form. Over-hedging can obscure a well-supported statement: It may perhaps possibly be the case that the meter is faulty stacks similar reservations without specifying the uncertainty. Prefer The meter may be faulty; a second test is needed. Conversely a legal requirement should not be weakened accidentally: Staff must report hazards is not equivalent to Staff might report hazards. Politeness may soften how a request is expressed without changing the speaker's practical expectation. Would you please send the invoice? still requests action, although its form is an interrogative about willingness. Scope distinguishes a possibility of a negative proposition from a denial of possibility: It may not be safe leaves open that it is unsafe; It cannot be safe presents safety as excluded by the evidence. An epistemic statement can still be mistaken, and a deontic rule can still be broken. Transparent analysis should therefore state the modal base in plain language: given the available evidence, under the rules, or with the person's present abilities. These are explanatory paraphrases, not rigid word-by-word translations. The goal is to preserve a writer's justified commitment and a reader's ability to see what supports it. may + base-form verb phrase The modal can express possibility and takes semantic scope over the proposition. must + base-form verb phrase The modal can express a requirement or inference, according to context. The device may fail at very low temperatures. A possibility is limited to a stated condition. Operators must disconnect the power before cleaning. The modal expresses a procedural obligation. The small trial suggests a benefit, but larger studies are needed before a general recommendation. The claim's scope and evidence are explicitly qualified rather than ornamented. The report may be inaccurate. The report must be inaccurate. Both grammatical; the second represents a much stronger inference in the same epistemic context. Formal hedging need not use a modal: The evidence is limited is a direct, precise statement of a limitation. A hedge must not silently weaken a quoted obligation. The rule requires disclosure: Applicants might disclose all fees. The rule requires disclosure: Applicants must disclose all fees. Might does not preserve the stated obligation. The data certainly prove a universal benefit. [one small pilot only] The pilot suggests a possible benefit in the sampled group. Limit commitment and population to the stated evidence; the issue is overclaiming, not merely word form. epistemic Concerning the assessment of knowledge or evidence. The lights are on; she must be there. deontic Concerning permission, obligation or norms. You must wear a badge. source-10e4340e83d799 source-3e3ac15bcaeafc

concepts.title: Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time
concepts.definition: A conditional construction presents one situation as a condition under which another claim, action or conclusion applies. Its verb forms express both time relationships and the speaker’s way of presenting the possibility.

glossary.definition: A conditional presenting fulfilment as unsettled rather than grammatically remote.
glossary.example: If she calls, I will answer.

glossary.definition: An imagined alternative contrary to an established fact.
glossary.example: If I had brought the key, we could have entered; I left it at home.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d18-m01 Conditional meaning: patterns, reality and time I J K gv5-topic-d18-c01 gv5-topic-d18-c02 gv5-topic-d18-c03 A conditional construction presents one situation as a condition under which another claim, action or conclusion applies. Its verb forms express both time relationships and the speaker’s way of presenting the possibility. Start with the intended relationship. If you heat this wax, it melts describes a recurring result under the relevant conditions; this is often called the zero conditional. If the repair is finished tomorrow, we will reopen presents an open future condition, commonly called a first conditional. Present is normally used for future time in that conditional clause. If the repair were cheaper, we would proceed presents a more remote alternative. Past-form were here indicates distance from the actual situation, not a repair that happened yesterday. The second-conditional teaching pattern commonly combines a past form in the if-clause with would, could or might in the result. The third commonly combines past perfect with would/could/might have plus a participle: If we had kept a copy, we could have restored the file. It imagines a different earlier situation. Mixed patterns connect different times: If we had kept a copy, we would have the file now. The condition is earlier; the result concerns the present. Do not add perfect have mechanically to both clauses if the intended result is current. These numbered categories are useful memory aids, not a complete grammar. Real past habits can use past forms in both clauses: If the roads flooded, we stayed home. Open conditions can contain a progressive, perfect or modal: If you have finished, send the form; If you can attend, call us. A condition may concern the appropriateness of a speech act: If you are hungry, there is soup in the kitchen offers useful information; hunger does not cause the soup to exist. Without your notes, I would have missed the detail expresses an implied condition without if. An open condition leaves its fulfilment unsettled in the discourse. A remote condition presents distance, often hypothetical or counterfactual, but remoteness is not a precise probability percentage. Context establishes whether an imagined alternative contradicts known facts. Will and would can occur legitimately in an if-clause when expressing willingness, insistence, politeness or a later consequence: If you will wait here, someone will help you. This differs from mechanically inserting future will in a neutral time condition. State the intended reading before judging a form; an assessment must supply enough context to distinguish a routine future condition from a modal exception. if + present, will/can/may + base A common open future pattern, with the result selected for meaning. if + past, would/could/might + base A common remote present/future pattern. if + past perfect, would/could/might have + participle A common imagined alternative past. if + past perfect, would + base + now An earlier condition with a present hypothetical result. If the sensor detects smoke, the alarm sounds. The present forms describe a designed recurring relationship, not a universal scientific law. If we had booked a room, we would not be searching for one now. The past-perfect condition connects to a present result. If you will sign the register, I can issue a visitor’s pass. Will can solicit willingness; it is not an automatic error inside if. If the door is unlocked, I will enter. If the door were unlocked, I would enter. Both grammatical; the first leaves an open possibility, while the second presents a remote alternative in the stated context. A main clause can be imperative: If you notice damage, report it. A condition can be implied rather than introduced by if: With a stronger signal, we could communicate. If the road were open now, we would have drive through it now. If the road were open now, we would drive through it now. For the intended present result, use would plus base drive; the original chain is malformed. If I had saved it yesterday, I would have it now. [declared impossible because “mixed”] No change. The earlier saving condition and present possession result legitimately have different time reference. open conditional A conditional presenting fulfilment as unsettled rather than grammatically remote. If she calls, I will answer. counterfactual An imagined alternative contrary to an established fact. If I had brought the key, we could have entered; I left it at home. source-9fcbdb35005527 source-1bb5d453fe6dc8 source-10e4340e83d799

concepts.title: Wishes, regrets, preferences and apparent situations
concepts.definition: Wish and related constructions can express a desired difference from reality, a regret about an earlier event, a preference or an impression; each construction has its own complement pattern.

glossary.definition: Were used with a singular subject in a remote or contrary-to-fact construction.
glossary.example: If I were available, I would help.

glossary.definition: A choice of one situation over another.
glossary.example: I would rather walk than wait.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d18-m02 Wishes, regrets, preferences and apparent situations I J K gv5-topic-d18-c04 gv5-topic-d18-c05 Wish and related constructions can express a desired difference from reality, a regret about an earlier event, a preference or an impression; each construction has its own complement pattern. A present regret commonly uses wish plus a past form: I wish I knew the address means that I do not know it now. A past regret normally uses past perfect: I wish I had checked the address means that I did not check it, and now regret that omission. If only can express the same kind of wish with greater emphasis: If only we had checked. These forms locate an imagined difference from reality; past form after wish does not automatically locate the desired situation in past time. For an open desired future outcome, hope is normally appropriate: I hope the parcel arrives tomorrow. Wish has other patterns. I wish to speak to the manager is a formal expression of wanting; I wish you success expresses a good wish with two objects. Wish plus would often concerns a desired change in behaviour or circumstances: I wish the neighbours would lower the volume. It is not an unrestricted replacement for any state after wish. Would rather takes a base form with the same understood subject: I would rather wait. With a different subject, a past clause is common for a present or future preference: I would rather you waited outside. A past-perfect clause can express an earlier preference: I would rather you had told me yesterday. It is time to leave is an ordinary infinitival expression. It is time we left also refers to the present or near future, despite the past form; it can imply that the action is overdue. As if and as though introduce an apparent or imagined comparison. He looks as if he is tired leaves tiredness plausible; He behaves as if he owned the office presents a distancing comparison. The construction does not always assert that its situation is false. Perfect reference is possible: She looks as if she has been running. Reduced forms also occur: She raised a hand as if to object. Irrealis were is available with be in remote comparisons and wishes, especially in formal prose: I wish I were there; she spoke as though she were the owner. Was is also established in many less formal standard contexts with first- or third-person singular subjects, so it should not be labelled universally ungrammatical. The deliberate choice of were can make the remote interpretation explicit. Subject identity matters in would-rather constructions; changing I would rather leave to I would rather you left changes whose action is preferred. Interpretation should therefore track the holder of the preference, the intended actor and the time of the preferred event separately. wish + past form Typically a desired difference in a present situation. wish + past perfect Typically regret about an earlier situation. would rather + base / would rather + subject + past clause Same-subject and different-subject preference patterns. I wish I knew how to repair this lock. Knew expresses a current desired difference from not knowing. I would rather you had spoken to me before sending it. The speaker prefers a different earlier action by another person. The cyclist looks as though she has been riding in the rain. The comparison is consistent with an actual recent activity; it need not be false. I hope she arrives tomorrow. I wish she were here now. Both grammatical; hope concerns an open desired outcome, while wish presents a desired difference from the current situation. Wish to means formally want to, not regret: We wish to renew the lease. As if can take a non-finite clause or a prepositional phrase: as if to protest; as though in pain. I would rather to wait here. I would rather wait here. Same-subject would rather selects a base form without to. I wish I have checked it yesterday. [regret] I wish I had checked it yesterday. Past regret requires an appropriate earlier perfect form in this construction. irrealis were Were used with a singular subject in a remote or contrary-to-fact construction. If I were available, I would help. preference A choice of one situation over another. I would rather walk than wait. source-e74cc44a499c12 source-bfa29371339537 source-04540f9554f61f source-bee4db2d8bf977 source-9fcbdb35005527

concepts.title: Formal conditional inversion and conditional links
concepts.definition: Conditional inversion places should, had or irrealis were before the subject in specified formal conditional patterns, normally replacing an if-clause without requiring a question meaning.

glossary.definition: A formal condition with auxiliary before subject and usually no if.
glossary.example: Had I seen it, I would have replied.

glossary.definition: A requirement without which a stated result cannot apply.
glossary.example: Entry is permitted only if a pass is shown.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d18-m03 Formal conditional inversion and conditional links I J K gv5-topic-d18-c06 Conditional inversion places should, had or irrealis were before the subject in specified formal conditional patterns, normally replacing an if-clause without requiring a question meaning. The common starting point is an if-clause: If you should need assistance, contact reception. In formal wording, omit if and place should before the subject: Should you need assistance, contact reception. This is a conditional statement with an imperative result, not an enquiry about whether assistance is needed. The form often presents a possible contingency politely or impersonally. It can be useful in notices and correspondence, but ordinary if is equally grammatical and often simpler. Inversion is therefore a resource for a particular register, not a compulsory sign of advanced writing. For an alternative past, Had I known the date, I would have attended corresponds to If I had known the date. Had is the auxiliary of the past perfect, and known remains a participle. For a remote present state, Were I free, I would join you corresponds to If I were free. Were followed by a subject and to-infinitive can present a remote future contingency: Were the supplier to withdraw, we would seek another. These patterns are limited: an ordinary lexical past verb cannot usually be moved in the same way. Wrote she earlier is not the normal conditional equivalent of If she wrote earlier. Negative conditional inversion usually places not after the subject: Had we not checked the figures, the error would have survived. Contractions such as Hadn’t we checked can have other, interrogative uses and should not be substituted mechanically in formal conditional prose. Keep the result clause's modal and time reference unchanged when converting: Had she called, we might have helped retains possibility rather than certainty. A transformation from might have helped to would have helped strengthens the claim. The grammatical operation changes word order and removes if; it does not license extra factual commitments. Other conditional links have their own meanings. Unless commonly means except if: We will proceed unless the regulator objects sets an exception to proceeding. Only if states a necessary condition: We will proceed only if approval is granted does not itself promise that approval guarantees proceeding. Provided that, on condition that and as long as establish conditions or limits with register differences. In case often motivates a precaution rather than stating the condition under which an action will occur: Take a copy in case the network fails instructs taking it beforehand. Replacing all these links with if can alter the logical relationship. Analyse the condition's role before attempting an equivalent inversion or paraphrase. should + subject + base form Formal possible contingency, replacing if + subject + should. had + subject + past participle Formal earlier hypothetical condition. were + subject + complement / to-infinitive Formal remote state or future contingency. Should the lights fail, use the marked exit. Should introduces a contingency; use supplies an imperative result. Had the clerk not kept a copy, we might have lost the record. Negation follows the subject, and might preserves a possible result. Were the lease to expire next month, the company would need alternative premises. Were to presents a remote future supposition. If you should require a receipt, ask at the desk. Should you require a receipt, ask at the desk. Both grammatical and close in meaning; the inverted version has a more formal register. Inversion applies to the licensed auxiliaries, not to every conditional verb. Retaining if as well as the inverted pattern is not the intended conversion: use If I had known or Had I known. If had I known, I would have replied. Had I known, I would have replied. Remove if when forming this conditional inversion. Had she knew, she would have objected. Had she known, she would have objected. Had selects the participle known, not past simple knew. conditional inversion A formal condition with auxiliary before subject and usually no if. Had I seen it, I would have replied. necessary condition A requirement without which a stated result cannot apply. Entry is permitted only if a pass is shown. source-1bb5d453fe6dc8 source-9fcbdb35005527

concepts.title: Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis
concepts.definition: Grammatical mood concerns conventional verb forms and clause patterns associated with statements, directives or non-actual situations; it is distinct from a speaker’s emotion and from the communicative function of a sentence.

glossary.definition: Concerning a proposed, required or desired situation.
glossary.example: They demanded that the gate be opened.

glossary.definition: A clause construction typically headed by a plain verb and understood addressee.
glossary.example: Read the notice before entering.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d18-m04 Mood, mandative meaning and cumulative analysis I J K gv5-topic-d18-c07 gv5-topic-d18-c08 gv5-topic-d18-c09 Grammatical mood concerns conventional verb forms and clause patterns associated with statements, directives or non-actual situations; it is distinct from a speaker’s emotion and from the communicative function of a sentence. Traditional teaching distinguishes indicative, imperative and subjunctive constructions. Most ordinary factual statements use indicative forms: The meeting starts at nine. An imperative typically uses a plain verb form with an understood addressee: Start at nine; do not enter. A sentence's grammatical form does not uniquely determine its social purpose. Can you wait? has interrogative form but usually functions as a request. Conversely an imperative can express an invitation or good wish rather than a harsh order: Have a seat; enjoy your visit. Analyse grammatical construction and practical purpose as separate questions. A mandative clause presents something as proposed, demanded or required. Formal examples include The policy requires that every visitor sign in and The adviser recommended that the hearing be postponed. Sign and be are plain forms, often called the mandative subjunctive. They do not acquire third-person -s or an ordinary tense ending in this pattern. British English also widely uses should: The adviser recommended that the hearing should be postponed. The plain form is especially characteristic of American formal usage but also standard in British English. These are established alternatives; changing should be to be is not a necessary correction. The preceding verb does not automatically create mandative meaning. She insisted that she was innocent asserts a proposition; she insisted that the inspector be present demands a situation. Suggest can similarly indicate evidence, as in The marks suggest that the box was moved, rather than recommend an action. Formulaic subjunctives survive in expressions such as Long live the king and Be that as it may. Irrealis were is sometimes included under a broad traditional subjunctive label, while modern grammars may analyse it separately. The terminology varies; the form, meaning and distribution should remain clear. For cumulative analysis, ask five connected questions: what are the clause boundaries; what functions do the clauses perform; which time is intended; how strong is the modal claim; and does the wording fit the register? A conditional can contain an embedded content clause, a relative and a mandative requirement: If the policy that we adopted requires that each visitor sign in, the receptionist should explain the rule. Parsing those units prevents an agreement rule from being applied across an unrelated clause boundary. Use the phase assessment to revisit Days 13–18, and treat uncertain written responses as material for explicit self-review rather than an automatically awarded mastery score. require/recommend + that + subject + plain form A formal mandative subjunctive pattern. require/recommend + that + subject + should + base A standard mandative alternative, particularly familiar in British usage. The contract requires that the tenant pay on the first day. Pay is plain form in a mandative clause, despite singular tenant. The consultant recommended that the data should be checked independently. Should be is a legitimate British mandative construction. The witness insisted that she had seen the vehicle. Insisted introduces an asserted report here, so an indicative perfect clause is appropriate. They suggested that she be invited. They suggested that she should be invited. Both standard mandative alternatives; the second is particularly familiar in British English. A verb such as insist or suggest has more than one meaning and complement pattern. A that-clause after it is not automatically mandative. Modern descriptions may separate irrealis were from the plain-form subjunctive. The rule requires that he signs in. [rewrite using the plain-form mandative] The rule requires that he sign in. The explicit transformation target selects the plain form; this does not declare every indicative mandative reading impossible. They recommended that the gate should is locked. They recommended that the gate should be locked. The auxiliary after should must have base form be. mandative Concerning a proposed, required or desired situation. They demanded that the gate be opened. imperative A clause construction typically headed by a plain verb and understood addressee. Read the notice before entering. source-3e6d246caea47b source-9fcbdb35005527 source-10e4340e83d799 source-63cc2ee69b424a source-7432e196e7a5da

concepts.title: Building the passive verb phrase
concepts.definition: A canonical be-passive uses a form of be plus a lexical past participle and normally presents as subject an element corresponding to an object in a related active clause.

glossary.definition: A grammatical contrast affecting how participants are expressed in a clause.
glossary.example: The clerk signed it / It was signed by the clerk.

glossary.definition: The participant carrying out an action, when the event has such a participant.
glossary.example: In The file was signed by Noor, Noor is the agent.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d19-m01 Building the passive verb phrase D J gv5-topic-d19-c01 A canonical be-passive uses a form of be plus a lexical past participle and normally presents as subject an element corresponding to an object in a related active clause. Compare The technician repairs the scanner with The scanner is repaired by the technician. The scanner is the object in the active and the subject in the passive. Be supplies the finite present form, and repaired is a participle. The subject of a passive is therefore not necessarily the performer of an action. Form a negative or a question through the first auxiliary: The scanner is not repaired here; Is the scanner repaired here? A by-phrase can identify the agent, but it is often omitted when unknown, obvious or unimportant. Preserve tense and aspect through the auxiliary chain. Active is repairing corresponds to passive is being repaired; was repairing corresponds to was being repaired. Has repaired corresponds to has been repaired; had repaired to had been repaired. A modal comes before base be: can be repaired. A modal perfect uses have been: must have been repaired. Future perfect reference can use will have been repaired. To-infinitives can likewise be passive: to be repaired; a perfect passive infinitive is to have been repaired. The lexical participle remains repaired through these changes; the preceding auxiliaries carry the grammatical distinctions. The sequence has been being repaired is grammatically available for a perfect-progressive passive, but it is uncommon and often cumbersome. In ordinary writing, an active clause such as technicians have been repairing it, or a suitably contextual recast, is often easier to process. Avoid calling a difficult but possible combination impossible. Conversely, do not lose duration by replacing has been being repaired for a month with was repaired a month ago: the latter presents a different time relationship. Choose a recast that preserves what is known about continuation or completion. Not every sequence of be plus a participial-looking word has a uniquely verbal passive analysis. The door was closed at six can report the closing event or describe the resulting state, depending on context. A clear agent phrase or an event-focused progressive can support a verbal reading, while a contrast of states can support an adjectival reading. Individual diagnostics have limits because words can belong to more than one construction. In analysis, describe the reading actually licensed by the discourse rather than assigning a label from the surface ending alone. In transformation, check the original verb's complements before selecting a new subject. finite be + past participle A basic passive; be carries tense and agreement. have + been + past participle A perfect passive. modal + be / modal + have been + past participle Simple or perfect passive under a modal. to be / to have been + past participle Passive infinitival patterns. The labels are checked before dispatch. Present passive describes the checking procedure; labels is the grammatical subject. The labels were being checked when the power failed. Past progressive passive presents checking as in progress at the interruption. The labels must have been checked before dispatch. The modal-perfect passive can express a deduction in an evidential context; context determines the modal reading. The clerk has stamped the form. The form has been stamped by the clerk. Both grammatical; the passive preserves the perfect and changes the information placed first. Perfect-progressive passives exist but are uncommon: the bridge has been being inspected. Prefer a clear recast without pretending that the form is universally ungrammatical. Be plus participle can also describe a state. The forms have been wrote. The forms have been written. The lexical verb requires its participle written after passive be. The form is being checked yesterday. [completed yesterday] The form was checked yesterday. Use a past form for the explicitly completed earlier event; preserve an ongoing reading only if the context supplies one. voice A grammatical contrast affecting how participants are expressed in a clause. The clerk signed it / It was signed by the clerk. agent The participant carrying out an action, when the event has such a participant. In The file was signed by Noor, Noor is the agent. source-b35577171ea742 source-445532eb0f5c35 source-6908b83f55a46c

concepts.title: Agents, reporting, get-passives and two-object verbs
concepts.definition: Passive constructions can background an agent, report a claim or promote different objects, while get-passives often present a dynamic event in a more conversational register.

glossary.definition: A passive without an expressed agent phrase.
glossary.example: The notice was removed.

glossary.definition: A passive construction attributing a report, belief or judgement.
glossary.example: The files are believed to be intact.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d19-m02 Agents, reporting, get-passives and two-object verbs D J gv5-topic-d19-c02 gv5-topic-d19-c03 Passive constructions can background an agent, report a claim or promote different objects, while get-passives often present a dynamic event in a more conversational register. An agentless passive is useful when the affected item is the continuing topic: The scanner arrived yesterday. It was installed this morning. Omitting an unknown agent avoids inventing one. It can also obscure responsibility, so the omission should serve the reader's purpose. A known, important agent may belong in a by-phrase: The decision was overturned by the appeal panel. Active and passive versions organise information differently; neither voice is a universal rule for professional writing. Some passive clauses describe states rather than obvious deliberate actions, so agent is not always the best semantic label for every by-phrase. Reporting passives include It is believed that the bridge is safe and The bridge is believed to be safe. The first uses impersonal it and a content clause; the second places bridge first with an infinitival complement. For an event earlier than the reporting belief, use a perfect infinitive where appropriate: The bridge is believed to have opened in 1980. The construction attributes a belief; it does not guarantee the proposition is true. Keep the source if it matters: The bridge is believed by local historians to have opened in 1980 is more informative than an entirely unattributed report. With suitable two-object verbs, either recipient or transferred item can become passive subject: The charity gave the school a printer; The school was given a printer; A printer was given to the school. The alternatives are not unlimited for every verb. Explain takes the pattern explain something to someone in the intended sense; The rule was explained to her follows that pattern, whereas She was explained the rule is not the ordinary standard counterpart. Learn the lexical pattern, not just an abstract two-object formula. Different dialects and particular verbs also differ in their preferred passive alternatives. A get-passive uses get plus a participle: The parcel got damaged. It is especially common in conversation and typically foregrounds an event or the affected participant. It is not confined to bad outcomes: She got promoted reports a desirable event in many contexts. Get does not by itself prove that the subject caused or deserved the outcome. Adding a reflexive, as in He got himself locked out, can suggest responsibility, but context still matters. A state such as The answer is known does not automatically have a natural equivalent with get. Keep meaning and register in view when choosing between be, get and an active clause. it + passive reporting verb + that-clause Reports an attributed proposition with impersonal it. subject + passive reporting verb + to-infinitive Puts a participant in the reported proposition first. recipient + be + participle + transferred item Possible with suitable ditransitive verbs such as give. get + past participle A commonly conversational event-focused passive. The museum was given a complete catalogue. Museum is the recipient promoted from a give construction. The manuscript is thought to have survived the fire. The perfect infinitive places survival before the present attribution of belief. The trainee got promoted after the trial period. Get-passive describes an event; a negative outcome is not required. The school was given a printer. A printer was given to the school. Both grammatical for the same transfer in context; they foreground different participants. Get-passives can report positive events and need not imply fault. Not all verbs allow both double-object/passive alternatives: lexical complementation must be checked. She was explained the rule. The rule was explained to her. The intended explain pattern takes the rule as object and to her as recipient phrase. The bridge is believed to opened in 1980. The bridge is believed to have opened in 1980. Use a perfect infinitive to express the earlier opening under the present reporting verb. agentless passive A passive without an expressed agent phrase. The notice was removed. reporting passive A passive construction attributing a report, belief or judgement. The files are believed to be intact. source-b35577171ea742 source-266c3ac8d0e174 source-a1d750e1351f47 source-6908b83f55a46c

concepts.title: Causatives and their complement patterns
concepts.definition: Causative constructions express arranging, causing or enabling another action, but have, get, make, let and help differ in grammar and in the kind of involvement they commonly convey.

glossary.definition: A construction expressing causing, arranging or enabling an event.
glossary.example: She had the printer serviced.

glossary.definition: An infinitival verb form without to.
glossary.example: In They let us leave, leave is bare.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d19-m03 Causatives and their complement patterns D J gv5-topic-d19-c05 gv5-topic-d19-c06 Causative constructions express arranging, causing or enabling another action, but have, get, make, let and help differ in grammar and in the kind of involvement they commonly convey. Have something done commonly describes arranging for someone else to act: We had the scanner repaired. The object scanner is followed by the participle repaired; the sentence does not say that we personally repaired it. Get something done can describe arranging or achieving a similar result: We got the scanner repaired before Monday. Here get is not simply an interchangeable auxiliary in every context. A causative sentence has its own subject and participant structure, so converting I repaired the scanner into I had the scanner repaired normally changes who performed or arranged the work. Have can also introduce a person and a bare infinitive: I had the technician check the wiring. Get commonly uses a person plus to-infinitive: I got the technician to check the wiring. In a suitable context it can suggest persuasion or successfully arranging cooperation. Make plus a person and a bare infinitive often expresses causing or compelling an action: The delay made us reconsider. Let normally expresses permission: The supervisor let us leave. Help accepts a bare or to-infinitive: She helped me check it; she helped me to check it. These patterns should be learned alongside their typical meanings. Passive make restores to: We were made to wait. In the permission meaning of let, be allowed to is the ordinary passive alternative: We were allowed to leave, rather than mechanically producing were let to leave. Some other uses of let, such as letting property or the fixed expression be let go, behave differently. Do not generalise a restriction on one meaning to every occurrence of a word. Help him to leave and help him leave are both standard; choosing one does not justify marking the other wrong. Register and local preference can affect frequency without changing grammaticality. Have plus object plus participle is not always an arranged service. We had our equipment stolen ordinarily reports an adverse experience, not an instruction to steal it. Context distinguishes that reading from a causative arrangement. Similarly, We had visitors waiting outside uses an -ing complement and can describe an experience or an ongoing state brought about by circumstances. The order of have and an object matters: We had repaired the scanner is past perfect, whereas We had the scanner repaired is the object-plus-participle construction. Analyse the complete verb phrase before inferring agency, time or responsibility. A meaningful transformation must preserve these distinctions rather than merely reproduce a familiar sequence. have/get + affected object + participle Often an arranged service or achieved result; context can supply an adverse-experience reading. have + person + bare infinitive / get + person + to-infinitive Related causative patterns with distinct lexical selection. make/let + person + bare infinitive; help + person + (to-)infinitive Complement patterns depend on the selected verb and meaning. We had the locks changed after the move. The subject arranged the service; the sentence does not identify the worker. The noise made the lecturer pause. Make introduces the person affected and the bare infinitive pause. The assistant helped the visitor to complete the form. To complete is standard after help; complete without to would also be standard. We had repaired the scanner. We had the scanner repaired. Both grammatical; the first is past perfect with us as repairers in the ordinary reading, while the second normally describes an arranged service. Have an object stolen can report an unwanted experience rather than deliberate causation. Help admits infinitives with or without to. Fixed be let go is not evidence for unrestricted passive permission constructions. The supervisor made us to wait. The supervisor made us wait. Active causative make takes a bare infinitive here. We were made wait outside. We were made to wait outside. Passive make uses the to-infinitive in this construction. causative A construction expressing causing, arranging or enabling an event. She had the printer serviced. bare infinitive An infinitival verb form without to. In They let us leave, leave is bare. source-481dd675b53cdd source-1faf37a18b3e37 source-f72ea287b27b1d source-a4b8f505f226f9 source-44d9470b0f7cc1

concepts.title: Passivisation limits, ergative alternation and meaning
concepts.definition: Passivisation depends on a licensed verb-and-complement pattern; an ergative alternation instead uses the same lexical verb transitively for causing a change and intransitively for the change itself.

glossary.definition: A pedagogical label for a transitive causative and related active intransitive change-of-state pair.
glossary.example: The sun melted the snow / The snow melted.

glossary.definition: A passive related to a verb-plus-preposition construction.
glossary.example: That problem has been dealt with.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d19-m04 Passivisation limits, ergative alternation and meaning D J gv5-topic-d19-c04 gv5-topic-d19-c07 gv5-topic-d19-c08 Passivisation depends on a licensed verb-and-complement pattern; an ergative alternation instead uses the same lexical verb transitively for causing a change and intransitively for the change itself. Some active clauses have no object available for the ordinary passive operation: The parcel arrived; the children slept. The parcel was arrived is not the standard passive equivalent of arrived. A subject complement after a linking verb is not a direct object: She became a doctor cannot be mechanically turned into A doctor was become by her. These restrictions follow from the construction, not from whether the event seems important or whether the subject is human. First identify objects and complements, then ask whether the lexical verb supports the intended passive. English also permits some prepositional passives: Someone looked into the complaint can correspond to The complaint was looked into. The preposition remains with the verb, even though the complaint is now subject. The bed has been slept in is another established example. Such constructions show why only verbs with a direct object can ever be passive is too broad. They do not mean that every prepositional phrase can be promoted naturally; lexical restrictions, idiomatic units and the relationship of the affected participant to the event matter. A learner's dictionary and established usage help resolve difficult individual cases. Many change-of-state verbs alternate: Heat cracked the glass; The glass cracked. In the first, heat is a cause and glass an object; in the second, glass is subject in an active intransitive clause. The glass was cracked by the heat is passive and expresses the cause differently. The active intransitive does not identify an external cause and must not be described as passive merely because its subject undergoes a change. Open, break, melt and increase permit comparable patterns in suitable senses, but not all transitive verbs alternate: A thief stole the bag does not license The bag stole with the same meaning. Meaning-preserving transformations require a final interpretation check. The scope of negation, quantifiers and modals can change when information is rearranged: Not every file was checked denies complete checking. Every file was not checked can be scope-ambiguous; use No file was checked for an explicit zero-checking claim. Keep a specific agent when that agent is part of the original informational task, preserve tense and aspect, and avoid changing an unsuccessful attempt into a completed event. Some stative transitive verbs have limited or unusual passives in ordinary senses; an awkward example is not automatically a universal ban on the verb. Distinguish syntactic possibility, normal collocation and discourse usefulness, and explain precisely which restriction an exercise intends to test. cause + transitive change verb + affected object A causative active use, such as heat melted the wax. affected subject + intransitive change verb An active intransitive alternation, such as the wax melted. promoted subject + be + past participle + retained preposition (+ by-agent) A licensed prepositional passive retains the preposition selected by the verb, as in The matter was looked into. The temperature rose overnight. Rise is intransitive here; no ordinary object can become a passive subject. The complaint was looked into by an independent reviewer. A prepositional passive retains into and identifies the reviewer. The window opened when the latch loosened. Opened is active intransitive, even though window undergoes the change. The heat melted the seal. The seal melted. Both grammatical active clauses; the second leaves the cause unexpressed and is not a passive transformation by form alone. Some clauses without a direct object permit prepositional passives. An affected subject does not by itself make a clause passive. Stative verbs require sense-specific and usage-sensitive analysis. The parcel was arrived before noon. The parcel arrived before noon. Arrive does not form the intended be-passive. The complaint was looked by an investigator into. The complaint was looked into by an investigator. Keep the verb-preposition unit in its normal passive order before the agent phrase. ergative alternation A pedagogical label for a transitive causative and related active intransitive change-of-state pair. The sun melted the snow / The snow melted. prepositional passive A passive related to a verb-plus-preposition construction. That problem has been dealt with. source-b35577171ea742 source-5532e2d7078060 source-a70db92421dbc9

concepts.title: Non-finite forms and grammatical functions
concepts.definition: A non-finite verb form lacks the ordinary independent tense/person agreement contrasts of a finite verb. Non-finite clauses may nevertheless express complex time, aspect, voice and participant relationships through their form and larger context.

glossary.definition: A clause built around a non-finite verb, interpreted within a larger linguistic or situational context.
glossary.example: To check every signature would take time.

glossary.definition: A modern umbrella label for verbal -ing forms used in several clause functions.
glossary.example: Checking every signature carefully takes time.
