concepts.searchText: gv5-d20-m01 Non-finite forms and grammatical functions D H J L gv5-topic-d20-c01 gv5-topic-d20-c02 gv5-topic-d20-c03 gv5-topic-d20-c04 A non-finite verb form lacks the ordinary independent tense/person agreement contrasts of a finite verb. Non-finite clauses may nevertheless express complex time, aspect, voice and participant relationships through their form and larger context. Begin with four useful shapes: to write, write after an appropriate selecting expression, writing and written. In The clerk hopes to write, hopes is the finite verb and to write is an infinitival complement. In The clerk may write, may is finite and write is the following plain form. In The clerk is writing, is is finite and writing is a participial form. Written combines with have in a perfect or be in a passive: has written; was written. The spelling alone is not a complete analysis, because many past-tense and participial forms are identical, as in checked. An -ing clause can fill several functions: Reading the instructions carefully takes time has a subject clause; She enjoys reading the instructions has a complement; Reading the instructions carefully, she noticed an exception has an adjunct. Traditional teaching often calls the first two gerunds and the last a participle. Some modern grammars use the combined label gerund-participial for the verbal form. Neither terminology makes every -ing word a verb. In the careful reading of the instructions, reading is a noun with a determiner and adjective; in reading the instructions carefully, the verb takes a direct object and adverb. Build longer forms by applying ordinary auxiliary selection. To have written is a perfect infinitive; to be written is passive; to have been written combines perfect and passive. Having written is a perfect -ing form, and having been written is perfect passive. These forms have no independently inflected tense, but the perfect commonly locates a situation before a contextual reference point. The committee claims to have checked the files attributes the earlier checking as a claim rather than independently guaranteeing its truth. A negative can precede the non-finite phrase: not to sign; not having signed. Present participle and past participle are traditional form names, not automatic time labels. The files being checked tomorrow refers to future checking even though being is an -ing form; the files checked yesterday has past time because the context supplies it. A non-finite clause may contain auxiliaries, an object and other dependants; it is not merely a loose phrase with no internal syntax. Conversely, a plain verb form does not prove non-finiteness in every context: an imperative such as Write clearly is a main-clause construction. Determine the clause type and selecting environment before assigning a form or function label. to + have + been + lexical past participle A perfect passive infinitive; the larger context supplies the reference point. -ing verb + object + adverb A verbal -ing clause can retain ordinary verb complementation and modification. The researcher plans to interview the witnesses. Plans is finite; to interview the witnesses is an infinitival complement. Carefully checking the figures revealed a discrepancy. The whole -ing clause functions as subject; checking takes figures as object and carefully as modifier. The letters are believed to have been destroyed. The perfect passive infinitive presents destruction as earlier than the attributed belief; the belief is reported, not proved. The careful reading of the report took an hour. Reading the report carefully took an hour. Both are grammatical. The first has a noun reading with adjective careful; the second has a verbal -ing clause with object and adverb. Traditional gerund/participle labels and modern gerund-participial terminology analyse the same many verbal forms differently. Identify the observable pattern before arguing about the label. Irregular forms need lexical checking: written is a participle; wrote is a past-tense form. The report appears to have been wrote. The report appears to have been written. The perfect passive chain ends in the lexical past participle written. The clerk enjoys to reading the files. The clerk enjoys reading the files. Enjoy selects an -ing complement in this intended activity sense; do not combine to-infinitival and -ing marking mechanically. non-finite clause A clause built around a non-finite verb, interpreted within a larger linguistic or situational context. To check every signature would take time. gerund-participial A modern umbrella label for verbal -ing forms used in several clause functions. Checking every signature carefully takes time. source-445532eb0f5c35 source-a70db92421dbc9 source-dab92de230863e source-6908b83f55a46c

concepts.title: Verb complementation and differences in meaning
concepts.definition: Verb complementation concerns the patterns licensed by a particular verb and its sense. An -ing complement and an infinitival complement may be restricted alternatives or may express different meanings.

glossary.definition: The syntactic frame licensed by a particular word and its sense.
glossary.example: Persuade someone to wait requires an object followed by an infinitive.

glossary.definition: An infinitive without infinitival to, licensed in specified constructions.
glossary.example: We heard the bell ring.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d20-m02 Verb complementation and differences in meaning D H J L gv5-topic-d20-c05 Verb complementation concerns the patterns licensed by a particular verb and its sense. An -ing complement and an infinitival complement may be restricted alternatives or may express different meanings. Learn a verb together with a complete pattern: avoid handling fragile objects; hope to finish; ask someone to wait. Avoid normally takes an -ing activity complement; hope normally takes a to-infinitive in this use. An object may belong to the pattern: The supervisor persuaded the clerk to wait. Leaving out or inserting a preposition by analogy can change or break the selected construction. To is not always infinitival: in look forward to meeting, to is a preposition followed by an -ing clause, whereas in hope to meet it marks an infinitive. Several verbs allow both forms with an important ordinary contrast. Remember to lock the cabinet concerns remembering a task before performing it; remember locking the cabinet concerns a memory of the locking. Stop to read the notice means pause another activity in order to read; stop reading means cease the reading activity. Try to restart the computer describes an effort; try restarting the computer proposes restarting as a method to see whether it helps. Neither try-pattern alone guarantees success. Go on checking continues checking; go on to check introduces a subsequent activity in an appropriate sequence. Perception verbs can license an object plus a bare infinitive or an -ing form: I saw the boat cross the channel; I saw the boat crossing the channel. The first often presents the event as a whole; the second presents a stage in progress. This contrast should not be exaggerated into a rule that the second event definitely failed to finish. Active causative make and let also normally take a bare infinitive: made us wait; let us leave. Passive made normally introduces to: we were made to wait. Help permits both help us carry and help us to carry. These are selected constructions, not exceptions to be erased by a single formula. Other pairs differ mainly in viewpoint or context: like swimming and like to swim can both be standard, and preferences vary with meaning and variety. Some patterns allow an explicit non-finite subject, while others require interpretation through the surrounding clause. A dictionary entry helps establish the complement frame; it does not remove the need to read the intended sense. When transforming a sentence, preserve participant roles, aspect and whether an event actually happened. Do not turn remembered to send into remembered sending merely because both phrases contain the same lexical verb: the memory relationship and the assumed event sequence have changed. avoid + -ing; hope + to-infinitive Selected complement patterns for these ordinary senses. stop + -ing / stop + to-infinitive Ceasing the activity contrasts with pausing for a purpose. We avoided disturbing the residents. The -ing clause is the selected activity complement of avoided. Mina stopped to compare the two maps. The infinitive expresses the purpose of pausing another activity. The mechanic saw the belt slipping but did not see it break. The -ing form presents an unfolding stage; the bare infinitive presents the breaking event as a whole in the negative perception report. Rafi remembered to post the invitation. Rafi remembered posting the invitation. Both are grammatical. The first concerns remembering a task; the second concerns recalling the posting event. Do not treat every pair as sharply different in the same way. Like reading and like to read overlap, while stop reading and stop to read usually have a substantial structural and meaning contrast. Help permits an infinitive with or without to. We look forward to meet the new colleagues. We look forward to meeting the new colleagues. To belongs to the prepositional pattern look forward to; the following activity clause uses -ing. The interruption made us to start again. The interruption made us start again. Active causative make normally selects a bare infinitive; passive were made to start has a different pattern. complementation pattern The syntactic frame licensed by a particular word and its sense. Persuade someone to wait requires an object followed by an infinitive. bare infinitive An infinitive without infinitival to, licensed in specified constructions. We heard the bell ring. source-ccfbea5f751a50 source-dab92de230863e source-a4b8f505f226f9 source-1faf37a18b3e37 source-f72ea287b27b1d

concepts.title: Purpose, participial clauses and meaning-preserving reduction
concepts.definition: A non-finite adjunct adds information such as purpose, time, reason or circumstance. Participial and infinitival clauses can make writing economical, provided their interpreted subject and their relationship to the main clause remain clear.

glossary.definition: An adjunct whose intended participant is not clearly or appropriately supplied by the surrounding construction.
glossary.example: Having read the draft, the mistake was obvious leaves the reader unclear.

glossary.definition: A supplementary clause with its own expressed subject.
glossary.example: The doors secured, the guards began their patrol.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d20-m03 Purpose, participial clauses and meaning-preserving reduction D H J L gv5-topic-d20-c06 gv5-topic-d20-c07 A non-finite adjunct adds information such as purpose, time, reason or circumstance. Participial and infinitival clauses can make writing economical, provided their interpreted subject and their relationship to the main clause remain clear. An infinitive can express purpose: The librarian moved the lamp to illuminate the desk. The purpose is not simply a second completed event; it explains the intended reason for moving the lamp. In order to can make that relation explicit. An -ing adjunct often shares the main subject: Checking the inventory, the librarian found a missing volume. The librarian is understood as the checker. A past-participial adjunct often gives a passive interpretation: Warned about the leak, the librarian moved the books. The librarian receives the warning rather than issuing it. Perfect participial clauses can make earlier completion explicit: Having checked the inventory, the librarian locked the store. A passive perfect is also possible: Having been warned about the leak, she moved the books. The grammatical form helps organise time and voice, but the exact logical link often comes from context. Warned about the leak may express background, reason or a concessive relation in a suitable sentence; do not translate every participial clause automatically as because. A reduced relative also needs its own interpretation: the letters written yesterday has a passive relation between letters and write, while the researcher writing today presents the researcher as the writer. A dangling adjunct arises when the understood participant is missing or misleadingly attached under the intended reading: Having inspected the roof, the leak was obvious does not clearly express who inspected it. If Samir inspected the roof, write After Samir inspected the roof, the leak was obvious to him. Replacing the main clause with Samir found the leak obvious is another valid repair. A passive main clause is not automatically incompatible with an opening participle: Warned about the leak, the tenants were evacuated is coherent because the tenants received the warning. State the intended actor before diagnosing an error. Not every opening non-finite expression shares the main subject. Absolute constructions have their own subject, as in The checks completed, the team left. Comment expressions such as strictly speaking relate to the speaker’s assessment rather than an ordinary main-clause agent. Purpose clauses can also have implicit agents recoverable in context, especially with passive main clauses; clarity, not an unconditional ban, guides editing. Reduction may remove tense, modality or emphasis: the forms that must be checked cannot simply become the forms checked without losing necessity. A sound transformation therefore compares what each version actually commits the writer to, including the role of every participant and every qualification. having + past participle, main clause A perfect -ing adjunct can make prior completion explicit. noun + past-participial modifier Often a reduced passive relative, subject to lexical meaning and context. The clerk opened the window to cool the room. The infinitive states an intended purpose; it does not guarantee that the room cooled. Having compared both estimates, Samir requested a third. Samir is understood as the person who compared the estimates. The folders damaged in the flood were photographed before disposal. Damaged in the flood modifies folders with a passive interpretation; it does not make folders the agents of damage. Warned about the closure, the visitors changed their route. Having warned the visitors about the closure, the guide changed the route. Both are grammatical. The first has a passive interpretation for the visitors; the second makes the guide the warning agent. An absolute such as Weather permitting, we will inspect the site has an explicit subject inside the opening clause. A comment expression such as frankly speaking is not evaluated by blindly assigning its speaking to the next noun. Having checked the lock, the key was returned to Amina; Amina performed the checking. After Amina checked the lock, the key was returned to her. An explicit finite subject repairs the intended actor relation without claiming that the key checked the lock. The documents that must be signed tomorrow are ready. Proposed equivalent: The documents signed tomorrow are ready. The documents that must be signed tomorrow are ready. The proposed reduction drops the original obligation. Retain the finite relative, or use a carefully qualified alternative that preserves must. dangling adjunct An adjunct whose intended participant is not clearly or appropriately supplied by the surrounding construction. Having read the draft, the mistake was obvious leaves the reader unclear. absolute construction A supplementary clause with its own expressed subject. The doors secured, the guards began their patrol. source-473784fba0527d source-a70db92421dbc9 source-6908b83f55a46c source-dab92de230863e source-b760c623998f7d

concepts.title: Control, raising and the interpretation of non-finite subjects
concepts.definition: Interpreting a non-finite clause often requires identifying its expressed or understood subject. Control and raising are analytical labels for important differences between constructions; their formal treatment varies between grammatical theories.

glossary.definition: A dependency in which a participant or the context supplies the interpretation of a non-finite clause’s unexpressed subject.
glossary.example: Rafi tried to wait makes Rafi the intended waiter.

glossary.definition: An analytical label for constructions such as seem, where the visible subject is interpreted with the lower predicate without an additional participant role from the raising predicate.
glossary.example: The parcel seems to have arrived.

glossary.definition: A notation for an unpronounced subject in a traditional generative analysis of control.
glossary.example: An analysis may represent Rafi tried [PRO to wait].

concepts.searchText: gv5-d20-m04 Control, raising and the interpretation of non-finite subjects D H J L gv5-topic-d20-c08 gv5-topic-d20-c09 Interpreting a non-finite clause often requires identifying its expressed or understood subject. Control and raising are analytical labels for important differences between constructions; their formal treatment varies between grammatical theories. Ask who is understood to perform the action. In Amina tried to unlock the cabinet, Amina is the person trying and the intended unlocker. In Amina persuaded Omar to unlock the cabinet, Omar is the intended unlocker, while Amina is the persuader. These are ordinary subject-control and object-control examples in traditional terminology. The first noun in the sentence does not control every following infinitive, and the nearest noun is not a universal answer either. Learn the selecting verb’s pattern and read the whole context before interpreting the missing participant. Some infinitives express their own subject: It would be useful for Omar to attend identifies Omar as the attendee. Others allow a general or contextual subject: To leave now would be unwise may concern us, another salient group, or people in general, depending on context. With a control verb, participant roles can remain stable under a main-clause passive: Amina persuaded Omar to attend; Omar was persuaded by Amina to attend. Omar is still understood as the attendee. The surface object/subject position changes, so a role-based explanation is more reliable than an instruction to select whichever noun appears immediately before to. Raising constructions behave differently. In The parcel seems to have arrived, the parcel is the understood subject of arrive, but seem does not describe an action performed by the parcel. Compare It seems that the parcel has arrived. Dummy there supplies a useful diagnostic: There seems to be a problem is grammatical even though there names no person who seems. A normal agentive control construction such as try does not simply accept dummy there in that way. The contrast concerns the intended dummy interpretation, not every possible use of the word there, which can also be an ordinary place expression. In one established generative account, control involves an unpronounced subject conventionally written PRO, whose interpretation is supplied by a controller or context. Raising instead relates the visible subject to a position associated with the lower predicate; seem does not assign it the additional participant role that try assigns its subject. These are theoretical analyses, not observable extra words to insert into finished prose, and other frameworks describe the dependency differently. Diagnostics should be used together with meaning and lexical selection, not as one automatic test for every adjective or verb. A further pattern illustrates the limits of a simple subject rule: in The report is easy to read, report is understood as the object of read, whereas in Amina is eager to read, Amina is the understood reader. Such differences make careful syntactic analysis useful, but a beginner can begin by asking who does what and which complement pattern is licensed. subject + try + to-infinitive A standard subject-control example: the subject is also the intended performer in the complement. There + seem + to be + noun phrase An established raising pattern with dummy there. Nora tried to repair the hinge. Nora is both the person trying and the intended repairer. Nora persuaded Imran to repair the hinge. Imran is understood as the repairer; Nora is the persuader. There seem to be several errors in the total. Dummy there has no semantic agent role; the plural associate supports seem in this careful formal version. The courier tried to arrive early. The courier seems to have arrived early. Both are grammatical. Try attributes an effort to the courier; seem presents an appearance or inference about the arrival without attributing an act of seeming to the courier. The subject of an infinitive can be explicit after for, contextually understood, controlled by a main-clause participant, or involved in another dependency. Do not teach that every infinitive has the subject of its nearest finite clause. Amina persuaded Omar to leave. Analysis: Amina must be the leaver because she is the sentence’s subject. Amina persuaded Omar to leave. In the ordinary intended reading, Omar is the leaver. Persuade licenses object/goal control; the matrix subject is the persuader. There seems to be a delay. Correction proposed: A person must replace there because every infinitive needs a human subject. No correction is needed: There seems to be a delay. The established dummy-there raising construction does not require a human agent. control A dependency in which a participant or the context supplies the interpretation of a non-finite clause’s unexpressed subject. Rafi tried to wait makes Rafi the intended waiter. raising An analytical label for constructions such as seem, where the visible subject is interpreted with the lower predicate without an additional participant role from the raising predicate. The parcel seems to have arrived. PRO A notation for an unpronounced subject in a traditional generative analysis of control. An analysis may represent Rafi tried [PRO to wait]. source-b61da788662118 source-a1d750e1351f47 source-a70db92421dbc9

concepts.title: Quoting, reporting and choosing a perspective
concepts.definition: Direct speech presents words as a quotation; indirect speech reports their content from the current speaker’s perspective. A report can preserve a message without reproducing its wording.

glossary.definition: A clause identifying a communication or thought.
glossary.example: The guide explained ...

glossary.definition: Reference tied to a speaking context, such as I, here and now.
glossary.example: She said she would stay here.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d21-m01 Quoting, reporting and choosing a perspective D I N gv5-topic-d21-c01 gv5-topic-d21-c03 gv5-topic-d21-c04 Direct speech presents words as a quotation; indirect speech reports their content from the current speaker’s perspective. A report can preserve a message without reproducing its wording. Begin with who said what to whom. In a direct quotation, the pronouns and expressions such as here and tomorrow belong to the original speaking situation: Mina said, “I will return tomorrow.” In an indirect report, the reporter constructs a new clause: Mina said that she would return the following day. That introduces the reported statement and can often be omitted after common verbs. Quotation marks are needed for a claim to reproduce words exactly; they are not needed merely because a sentence mentions someone’s ideas. Change reference by identifying actual people, places and times, rather than by applying a substitution list blindly. If I report my own promise, I remains I. If the report occurs in the same room on the same day, here and today may remain appropriate. A reporting verb can be present when a statement is current: The notice says that applications close on Friday. Past reporting locates the act of speaking before now. The reported clause then locates its own event relative to that act and the reporter’s present. Thought reporting follows comparable patterns: Rafi thought that the entrance was locked. It need not describe spoken words. Reporters must distinguish a source’s claim from their own endorsement. The manager claimed that the stock was safe does not establish that it was safe. Words such as admitted, alleged and confirmed introduce evidential and evaluative meanings beyond said. A faithful transformation therefore preserves uncertainty and attribution, not just tense forms. Do not turn “I may resign” into a statement that the person definitely resigned or promised to resign. Direct and indirect are constructions, not degrees of factual accuracy. An exact quotation can be misleading if its context is removed; a carefully attributed paraphrase can be accurate. Traditional transformation exercises often supply a single decontextualised reporting time. Real discourse permits several perspectives, so a defensible answer states its assumed reporting situation. Free indirect discourse blends a narrator’s voice with a character’s viewpoint without a reporting clause; it is useful to recognise in literary prose, but ordinary formal reports should make attribution clear whenever readers might otherwise confuse the source with the writer. X said (that) + finite clause Reports a proposition; reference is interpreted from the reporting context. Nida said, “I need this key.” I and this are anchored to Nida’s original situation. Nida said that she needed that key. The report changes person and points back to the identified key. I said that I would remain here until Friday. Self-report preserves I; here is valid if the reporter is still in the relevant place. The witness said, “I saw a van.” The witness said that she had seen a van. Both report a message; only the first claims to quote those words. If the reporter and original speaker are the same person, a first-person pronoun need not change: I said I was ready. Ali said me that he was ready. Ali told me that he was ready. Tell takes a recipient object here; said to me is another valid pattern. The notice says that applications closed tomorrow. The notice says that applications close tomorrow. For a current notice announcing a future deadline, close gives scheduled future reference. reporting clause A clause identifying a communication or thought. The guide explained ... deixis Reference tied to a speaking context, such as I, here and now. She said she would stay here. source-89176b529bbc02 source-93f2b5c2495752

concepts.title: Backshift and temporal relationships
concepts.definition: Backshift is the use of a more remote tense form in a reported clause, commonly after past reporting. It does not necessarily mean that the reported situation has ceased to be true.

glossary.definition: A shift to a more remote tense form in reporting.
glossary.example: am ready → was ready

glossary.definition: A future viewed from an earlier reference point.
glossary.example: She said she would telephone.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d21-m02 Backshift and temporal relationships D I N gv5-topic-d21-c02 gv5-topic-d21-c08 Backshift is the use of a more remote tense form in a reported clause, commonly after past reporting. It does not necessarily mean that the reported situation has ceased to be true. A common reporting sequence moves present to past: “I am tired” becomes She said she was tired. A present perfect can become a past perfect, and will can become would. These changes allow the report to be viewed from the earlier speaking time. The past form in She said she lived nearby can describe residence simultaneous with her speaking, not residence before it. Keep separate the time of the report, the time of the original statement and the time of the event described. Backshift is often optional when information remains true or relevant: He said that his sister works in a laboratory is normal if her work continues. He said that his sister worked in a laboratory can be equally appropriate and does not itself prove that she has left. A clear past sequence can also be reported without changing every past simple to past perfect. In a conventional transformation exercise, use the specified reporting viewpoint; in actual writing, choose the form that accurately communicates the intended relationships. Backshift is more strongly motivated when a current-tense report would suggest a present truth that the writer does not intend. On Monday she said that the bridge was closed; it reopened on Tuesday. Describing that Monday message as she said the bridge is closed in a Wednesday report would be misleading without a special quotation-like perspective. Past perfect normally remains past perfect. Could, should, would, might and ought to often remain unchanged, while must may remain or become had to depending on whether it expresses continuing necessity, an earlier obligation or a deduction. The term sequence of tenses describes relationships, not a mechanical rule requiring all verbs in a sentence to share tense. A past reporting verb can combine with a present generalisation, a past event and a future-in-the-past prediction in one grammatical report. Modal past forms may express politeness or hypothesis rather than earlier time. In expert analysis, distinguish absolute time reference to the reporter’s now from relative time reference to an earlier viewpoint. If two answers differ only in a legitimate viewpoint, explain the difference rather than treating one as a grammatical failure. said + past clause Often simultaneous with the original speaking time. said + had + past participle Often places an event before an earlier speaking viewpoint. In April, she said that she was applying for funding. The application was current at the April speaking time. He said that water expands when it freezes. The present reports an enduring generalisation. The pilot said that the aircraft had landed before dawn. The landing precedes the past report. She said she is unwell. She said she was unwell. Both can be valid; the first highlights continuing relevance, the second adopts the earlier viewpoint. The past perfect is not shifted into an invented earlier tense: She said she had already paid remains possible. She said that she had had had enough. She said that she had had enough. Past perfect had had is possible; an additional had has no grammatical role. Reporting Wednesday, after reopening: On Monday he said the bridge is closed. On Monday he said the bridge was closed. The supplied context calls for the earlier closure, not a current closure. backshift A shift to a more remote tense form in reporting. am ready → was ready future-in-the-past A future viewed from an earlier reference point. She said she would telephone. source-89176b529bbc02

concepts.title: Reported questions and embedded interrogatives
concepts.definition: An embedded interrogative is a question-like clause functioning inside a larger construction. Its word order normally differs from that of an independent question.

glossary.definition: An interrogative clause inside a larger construction.
glossary.example: I know where she works.

glossary.definition: A question whose question word functions as subject.
glossary.example: Who called?

concepts.searchText: gv5-d21-m03 Reported questions and embedded interrogatives D I N gv5-topic-d21-c05 An embedded interrogative is a question-like clause functioning inside a larger construction. Its word order normally differs from that of an independent question. Compare Where is the archive? with She asked where the archive was. The reporting clause supplies the act of asking; the embedded clause uses the order where + subject + verb. For yes–no questions, use whether or if: He asked whether the office was open. These words introduce alternatives rather than an asserted fact. Do not add that before whether or a question word in this pattern. Punctuation belongs to the whole sentence: She asked where it was. ends with a full stop. The whole sentence can itself be a direct question: Do you know where the archive is? takes a question mark because Do you know ...? is interrogative. Inside it, the archive is retains embedded order. Subject questions need special care: Who signed the register? becomes She asked who signed the register. Here who is the subject, so there is no separate subject to move in front of signed. Do-support disappears in ordinary embedded questions: Why did they leave? becomes He asked why they had left or why they left. If and whether overlap but are not interchangeable everywhere. Use whether before a to-infinitive (whether to apply), after a preposition (about whether it is safe), and immediately before or not (whether or not we agree). If is common for indirect yes–no questions, though it can be confused with a condition in some contexts. Ask may take a recipient (She asked me where I lived), but wonder normally does not: She wondered where I lived. A request shaped as a question may need reporting by communicative purpose rather than literal interrogative form. Embedded questions need not report an earlier spoken question. The issue is whether the evidence is sufficient and I know how the device works contain interrogative content without a speech event. An exclamative such as how quickly they responded has a different meaning from the question how quickly did they respond? Some varieties and informal echoes permit patterns resembling direct-question order inside a report; this course’s formal edited default uses ordinary embedded order. Quoted questions remain direct speech and retain their own order: She asked, “Where is the archive?” Distinguish that quotation from an unquoted embedded clause. asked + wh-word + subject + verb Reports a wh-question without question inversion. asked + whether/if + clause Reports a yes–no question. The clerk asked whether I had an appointment. Whether introduces the yes–no alternatives. Do you remember where we stored the backups? The outer question requires ?, while the embedded clause uses we stored. She asked who had authorised the payment. Who is the embedded subject; the sequence is already correct. He asked where was the exit. He asked where the exit was. The first is faulty in the course’s formal embedded-question pattern; the second retains subject–verb order. A subject wh-question may look unchanged when embedded: Who arrived? → She asked who arrived. I wondered that whether the gate was locked. I wondered whether the gate was locked. Whether itself introduces the embedded interrogative. They discussed if to appeal. They discussed whether to appeal. An interrogative to-infinitive takes whether, not if. embedded interrogative An interrogative clause inside a larger construction. I know where she works. subject question A question whose question word functions as subject. Who called? source-89176b529bbc02

concepts.title: Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns
concepts.definition: A reporting verb selects a grammatical complement and contributes its own meaning. Reporting an instruction, promise, suggestion or exclamation requires preserving that communicative meaning.

glossary.definition: A construction selected by a head word.
glossary.example: advise someone to wait

glossary.definition: The part of a message affected by not.
glossary.example: promise not to publish

concepts.searchText: gv5-d21-m04 Commands, requests and reporting-verb patterns D I N gv5-topic-d21-c06 gv5-topic-d21-c07 gv5-topic-d21-c09 A reporting verb selects a grammatical complement and contributes its own meaning. Reporting an instruction, promise, suggestion or exclamation requires preserving that communicative meaning. Commands and many requests can be reported with a recipient and a to-infinitive: “Close the hatch” becomes She told us to close the hatch. Put not before to for a prohibition: She warned us not to touch the cable. Asked us to can report a polite request, while ordered us to makes it stronger. These choices matter: an invitation is not automatically an order. A reported exclamation may use a content clause or an evaluative verb: “What a useful guide!” can become She exclaimed that the guide was very useful. Learn a verb’s complete pattern. Say that ... and say to someone that ... differ from tell someone that ... . Advise someone to apply, promise to return and apologise for arriving late have different complement structures. Suggest allows an -ing clause or a finite content clause: They suggested waiting; they suggested that we wait or should wait. It does not normally take a recipient plus to-infinitive with that meaning: suggested us to wait is not the standard pattern. Deny taking the money and deny that one took it likewise offer different grammatical forms. Reporting verbs can change the message if selected carelessly. Promise implies commitment, admit implies acceptance of an unwelcome fact, and persuade describes successfully influencing someone rather than merely advising them. He advised me to appeal does not entail I appealed. Negation also has a scope: He did not promise to return denies a promise; He promised not to return reports a promise of non-return. A formal transformation must preserve agency, addressee, obligation, uncertainty and time relations, even if a more elaborate sentence sounds impressive. Traditional reported-speech exercises sometimes treat every question as a request for information and every imperative as an order. Actual utterances can have indirect functions: “Could you lower the screen?” is usually a request, while “Have a seat” can be an invitation. Choose the reporting construction from the supplied situation. A reporting passive such as Participants were advised to retain copies can appropriately background the adviser; it does not make an instruction more authoritative by itself. When a verb’s possible complements vary with meaning or register, consult a learner’s dictionary and compare complete original sentences before ruling out an unfamiliar form. tell/ask/advise + person + (not) to-infinitive Reports directives while retaining an addressee. suggest + -ing / that-clause Reports a proposal without the nonstandard suggest-person-to pattern. The technician warned visitors not to unplug the server. Not scopes over unplug; visitors are the understood actors. The committee suggested that the trial should continue. Mandative should is a standard British pattern. He promised not to disclose the names. The commitment concerns non-disclosure, not absence of a promise. She advised me to resign. She persuaded me to resign. Both grammatical; the second normally entails successful influence, so it cannot automatically replace the first. Help can allow a to-infinitive or bare infinitive, but that flexibility must not be transferred to every reporting verb. The officer suggested me to appeal. The officer suggested that I appeal. Suggest takes an appropriate content clause here; advised me to appeal changes the force. She told that the meeting was cancelled. She said that the meeting was cancelled. Tell normally requires an object recipient in this reporting pattern. complement pattern A construction selected by a head word. advise someone to wait scope of negation The part of a message affected by not. promise not to publish source-89176b529bbc02 source-f7c1a80292d10b

concepts.title: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects
concepts.definition: A modifier adds descriptive or limiting information to another expression. A misplaced modifier suggests an unintended attachment; a dangling modifier lacks a suitable understood participant in its grammatical context.

glossary.definition: An expression supplying an understood participant of a non-finite clause.
glossary.example: Shaking, the visitor spoke.

glossary.definition: A supplementary construction with its own subject.
glossary.example: The rain having stopped, we left.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d22-m01 Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects H K Q gv5-topic-d22-c01 A modifier adds descriptive or limiting information to another expression. A misplaced modifier suggests an unintended attachment; a dangling modifier lacks a suitable understood participant in its grammatical context. Start by asking what each description is meant to describe. In a blue folder on the desk, blue describes the folder and on the desk locates it. In an opening participial clause such as Carrying a blue folder, Leena entered, Leena is normally understood as the person carrying the folder. Writing Carrying a blue folder, the door opened instead makes the door the expected carrier. The problem is not that the sentence begins with an -ing form; it is that the grammatical connection does not fit the intended event. Place a modifier close enough to its target that readers can recover the intended relationship. A notice reading We sell bags for children made of recycled fabric invites the absurd reading that children are made of fabric. We sell recycled-fabric bags for children removes that attachment risk. An introductory past-participial clause can correctly attach to a passive subject: Damaged in transit, the equipment was returned. Equipment is both what was damaged and what was returned; a passive main clause is not automatically a dangling construction. A squinting modifier lies between expressions it could modify in either direction: Students who revise regularly improve. Regularly may describe revising or improvement. Rewrite around the intended message rather than move the word mechanically: Students who revise on a regular schedule improve, or Students who revise show regular improvement. Purpose infinitives need semantic care too. To reach the balcony, take the stairs has an understood imperative you; the absence of a printed subject does not make it faulty. To reach the balcony, the staircase is narrow gives no suitable controller of reach. The subject-sharing guideline governs ordinary subjectless adjunct clauses, not every initial expression. An absolute construction supplies its own subject: The inspection complete, the team left. Conventional comments such as generally speaking or to be honest concern the speaker’s stance and need not describe the next noun as an action. Some apparent dangling expressions are established discourse constructions; others create a real unintended assertion. Expert revision identifies the construction before applying a rule. If a person’s identity is unknown, use a finite clause or an impersonal alternative instead of inventing a named agent to repair the sentence. Subjectless participial adjunct, + main subject + predicate The understood participant normally matches the main subject. Noun phrase + participle, + clause An absolute can supply a different explicit subject. Walking beside the canal, Farah noticed the damaged railing. Farah is the walker and the observer. Stored below zero, the samples were stable for a week. The passive main subject also receives the storage action. The access road having flooded, the engineers postponed the visit. The absolute has its own subject, the access road. After examining the map, the route was obvious. After we examined the map, the route was obvious. The finite after-clause supplies the examiner; choose an actor only if the context identifies one. Conventional speaker comments such as Frankly speaking, the proposal is expensive do not require the proposal to speak. Packed in ice, the courier delivered the fish. The courier delivered the fish packed in ice. The intended chilled entity is the fish, not the courier. To pass the interview, punctuality is important. To pass the interview, applicants should arrive punctually. The revised infinitive has an understood actor; use this only where punctual arrival is actually the intended advice. controller An expression supplying an understood participant of a non-finite clause. Shaking, the visitor spoke. absolute construction A supplementary construction with its own subject. The rain having stopped, we left. source-43eb829d65d5b4 source-445532eb0f5c35

concepts.title: Attachment, scope and reference
concepts.definition: Ambiguity occurs when a form supports more than one interpretation. Attachment concerns which expression a modifier belongs to; scope concerns how much of a message an operator such as only or not affects.

glossary.definition: The structural connection between a dependent and its head or clause.
glossary.example: the child with the red bag

glossary.definition: The domain over which a meaning operator applies.
glossary.example: not every file

concepts.searchText: gv5-d22-m02 Attachment, scope and reference H K Q gv5-topic-d22-c02 gv5-topic-d22-c05 Ambiguity occurs when a form supports more than one interpretation. Attachment concerns which expression a modifier belongs to; scope concerns how much of a message an operator such as only or not affects. A grammatical sentence can be ambiguous without containing an error. I photographed the guide with the telescope may mean that I used the telescope or that the guide had it. The prepositional phrase can attach to the photographing event or to the noun guide. To revise, state the intended interpretation: Using the telescope, I photographed the guide; or I photographed the guide who was carrying the telescope. Neither rewrite is the universally correct answer because the original supplies no decision between the two meanings. Scope differences are often created by focusing words. Only Salma reviewed the draft contrasts Salma with other possible reviewers. Salma reviewed only the draft contrasts that document with other possible objects. Salma only reviewed the draft can emphasise that she reviewed it rather than approved it, although spoken stress and context may support other readings. Keep the intended contrast explicit in formal prose. Negation interacts with quantifiers too: Not all the samples failed means at least some did not fail; none of the samples failed says that every sample avoided failure. Pronoun reference requires a recoverable intended person or thing, but not every pronoun needs a single preceding noun. This can refer to an entire event: The lift stopped between floors. This delayed the delivery. That is a legitimate propositional reference. By contrast, When Hina met Sara, she was worried does not establish which woman was worried. Repeat a name or restructure the sentence if the distinction matters. Avoid solving ambiguity by guessing gender, role or a stereotype; preserve uncertainty when the source does not identify the intended referent. Grammatical ambiguity can coexist with pragmatic clarity. Context may make one reading overwhelmingly likely even though the structure permits another. Expert analysis separates a possible parse from a plausible intended meaning and identifies the evidence for each. Bound-variable readings also go beyond simple name replacement: Every researcher filed their own notes can vary the referent of their with each researcher. Do not replace such pronouns with one fixed name without changing meaning. Scope can remain underspecified intentionally, as in diplomatic language, but assessments must either supply enough context for one answer or explicitly reward the analysis of multiple readings. only + focused constituent Sets the constituent against contextually relevant alternatives. not all + plural noun phrase Denies universality; it does not assert none. Only the backup server failed. The focus excludes the other relevant servers from the set that failed. The manager did not approve every claim. This need not mean that the manager approved no claims. Each student labelled their own specimen. Their varies with each student; singular they need not identify one fixed person. The director spoke to the editor after her meeting. After the director’s meeting, the director spoke to the editor. The second explicitly selects one referent; it is appropriate only if that is the intended reading. Bare this is acceptable when its propositional referent is clear; adding a summary noun is a clarity tool, not a universal grammatical requirement. Intended: some passed. None of the applicants failed the test. Not all the applicants failed the test. The original asserts universal success, which is stronger than the supplied meaning. Intended meaning: I used my telescope to watch the visitor. Ambiguous wording: I watched the visitor with a telescope. Using my telescope, I watched the visitor. The revision fixes attachment without attributing a telescope to the visitor. attachment The structural connection between a dependent and its head or clause. the child with the red bag scope The domain over which a meaning operator applies. not every file source-16d109b31fac43 source-2e5cd32b34733d

concepts.title: Parallelism, correlatives and comparisons
concepts.definition: Parallelism presents related elements in comparable grammatical or conceptual forms. It supports clear comparison and coordination, while grammatical coordination ultimately depends on the functions and constructions involved.

glossary.definition: Comparable form or organisation among related expressions.
glossary.example: to read, to draft and to edit

glossary.definition: One of a paired set signalling coordination.
glossary.example: either ... or

concepts.searchText: gv5-d22-m03 Parallelism, correlatives and comparisons H K Q gv5-topic-d22-c03 gv5-topic-d22-c04 Parallelism presents related elements in comparable grammatical or conceptual forms. It supports clear comparison and coordination, while grammatical coordination ultimately depends on the functions and constructions involved. Lists are easier to process when their parts follow a recognisable pattern: The role involves scheduling visits, checking records and answering enquiries. Each -ing clause fills the same complement position after involves. A mixture such as involves scheduling visits, record checks and to answer enquiries becomes awkward because the last infinitive does not fit the pattern. Try each element after the shared opening. If an item cannot combine with that opening, repair the structure rather than merely changing its ending to resemble the neighbouring words. Correlative pairs make structural expectations visible. The course is useful both for teachers and for editors places parallel prepositional phrases after both and and. The course both supports teachers and provides exercises coordinates verb phrases. Not only and but also can coordinate words, phrases or clauses. Fronted not only may require inversion in the clause it introduces, but it does not require every following item to be a full clause. Not only was the route shorter but also safer is a possible shared-copula construction; adding it was is another grammatical version. Parallelism is not a rule that every coordinated unit must have an identical category label. A complement may coordinate expressions with a shared function: She is a capable editor and easy to work with can be understood as two predicative descriptions. Some mixed constructions are fully acceptable; others are confusing or disallowed by a particular head. In comparison, identify what is compared and what has been omitted. The new office is larger than the old one compares offices. The cost of the new office is higher than that of the old one compares costs, with that substituting for cost. Reduced comparison clauses rely on recoverable material: Mei reads more articles than I do clearly compares readers; Mei reads more articles than me may also have that informal standard reading. Mei likes Jo more than I can mean more than I like Jo, whereas Mei likes Jo more than me can mean more than she likes me. Avoid using a case preference to erase a genuine reading. Formal revisions can expand ellipsis to show the intended relationship. At expert level, examine syntactic compatibility, omitted material and logical comparability separately; rhythmic symmetry alone does not prove grammatical or semantic equivalence. both X and Y / either X or Y The paired constituents should fit the same construction and intended relationship. comparative + than-clause Recover omitted material from context, or make it explicit. She plans to inspect the roof and to test the alarm. The two to-infinitives share a complementation role. Not only was the hall warmer but also quieter. The copula is shared with coordinated predicative adjectives. This week’s output exceeded last week’s output. The compared quantities are of the same relevant type. He enjoys reading and to cycle. He enjoys reading and cycling. Enjoy selects the relevant -ing complements; the repair addresses verb pattern as well as symmetry. Different forms can share a predicative function; evaluate the actual construction before declaring mixed categories ungrammatical. She is interested in restoring clocks and to repair radios. She is interested in restoring clocks and repairing radios. The preposition in supports the coordinated -ing complements. For a comparison of fares: The bus fare is lower than the train. The bus fare is lower than the train fare. The intended comparison is between fares, not a fare and a vehicle. parallelism Comparable form or organisation among related expressions. to read, to draft and to edit correlative One of a paired set signalling coordination. either ... or source-42dc4d1cdfd2d8 source-8db1cebfd15ccb source-028b7ffa729def

concepts.title: Predication and meaning-preserving revision
concepts.definition: Predication attributes a property, identity or event to a subject. Faulty predication occurs when the expressed grammatical relationship fails to convey the intended logical relationship.

glossary.definition: Attributing an event, property or identity to a subject.
glossary.example: The route is steep.

glossary.definition: A meaning that necessarily follows if a statement is true.
glossary.example: They left entails that departure occurred.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d22-m04 Predication and meaning-preserving revision H K Q gv5-topic-d22-c06 gv5-topic-d22-c07 gv5-topic-d22-c08 Predication attributes a property, identity or event to a subject. Faulty predication occurs when the expressed grammatical relationship fails to convey the intended logical relationship. A sentence can be structurally well formed yet say something the writer did not intend. The aim of the workshop is improving attendance can be grammatical as an identification of an aim, whereas The cost of the workshop is because transport is expensive mixes a thing being measured with an unexplained causal clause. A clearer version is The workshop is expensive because transport costs are high. First decide what the subject refers to, then decide what the predicate says about it. Do not use logical oddness as an excuse to ban every uncommon subject–complement combination. Faulty comparison often arises when an abbreviated form conceals the wrong relationship. For the intended claim about income, Her salary is higher than her assistant invites comparison with a person rather than that person’s salary. Her salary is higher than her assistant’s makes the relation clear. Some compressed expressions are familiar idioms and need no repair: He earns more than his assistant can be a complete comparative clause with earns understood. The appropriate revision depends on what is syntactically omitted and what readers can reliably reconstruct. Preserving meaning requires checking more than the topic. Did the original express every item or some items, possibility or certainty, a decision or a completed act, cause or sequence? The supervisor decided to close the office does not entail that the office closed. Because the equipment failed, the demonstration stopped asserts causation; The equipment failed and the demonstration stopped may leave the relation open. A grammatical revision that strengthens or changes these relationships is not a faithful correction, even when it sounds clearer. If the intended meaning is unavailable, offer alternatives and label their assumptions. Revision proceeds through diagnosis, interpretation, reconstruction and verification. Identify the smallest relevant structural unit, paraphrase its plausible readings, choose the intended one from evidence, then rebuild. Finally compare both versions for participants, time, polarity, quantification, modality, focus and register. Minimal editing is useful because it reduces unintended changes, but a small change is not automatically the best repair: it may preserve ambiguity or create a new presupposition. Expert editing sometimes needs a full finite clause rather than a compressed modifier. The objective is a defensible expression of the writer’s meaning, not obedience to a mechanical number-of-changes rule. subject + linking verb + predicative complement Attributes or identifies; check that the semantic relation is intended. reconstruct → compare meaning dimensions Verification includes scope, time, modality and participants. The reason for the delay was a missing permit. The complement identifies a cause rather than an unrelated location. The workshop was expensive because transport costs had risen. The because-clause gives the cause of expense. The board decided to suspend the scheme, but suspension had not yet begun. A decision is distinguished from its implementation. They planned to evacuate. They evacuated. Both grammatical, but only the second asserts the action occurred. The reason ... is because occurs in established English; prefer an economical alternative where useful, but do not label every occurrence inherently ungrammatical. Intended: costs are being compared. The repair cost is higher than a replacement device. The repair cost is higher than the cost of a replacement device. The supplied interpretation requires comparing two costs. Original: Some inspections may be delayed. Proposed revision: All inspections will be delayed. Some inspections may be delayed. The proposed rewrite wrongly changes quantification and modal certainty. predication Attributing an event, property or identity to a subject. The route is steep. entailment A meaning that necessarily follows if a statement is true. They left entails that departure occurred. source-42dc4d1cdfd2d8 source-2ce8f4ad32dfe5 source-10e4340e83d799

concepts.title: Negative, concessive and conditional inversion
concepts.definition: Inversion changes ordinary subject–verb order. Subject–auxiliary inversion places an auxiliary before its subject; other marked constructions front a complement or place a lexical verb before a following noun-phrase subject.

glossary.definition: An auxiliary precedes its subject.
glossary.example: Seldom do we agree.

glossary.definition: A fronted expression marks a contrast despite an acknowledged fact.
glossary.example: Young though she is, she leads the team.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d23-m01 Negative, concessive and conditional inversion J K M gv5-topic-d23-c01 gv5-topic-d23-c02 Inversion changes ordinary subject–verb order. Subject–auxiliary inversion places an auxiliary before its subject; other marked constructions front a complement or place a lexical verb before a following noun-phrase subject. Ordinary statements usually place the subject before the finite verb: We had never seen the original map. With a fronted negative or restrictive adjunct, formal English uses inversion: Never had we seen the original map. Move the existing finite auxiliary; if a simple present or past lexical verb has no auxiliary, add do, does or did and use the base verb: Rarely does the museum open at night. The sentence remains a statement. The inverted order does not by itself turn it into a question. Scope determines where inversion occurs. Only after the review did the panel approve the grant inverts the main clause, not the after-clause. Not until the rain stopped did we leave likewise leaves the subordinate order unchanged. A negative or only-containing subject is different: Not a single applicant complained and Only Nida knew the code have ordinary subject–verb order. Hardly ... when and no sooner ... than commonly express rapid succession, often with the past perfect, but the construction does not require past perfect in every context. Conditional inversion offers formal alternatives to some if-clauses: Had I known ... corresponds to If I had known ...; Should you need assistance ... corresponds to If you should need assistance ...; Were the machine to fail ... corresponds to If the machine were to fail ... . Do not simply remove if from any condition or combine both markers. Concessive patterns such as Tired though she was, she continued front the predicative expression; they do not normally invert she was. Child as he was, he understood uses an articleless fronted noun in this marked construction. Locative full inversion is a different pattern from subject–auxiliary inversion after a negative. With a full noun phrase, Here comes the courier or At the far end stood a guard can present a newly mentioned entity. With an ordinary unstressed personal pronoun, the usual order is Here she comes, not Here comes she. The construction depends on the verb, the locative and information structure; not every verb allows the same pattern. In particular, a fronted place expression does not mechanically require inversion. Compare At the far end, she waited, which preserves subject–verb order. Traditional teaching sometimes calls all marked order inversion, but distinguish subject–auxiliary inversion, full verb–subject inversion and concessive complement fronting. Each has different constraints. Conditional should can suggest a tentative possibility; replacing an ordinary if-condition may therefore alter register and nuance even when the broad condition survives. Use these constructions to emphasise a restriction or fit a formal genre, not to decorate every sentence. A direct neutral statement is often clearer in instructions and reports. When transforming, retain negation, temporal relationships and the scope of the limiting expression rather than merely moving the first two words. negative/restrictive adjunct + auxiliary + subject + remainder Marks emphasis within a statement. Had + subject + past participle, ... Formal conditional alternative to an if-past-perfect clause. predicative expression + though/as + subject + verb, ... Marked concessive fronting without ordinary question inversion. Only after the labels were checked did the team seal the crates. Inversion belongs to the main clause; labels were checked retains normal order. Should the printer stop, use the spare terminal. Should introduces a tentative future condition. Exhausted though the volunteers were, they completed the inventory. The adjective is fronted; the volunteers were is not inverted. Only Farah found the key. Only then did Farah find the key. Only modifies the subject in the first and an adjunct in the second, producing different order requirements. A negative subject does not trigger the adjunct-inversion rule: Nobody complained is correct without did. Never I had seen the original. Never had I seen the original. The fronted negative adjunct triggers subject–auxiliary inversion. If had we known, we would have waited. Had we known, we would have waited. Do not retain if when using this conditional inversion. subject–auxiliary inversion An auxiliary precedes its subject. Seldom do we agree. concessive fronting A fronted expression marks a contrast despite an acknowledged fact. Young though she is, she leads the team. source-f36cfc25889ed4 source-52104a3b64e06c source-1bb5d453fe6dc8

concepts.title: Fronting, clefts and organising focus
concepts.definition: Information structure concerns how a sentence packages its message for a particular context. Fronting and cleft constructions can establish a topic, highlight a contrast or place an important constituent in focus.

glossary.definition: The part highlighted against relevant alternatives or as a key contribution.
glossary.example: It was Monday that we met.

glossary.definition: A wh-clause plus be and a focused value.
glossary.example: What she wants is clarity.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d23-m02 Fronting, clefts and organising focus J K M gv5-topic-d23-c03 gv5-topic-d23-c04 gv5-topic-d23-c08 Information structure concerns how a sentence packages its message for a particular context. Fronting and cleft constructions can establish a topic, highlight a contrast or place an important constituent in focus. Compare I can repair this lock with This lock, I can repair. The fronted object remains the thing repaired; its position makes it a useful point of contrast with other locks. Fronting does not automatically require question order. In conversation, a speaker may instead use a detached topic and a resumptive pronoun: That old lock, I can repair it. This left-dislocation is established informal discourse, though formal edited writing often prefers an integrated clause. Different structures should not be treated as one interchangeable formula. An it-cleft divides a message between a focusing clause and a cleft clause: It was Nida who found the error. The construction highlights Nida against relevant alternatives while treating the finding of an error as background. The initial it + be remains singular even with a plural focus: It was the auditors who found the error. In a pseudo-cleft, a wh-clause sets up an open value: What we need is a reliable backup. The following phrase supplies the focused value. These structures are useful when answering or correcting a specific contextual question. Focus is not identical to new information. Known information can be contrastively focused: “Was it the director?” “No, it was the clerk.” Likewise, topic is not simply the first noun in every sentence. A topic identifies what a discourse contribution is about, while a grammatical subject fulfils a syntactic function. In thematic descriptions, theme often refers to a clause’s point of departure and rheme to the remainder, but linguistic frameworks use these terms differently. Explain the actual distribution of familiar information and emphasis rather than assume one universal terminology. Clefts can carry presuppositions and contrast. It was the red cable that failed normally treats a failure as given and identifies its source; The red cable failed can introduce the entire event. Transforming freely between them may change what readers are invited to take for granted. Pseudo-cleft agreement can vary when a plural complement follows, as in What we need is/are stronger checks; avoid forcing such a contested case into a context-free single-key test. Use unambiguous singular models first, and at the expert layer explain that agreement and interpretation interact. Marked structures work best where their focus matches a real communicative need. focused constituent, + subject + verb ... Integrated fronting gives prominence without necessarily requiring inversion. It + be + focus + who/that-clause Identifies or contrasts a focused constituent. What-clause + be + focused value A pseudo-cleft supplies a value for the wh-clause. The first proposal I support; the second I oppose. The first proposal and the second are fronted objects of support and oppose. Each clause keeps I as its subject; the fronting makes their contrast explicit. It was the night shift that detected the leak. The cleft identifies the detector while retaining the leak event as background. What the archive needs is a second scanner. The wh-clause sets up a need and the final noun phrase supplies its value. The clerk corrected the date. It was the date that the clerk corrected. Both report the correction; the cleft focuses the date against alternative things corrected. A fronted object does not ordinarily cause do-inversion: This report I understand is grammatical; This report do I understand is not the normal modern pattern. It were the drivers who reported the fault. It was the drivers who reported the fault. The cleft’s initial subject is singular it; the following clause has plural drivers. What we need a spare key. What we need is a spare key. The pseudo-cleft needs a linking verb connecting the wh-clause and focused value. focus The part highlighted against relevant alternatives or as a key contribution. It was Monday that we met. pseudo-cleft A wh-clause plus be and a focused value. What she wants is clarity. source-897ffbdb4059a3 source-d20d5991870574

concepts.title: Extraposition, existential presentation and end-weight
concepts.definition: Extraposition places a clausal constituent later while a dummy it occupies a grammatical position. Existential there introduces the presence of an entity or situation. Both can shape information flow without referring like ordinary pronouns.

glossary.definition: A grammatical subject without an ordinary referent.
glossary.example: It is raining.

glossary.definition: A tendency to place structurally heavier material late.
glossary.example: We gave them a report with three annexes.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d23-m03 Extraposition, existential presentation and end-weight J K M gv5-topic-d23-c05 gv5-topic-d23-c09 gv5-topic-d23-c10 Extraposition places a clausal constituent later while a dummy it occupies a grammatical position. Existential there introduces the presence of an entity or situation. Both can shape information flow without referring like ordinary pronouns. A long subject clause can be difficult to process at the start: That the shipment arrived before the deadline surprised us. An extraposed version is It surprised us that the shipment arrived before the deadline. The initial it does not refer to the shipment; it supports a construction with the content clause later. Similarly, It is useful to retain receipts is often more natural than To retain receipts is useful. Both are grammatical. The later clause is not an object merely because it appears after other material; analysis must consider the whole construction. Existential there presents existence or availability: There are two spare chairs in the corridor. It differs from locative there meaning in that place: Put the chairs there. In formal edited writing, use are with plural chairs and is with a singular presentational noun phrase. Contracted there’s with a following plural occurs in conversation, but a formal assessment can explicitly ask for the edited agreement convention. Some analyses call existential there the grammatical dummy subject and the following noun phrase the displaced or notional subject; school grammars often call only the latter the real subject. End-weight is the tendency to place structurally long material later; end-focus is a common tendency for important focal material to occur near the end. They interact but are not identical. We sent the committee a report containing the full sequence of maintenance logs puts the heavy report phrase last. Passive voice can maintain a familiar topic while allowing a new agent late in the clause: The mural was restored by a team from the local college. Neither subject length nor passive voice is a grammatical defect. Choose the order according to what the reader already knows and needs to learn. These tendencies are defaults, not bans on long initial clauses or final given material. Legal drafting, literary rhetoric and contrast may justify marked weight. Extraposition is also construction-specific: I find it surprising that nobody called requires anticipatory it in that pattern, while I know that nobody called does not take an inserted dummy object. Existential presentation commonly favours indefinite or newly introduced entities, but definite phrases occur in list-like or reminder contexts: There is still the matter of the deposit. A reliable analysis considers discourse purpose, syntactic licensing and register together before classifying an unusual sentence as erroneous. It + predicate + that/to-clause A dummy it supports a later clausal constituent. There + be + presentational noun phrase Introduces existence, presence or availability. It is essential that the seals remain intact. It is anticipatory rather than a reference to a previously named object. There is one unresolved claim. The clause introduces a remaining issue. I find it reassuring that the alarm has been tested. The find + it + adjective + content-clause pattern licenses anticipatory object it. That nobody objected was surprising. It was surprising that nobody objected. Both grammatical; the second places a heavier content clause later. Existential there can introduce a definite item in a reminder or list context: There is the signed copy you requested. Formal edited agreement: There is two urgent messages. There are two urgent messages. The supplied formal convention uses plural are with messages. I find surprising that the records survived. I find it surprising that the records survived. This anticipatory-object pattern requires it. dummy subject A grammatical subject without an ordinary referent. It is raining. end-weight A tendency to place structurally heavier material late. We gave them a report with three annexes. source-f3cb8cbb1e0c8b source-b04555eae72042 source-d20d5991870574

concepts.title: Emphatic auxiliaries, substitution and ellipsis
concepts.definition: Emphatic do adds positive emphasis to a lexical verb. Substitution replaces recoverable material with an expression such as do so or one; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unexpressed.

glossary.definition: Recoverable material left unexpressed in a licensed construction.
glossary.example: She can help, and I can too.

glossary.definition: A word or expression stands for recoverable material.
glossary.example: The blue one is mine.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d23-m04 Emphatic auxiliaries, substitution and ellipsis J K M gv5-topic-d23-c06 gv5-topic-d23-c07 Emphatic do adds positive emphasis to a lexical verb. Substitution replaces recoverable material with an expression such as do so or one; ellipsis leaves recoverable material unexpressed. A neutral statement can be strengthened with do, does or did: I do understand your concern. The auxiliary carries tense and agreement, while understand is a bare form. Do not write does understands or did understood. If an auxiliary already exists, stress that auxiliary instead: I have checked it; She can help. Emphatic do can also make an invitation warmer or an instruction more insistent: Do come inside. Emphasis changes the speaker’s stance, not necessarily the event described. Substitution and ellipsis avoid repetition when the missing content is clear. The archivist promised to inspect the box and did so before lunch uses did so for inspecting the box. In I could open it, but I would rather not, the omitted complement of not is recoverable. One and ones substitute for count noun phrases: The blue folders are full; use the green ones. Do not substitute one for an uncountable mass reading: If this equipment is faulty, get better equipment or a better item, not automatically a better one. Ellipsis is licensed by a construction and context, not by a general permission to delete any repeated-looking word. In The first draft was accepted; the second, rejected, gapping removes was and retains a contrasting remnant. The remaining material still supports the intended clause relationship. Informal conversational ellipsis such as Seen the new notice? is established but may not fit a formal report. Leaving a relative pronoun unexpressed is possible in some defining object relatives, not in subject relatives merely to shorten them. Make missing material explicit when readers could recover more than one proposition. Auxiliary choice preserves the structure of the understood material. “Has she filed it?” “She has” retains the perfect auxiliary; “Did she file it?” “She did” uses do. Substitution may preserve meaning only approximately if tense, agency or object reference shifts. Interpret do so and do it from context rather than regard them as universally interchangeable with every predicate, especially stative ones. In discourse, efficient ellipsis supports cohesion, while excessive compression can hide comparisons or agency. Expert control therefore includes the ability to expand a reduced construction and verify exactly which words, participants and time relations a reader must reconstruct. do/does/did + base verb Adds positive emphasis while the auxiliary carries tense/agreement. auxiliary + recoverable omitted predicate Retains relevant tense/aspect/modal structure in ellipsis. The replacement did arrive, despite the earlier warning. Did emphasises the positive event; arrive remains bare. The analyst checked the totals, and the editor did so too. Did so substitutes for the recoverable checking action. The first box was sealed; the second, left open. The second clause omits was; the contrast and passive interpretation remain recoverable. She did check the log. She checked the log. Both assert checking; the first contrasts with doubt or denial. With existing perfect have, do not add emphatic do: I have checked it can be emphatic through stress on have. She does understands the issue. She does understand the issue. The finite auxiliary takes agreement; the lexical verb is bare. “Has the parcel arrived?” “It did.” [same perfect viewpoint intended] “Has the parcel arrived?” “It has.” Keep the perfect auxiliary when supplying the corresponding elliptical answer. ellipsis Recoverable material left unexpressed in a licensed construction. She can help, and I can too. substitution A word or expression stands for recoverable material. The blue one is mine. source-028b7ffa729def source-773e3d2df84661 source-8cf60a1688508e

concepts.title: Clause boundaries, commas and semicolons
concepts.definition: Punctuation marks grammatical boundaries and guides interpretation. Some choices repair an incomplete or incorrectly joined structure; others offer legitimate stylistic alternatives. A pause in speech is evidence about rhythm, not a sufficient rule for inserting a comma.

glossary.definition: Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone in a context requiring a stronger boundary.
glossary.example: The alarm rang, we left.

glossary.definition: A relative clause adding a separate comment about an identified referent.
glossary.example: Mina, who lives nearby, helped.

concepts.searchText: gv5-d24-m01 Clause boundaries, commas and semicolons O P gv5-topic-d24-c01 gv5-topic-d24-c06 gv5-topic-d24-c10 Punctuation marks grammatical boundaries and guides interpretation. Some choices repair an incomplete or incorrectly joined structure; others offer legitimate stylistic alternatives. A pause in speech is evidence about rhythm, not a sufficient rule for inserting a comma. A full stop normally closes a complete written statement. A comma can separate list items, enclose supplementary material and set off many introductory elements. It does not normally join two independent clauses by itself in formal edited prose: The printer failed, we used another office is a comma splice. Write two sentences, use a semicolon or add a suitable coordinator. Choose the relationship you mean rather than treating all repairs as interchangeable: because introduces a cause, whereas and merely adds information. A semicolon can link closely related independent clauses: The entrance was locked; the caretaker had gone home. A conjunctive adverb such as however does not become a coordinating conjunction. The entrance was locked; however, the side gate remained open is one defensible pattern. A semicolon can also separate complex list items that already contain commas.
